items.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
paragraphs: UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".
He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".
He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."

items.title: TRNSMT: What's the future for Scotland's largest music festival?
paragraphs: No details have been announced for next year's TRNSMT festival
We're just weeks away from Christmas but for many music fans their thoughts have already turned to next summer's festival season.
Glastonbury announced its line-up this week, tickets are on sale for Reading and Leeds and the headliners for Belladrum have been announced.
But there is silence surrounding the TRNSMT plans for next year. Event promoters DF Concerts has declined to confirm whether it will return in 2027.
No dates, ticket sales or acts have yet been announced for the Glasgow Green festival, which has been running since 2017.

BBC Scotland News has spoken to several music industry professionals who have been involved with the event previously. All said they had yet to hear any details about 2027 - something described as unusual and different to past years.
It follows a 2026 edition where reduced tickets were being offered on discount websites.
The concert promoter is understood to have several dates booked in for Glasgow Green next year, but it is unknown whether these are for a festival or for one-off big shows on the green.
Two large gigs have already been announced for the green space by rock band Fontaines D.C. and the singer Alex Warren.
Both of those gigs have been advertised by DF under branding saying Live At Glasgow Green.
Multiple sources told BBC Scotland News they would not be surprised if several large gigs replace TRNSMT going forward.
DF Concerts previously claimed TRNSMT was worth an estimated £16.6m to Glasgow.
However it has faced criticism in recent years over lack of diversity among headliners - with no women topping the bill in the event's history - and the same acts regularly playing the festival.
BBC Scotland News has spoken to people in a number of roles across the music business, from band management to PRs and people involved with setting up stages.
All said there had been silence regarding any plans for TRNSNT, and none knew of any bands booked for it.
When asked for information about TRNSMT, DF Concerts said there was no information on the event it could share at this time.
A follow-up question that asked if the promoter could confirm if the festival was being planned for next year was given the same response.
TRNSMT sold some tickets at half price for this year's event
Last year the festival's dates for 2026 were announced on 3 November with the line-up revealed three days later.
Richard Ashcroft, Kasabian and Lewis Capaldi topped the bill, with the event held in June this year - a month earlier than usual.
Other acts who played included Wolf Alice, CMAT, the Fratellis and the Snuts.
Discount platform itison later offered tickets for the festival at £49 a night, considerably down from the £82 they were initially offered at - although the reduced tickets did sell out.
Music journalist Craig McConnell, deputy editor with long-running Scottish fanzine is this music?, external and a regular at TRNSMT, said he would not be surprised if the festival does not go ahead.
He believes the likes of Summer Sessions - large outdoor shows at venues like Bellahouston Park - have supplanted TRNSMT.
"Over the past few years it's been clear that big summer gigs such as the Summer Sessions attract a larger and more engaged audience than TRNSMT, regardless of respective capacity," he said.

"Where TRNSMT has appeared to try to appeal to everyone with their line-up and ended up pleasing no-one, Summer Sessions allows for a tightly curated bill of aligned artists with a much more flexible schedule. It would make business sense to make a shift."
Several music festivals in Scotland did not go ahead in 2026, repeating a wider pattern across the UK.
Over the past decade other Scottish events like the Wickerman and Connect - another DF event - have also gone.
Rebecca Wallace, an associate lecturer in popular music at the University of the West of Scotland, believes the cost of living crisis has had an impact on festival attendances.
"We are living in a time of austerity and people, especially young people, are having to make decisions between, say, going to big gigs or the rest of their social life. No-one can pay for anything."

However Wallace, who performs as a musician herself and previously worked at DF Concerts when it was holding TRNSMT's famed predecessor T In The Park, also feels the Glasgow Green event struggled to establish a musical identity for itself.
"The programming of T In The Park was in line with the promoter's tastes, but also in alignment with young people's tastes, and T became this rite of passage for so many young people," she said.
"It was part of this Scottish identity and had this identity of its own, which I don't think TRNSMT ever really grasped. It just did not meet the cultural moment of the time."
Biffy Clyro are among the past headliners of TRNSMT
TRNSMT launched in 2017, a year after the long-running T In The Park ended following a festival that saw the deaths of two teenagers and a host of organisational problems.
Unlike T, TRNSMT was based in a city and did not have camping, with Radiohead and Biffy Clyro among the early headliners.
McConnell told BBC Scotland News that if the festival doesn't go ahead it will be a blow to Scotland's music scene, as smaller stages there - like the BBC Introducing stage - can help emerging acts.
"There is a cultural loss that would come with this," he says.

"For better or worse, TRNSMT is Scotland's festival. Yes, we have Belladrum, Heartlands, Back Doune The Rabbit Hole and more independent festivals, but as the replacement for T in the Park, TRNSMT was the jewel in the crown of Scotland's festival scene.

"More importantly it is something for grass roots bands in Scotland to aspire to play. Local acts who were playing venues like McChuills in Glasgow last week are never going to be offered a slot at Summer Sessions.

"DF may be tight lipped about their plans - and the majority of music fans are hoping they actually have one - but until the public are told what's going on, they have no option but to assume that there are no plans."

items.title: 'Somebody has to stand up to that guy' - and Russell has his chance in Vegas
paragraphs: Max Verstappen (left) and George Russell (right) will start on the front row in the Las Vegas Grand Prix
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".
"That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.
Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.
Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.

Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.
They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".

After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

"He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."
Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.
Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."
When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.
But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."
George Russell and Max Verstappen battling for track position during final practice in Las Vegas

These two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position.
They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."
Verstappen called Russell a "backstabber" and a "loser".
That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".
And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.

Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.
He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour.
Verstappen goes off track after clashing with Russell in Las Vegas
All this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.

This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.

Despite widespread disquiet about going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, everyone has been towing the party line on that one recently in public, that they trust governing body the FIA and Formula 1 to have made the right decision.

After qualifying, though, Verstappen came close to becoming the first to break the omerta, when he told the Dutch media "of course I would rather be at home", before repeating that he trusted the sport's bosses on the matter.
BBC Sport has been told of at least one other major driver who would rather not be going to the Middle East specifically because of concerns about safety.
As for the racing here in Sin City, it is set up beautifully.
The two drivers on the front row, as well as not troubling to hide their distaste for each other, are also the only two to have won here.
Verstappen has won two of the three events on the Strip circuit, sandwiching Russell's victory in 2024.
In theory, that could give an opportunity to McLaren's Lando Norris, who qualified fourth, and starts third as a result of Antonelli's penalty.
But the 2025 world champion was concerned about the McLaren's lack of straight-line speed.

"The pace in the car is not bad," he said. "The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we are not going to be able to overtake someone, so I think it's going to be a tough day."
His team principal Andrea Stella was more optimistic.
McLaren's battle with Red Bull for third in the constructors' championship - the two are separated by just 17 points - is one of the few major issues still to be settled this year.
Stella saw the fact that Norris had missed out on beating Russell by just 0.02secs, despite having a plastic bag caught in his floor that he said had cost 0.1secs, as reason for optimism.
As were the lessons of the Italian Grand Prix - held on a track with similarly long straights and big braking zones.

"We saw that because of this towing effect you actually can stay tangled, linked to the other cars," Stella said. "So we are definitely looking forward to tomorrow and encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive.
"Because the tow effect is so big and because it's bigger than Monza, racing will be difficult to predict.
"So we need to make sure that from a driver's team point of view, we are ready for all the situations.

"It's also a circuit that may offer quite a few safety cars, and will be interesting, for instance, restarting from safety car with a tyre warm-up. Definitely an interesting one to be part of and to follow."
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live with build-up from 03:30; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

items.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
paragraphs: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

items.title: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
paragraphs: An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29. Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate," and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to "pushing the can down the road for two more years."

They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: "States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities."

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

"Technology is moving faster than diplomacy," said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. "Diplomats are very slow."

After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn't happened.

Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

items.title: Why has North Korea redesigned its flag? It's not about aesthetics...
paragraphs: Despite being a failed nation in most regards (60% are thought to be below the poverty line, and reports of widespread starvation have surfaced as recently as 2021), North Korea continues to fascinate us. Even this week, as Trump, Putin and Xi prepared to meet in Shenzhen, China the media was playing "Where's Kim?" after Trump told reporters North Korean leader Kim Jong Un "would like to" attend, and that whether he came was "up to President Xi".

As the summit wrapped up today, though, Kim Jong Un was nowhere to be seen. Instead, state media showed him touring a half-built ski resort at home. Which is shame for a design obsessive like me. Because if he had turned up, I'd have been watching the flagpoles rather than the handshakes.
Why? Well, earlier this month it emerged that the highly secretive and repressive nation has changed the shape of its flag for the first time since 1948.

The revised constitution, ratified in March but only recently published on the state website, sets the ratio at 1:1.65 rather than the old 1:2. The white stripes look noticeably thicker, and the red star in its white circle now sits closer to the centre. The government, though hasn't explained why, so it's up to us to have an educated guess.

It's tempting to read this in pure design terms, as a long overdue tidy-up. Indeed, as long ago as 1948, one delegate worried the long, thin flag would fold too easily on the pole. And things do move slowly in state bureaucracies, after all. Not usually this slowly, but could it just be that sorting out the flag's ratio has finally just floated to the top of a long list of priorities?

If it were as simple as that, though, North Korea would presumably have gone for the standard ratio of 2:3, the one seen in over 80 national flags. France, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, China, Russia, Ukraine… you get the picture. Instead Pyongyang has opted for on 1:1.65, a ratio seen in… absolutely no other national flag on Earth. Which kind of suggests they're trying to make a point.

The professed meaning behind the design has shifted too. The white elements once stood for the purity of a single Korean people. Naenara now says they represent the loyalty of people who support the Party and the leader.

You might think "so what?", but this actually a very big deal. Ever since North and South Korea were split between the communist and capitalist powers in 1945, both sides have dreamed the unification of the country (albeit under their control, of course).

In 2023, though, Kim expounded the "two hostile states" doctrine, which said that reunification “can never be achieved” with South Korea. In 2024 he rewrote the national anthem along these lines, and the new flag design should be seen in the same light.
It's a bit like when you give up on getting back with an ex-partner: you go out and buy a whole new outfit to cheer yourself up and show them you're doing just fine without them.

So while the flag design that has barely changed, that's doesn't mean it's not significant. The fact that it's changed at all actually says a lot about the future of 70 million Koreans, and the global world order as a whole.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: How to pick the right website template for your creative business
paragraphs: Even if you're using one of the best website builders, I recommend taking your time when choosing your template if you're going that route. A website template provides the foundation for everything, and choosing wisely at the beginning can save you time and energy further down the line.

Templates can still offer substantial value by handling the heavy lifting of page structure, navigation, and responsive design. But with countless websites vying for attention, you'll want a starting point that aligns with your brand while leaving plenty of scope for customisation so you can make the site stand out and add features or adapt the site later without requiring a complete overhaul.
In this guide, we'll cover the key factors to consider when evaluating templates, and also what other options are available if a template-based approach isn't the best match for your project.

Modern templates aren't intended to be finished websites but to provide a flexible framework that can be reshaped to fit your needs. That said, it's still important to check that a template includes all the layout and navigation features you think you're going to need. Success comes down to choosing a template that's already close to your brand's requirements, then refining and personalising it until the final result feels unique and tailored rather than generic.

Pay close attention to the underlying framework, including page layout, content hierarchy and overall site structure. Modern website builders make it relatively simple to update colors, typography, images and other visual details, but altering navigation systems, restructuring pages, or reworking the flow of content can be far more time-consuming, so these are areas to check.

Make sure the template offers the sections or content blocks that you need. This might include a hero image, features, testimonials and galleries. You might only want a simple one pager, but remember that it's easier to simplify a complex template than it is to add structure to one that's overly basic. Templates that provide little flexibility could limit future content growth.

Check the menu organisation fits with the structure you want before committing. Look for a clear visual hierarchy that guides visitors to important content, intuitive menus that make sections easy to find, flexible page layouts that support your content requirements and logical placements for calls to action, such as contact forms or portfolio links.

Avoid choosing a template based solely on appearance without considering usability or selecting complex navigation structures that confuse visitors. Overcrowded layouts can confuse viewers with elements that compete for attention.
The visual style of a template should complement your brand rather than dominate it, and design elements should align with your brand identity and audience expectations.

Most modern templates will allow considerable customisation, so you don't necessarily need one that resembles your branding from the start, but it can save time. Even then, publishing a template without significant customisation is rarely enough so check that typography and spacing can be easily adapted and that the colour palette can be customised. Also check that visual styling is consistent throughout the template.

Web design trends come and go. In 2026, we're seeing a lot of glassmorphism, immersive 3D visuals and storytelling through motion. But avoid picking a trendy design that may date quickly. Using a template with excessive animations or visual effects can also cause a site to date, while also potentially impacting on loading times and user engagement.

With visitors browsing on desktops, tablets and smartphones, responsive design is essential. Check how the template adapts across devices, as restructuring mobile layouts requires advanced customisation.

That means more than just checking that the layout adapts to the different screen size and orientation. Also evaluate whether animations, transitions, and interactive components work across platforms and match your brand's personality.

While most templates today are responsive, don't assume completely responsive behaviour without testing it. Look for layouts that adapt smoothly to different screen sizes, readable text and appropriately sized buttons on mobile devices and fast-loading pages across platforms. Functionality should ideally be consistent regardless of device.

Prioritising responsiveness can also mean avoiding designs that rely heavily on large images or complex interactions. Make sure you remember to check how portfolios, galleries or forms display on smaller screens.

Most websites need to connect with external tools and services. Your template should support these integrations without unnecessary complications, so ensure the template is compatible with features like ecommerce tools, booking systems, or membership areas even if you're only considering adding these at a later stage. It could set you back a lot if you decide to add a store in the future and find that the template doesn't readily support it.

Look for compatibility with your preferred content management system (many people use WordPress), and support for e-commerce, booking systems or payment gateways if required. You might also want easy integration with analytics, marketing and social media tools, regular updates and compatibility with third-party plugins.
Avoid assuming that all integrations will work out of the box. At the same time, don't overcomplicate the site with unnecessary third-party features that you don't think you'll really need.

Using a template can still be an efficient way to get online, but advances in AI mean that there are now alternatives that exist, still without having to code anything from scratch. AI website builders have become sophisticated enough to serve as legitimate starting points, with platforms like Bluehost creating custom designs based on conversational inputs.

The Bluehost AI Website Builder can turn a simple business description into a complete, working WordPress website in minutes. The platform guides you through a few basic questions about your business, or you can simply enter a prompt about your goals and brand style.

The AI builds a full layout that's automatically populated with pre-written text, navigation so you can get a good sense of how the site will look. You can then interact conversationally with an AI assistant to rewrite the copy, adjust tone, add pages or replace images.

You can also get more granular and fine-tune text, images and layouts using a visual drag-and-drop editor like you would with a template. And unlike closed website builders, the builder runs on WordPress. You keep full content ownership, and you can access the WordPress dashboard, install plugins, or use WooCommerce for online stores.

Paid plans bundle reliable hosting, free SSL security, a Content Delivery Network (CDN), weekly automated backups, malware scanning, and a free custom domain for the first year. You can also take advantage of tools like Yoast SEO Premium access to help optimise page titles, meta descriptions and readability.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
paragraphs: Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," said France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
Arguing that this COP was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their power to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn by 2035 - that has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

items.title: The film about fencing set between two cultures
paragraphs: Touché tells the story of Deep who seeks to change her life by taking up fencing
It was Hollywood more than Bollywood that British Indian filmmaker Parvinder Shergill grew up on, with Karate Kid, Rocky, A Few Good Men and ET among her favourite films.
The actor, writer and producer, who lives in Berkshire, says she feels "really lucky" that she comes from "two worlds".
Shergill says she builds stories around both cultures, the latest of which are her new film Touché and her first play Threads of Healing.
As she talks about wanting to "inspire" with her work, she says "it's an exciting time to embrace who you are, whatever that means to you".
Shergill says a lot of the work she consumed growing up was "very male-driven, global, mainstream, commercial".
But even though she wants to make work for the Western audience, she says her perspective "has an added layer of always having a female South Asian protagonist".
"I'm also going to be doing a sci-fi next year, there happens to be a brown woman in it, but it's not about her being brown. It's just she's in the sci-fi world."
She says she considers having a perspective from two cultures "a blessing".
"My sister does polo, I've done fencing and chess but we're British Indian women in a sari - that's wicked."
Parvinder Shergill says she "couldn't believe" the cast she assembled, including comedian Paul Chowdhry
Shergill says the world of Bollywood world as "very visual, it's very culture rich, it's very high on emotions".
In contrast she says "especially [in] Britain, our work is very deep thinking, it's very articulate, it's very heavy on the words".
She says she has projects in the pipeline that will "honour both worlds in a global audience".

"I think there is a way to combine great emotion and visual storytelling the way Bollywood does, especially with the soundtracks, but with excellent writing and what British playwrights and screenwriters have to offer."
Her approach is through subtlety, such as making sure the accents of her characters reflect the area they are from.
"Instead of drinking tea she might drink chai or instead of wearing a simple studded earring it might be a beautiful intricate Indian earring.
"Once you make it normal, it's normal for the audience."
Threads of Healing is Shergill's first play, starring Parminder Nagra and Dame Meera Syal
Shergill, who is also an NHS psychiatrist, says exploring mental health "will always be in all of my work".
Her play for BBC Radio 4 Drama, also available in print, explores personal trauma and overcoming it - a topic which she says is "really stigmatised still" in the South Asian community.
"It's a very difficult conversation and it's something I really try to look at."
She says trauma in all its forms is something that especially women in the community do not come forward with because they fear the consequences.
Bend It Like Beckham star Parminder Nagra plays the lead in Threads of Healing, which Shergill describes as "such a 360 moment".
"And Meera Syal, who plays her mother, I thought, 'we really look up to them in the community, hopefully people will listen and it will come more of a conversation piece'," she added.
Dame Meera has spoken openly about having been sexually harassed and assaulted.
Even though Shergill wants to make work for the Western audience, she says her perspective "has an added layer of always having a female South Asian protagonist"
On Touché, which will be screened in cinemas from 27 November, Shergill says she has "a soft place".
The film tells the story of a British South Asian woman named Deep, played by Shergill, who seeks to change her life by taking up fencing.
The actress had fenced in school and at university and describes it as "a mix of chess with pilates and yoga and weights".
"We were meant to get stunts and cranes and a stunt double but the ironic thing is, I could not find a stunt double who looked like me.
"That was just wild to me, so I thought, 'right, this is another reason to make the film'."
She says she "couldn't believe the cast we got", including Harry Potter star Matthew Lewis, comedian Paul Chowdhry and writer and actor Stephen Fry.
Shergill says there is also "an underlying mental storyline that I've dedicated the film to my grandfather who passed this year for that".
Shergill considers having a perspective from two cultures "a blessing"
Of her own role she says it was inspired by the theme of the underdog who becomes a hero "but it happens to not be a boy [but] someone that looks like me and other women".

"I really wanted to make something where girls can look at and be like, 'you know what? I can be a good person despite what happens in life if I just try really hard', so I wanted it to be an inspiring story," she says.
The film won the Tongues on Fire Flame Award at the 28th UK Asian Film Festival and Shergill says she is now "really excited" for her "first ever theatrical release".
"We actually had a little South Asian boy who's now fencing, which is so cool, so you don't know how you can inspire people."

items.title: Why is Blackpool such a Strictly highlight?
paragraphs: The Blackpool show has become synonymous with big staging and unforgettable routines

From Halloween high kicks to magical Movie Week moves, Strictly Come Dancing's highlights can often come thick and fast, but once a season, there is a particular peculiarity that has become a much-loved tradition - the annual decamp to Blackpool.
The seaside resort was a location in the first series of the BBC programme back in 2004 and went on to become a mainstay moment.
The show returns to the town on Saturday and will see eight couples taking to the dancefloor in the magnificent Blackpool Tower Ballroom.
But how did Blackpool become such a Strictly highlight and what does it mean to the town?
Blackpool Tower Ballroom sits underneath its most famous landmark
The show is usually made at the Elstree studios in Hertfordshire, but for one week each year, it goes north to the Tower Ballroom in Blackpool.
The ballroom regularly hosts World and all-England dance championships, and the Blackpool Junior Dance Festival has been held there every year since 1964.
As such, many of Strictly's dancers already know the venue well from their earlier careers.
Speaking in 2023, Lauren Oakley said she was seven when she first took to the dancefloor there.
"I just got my first dance partner and I remember being taken aback by how amazing it was and how dancers from all over the world were there performing and competing," she said.
Strictly's visit to the resort has become a firm favourite with fans of the show
It is little wonder that the dancers find it such an awesome venue.
The famous ballroom dates back to 1894 and is made from about 30,600 pieces of oak, mahogany and walnut wood.
The dancefloor is also sprung, which means it is supported underneath by wooden strips or foam, making it slightly bouncy.
It is also enormous, measuring about 121ft by 101ft (37m by 31m), which makes it about nine times bigger than the one at Elstree.
The cast of Strictly 2017 opened Blackpool with a dance to Let Me Entertain You
The ballroom regularly hosted Strictly's predecessor Come Dancing during that programme's almost 50-year run.
That made it a prime candidate for a visit when that show was upgraded and rebooted into Strictly Come Dancing in 2004.
Sure enough, the third episode of that first series came from the Tower Ballroom, with the dancefloor then hosting the final the following year.
Blackpool Week became a regular thing on the show from 2009, when Children In Need temporarily took over the Strictly studio at the old BBC Television Centre every November.
Since 2013, only the Covid pandemic has stopped the programme decamping to the seaside resort for an episode.
Anton Du Beke scored his first ever 10s in Blackpool
The sheer size of the Tower Ballroom means the dancers often go large in Blackpool Week in terms of both routines and staging.

Few Strictly fans will forget the splendour of Emma Barton and Anton Du Beke's American Smooth to Let's Face the Music and Dance in 2019, a routine which earned the now-Strictly judge his first 10s and highest ever score on the show.

Equally memorable from the same show was eventual winner Kelvin Fletcher's Jive with partner Oti Mabuse to Jailhouse Rock, which lived as long in the memory for Fletcher's impressive quiff as it did for their near-perfect performance.
Ed Balls produced many memorable performances, not least of which came in Blackpool
Blackpool was also the venue for another utterly unforgettable Jive, performed in 2016 by Ed Balls and his partner Katya Jones.

It featured the former politician being held aloft by Jones and four of her fellow dancers and throwing himself wholeheartedly into the dance in front of flames and a piano backdrop, all to the sounds of Great Balls of Fire.
Blackpool performances are often a case of go big or go home

Other Blackpool highlights include Jamie Borthwick being lowered to the dancefloor on a giant sparkly ketchup bottle in 2024, Fleur East and Vito Coppola getting straight 10s for their amazing Couple's Choice in 2022, Ashley Roberts and Pasha Kovalev's fish and chip shop-based Jive in 2018 and Frankie Bridge and Kevin Clifton's matching haircuts and thrilling Quickstep in 2014.
Ann Widdecombe and Anton du Beke perform a Samba in Strictly Come Dancing
But no highlights reel from Blackpool would be complete without a mention of the late Ann Widdecombe's Samba with Anton Du Beke in 2010.
Staged to Heaven Must Be Missing An Angel in canary yellow outfits, the routine saw Du Beke swing the politician round by her arms and legs.
While it may have been a miss with the judges - the combined total of 13 included a one from Craig Revel Harwood - it was a huge hit with viewers, who saved the couple in the public vote.
Katya Jones said being in Blackpool was "like coming home"
The majority of the professional dancers have a long history with Blackpool Tower Ballroom, having danced their competitively in their pre-Strictly careers.
Speaking in 2024, Katya Jones said "if you could describe Blackpool week in one word or phrase... it would be like coming home".
"It's bringing dancing back to where it belongs," she said.
"The energy in Blackpool is always different.
"The hall is bigger, so you have to really fill that space with your performance, with energy and spark, which sort of comes quite naturally because it's an epic room to be dancing in."
Sarah Hadland and Vito Coppola performed a Couple's Choice in Blackpool in 2024
Fellow pro Vito Coppola said it was a combination of history with the venue and the splendour of Strictly that made the trip special.
"I love Blackpool. I won the Blackpool Tower competition in 2008 when I was 15," he said.
"Every time I'm in Blackpool, I can feel the energy of years and years of dancing and all the big legends that have danced there.
"Words cannot describe how amazing the feeling of dancing on the ballroom in Blackpool is.
"Every week is beautiful and different, but Blackpool is just Blackpool."
Dazzling routines, outrageous sets, flamboyant costumes and the occasional dance dis-aaa-ster.
Like Vito, Nikita Kuzmin is a huge Blackpool fan, but for him, it is not just about the joy of dancing, but also the resort's more-varied delights.
Speaking on Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two on Tuesday, he said he loved getting a chance to enjoy Blackpool's amusements.
"I've said it a million times... it's the best arcades in the world," he said.
Johannes Radebe was one of the only dancers who had not performed in Blackpool before Strictly
But not all the professionals have such a long history of visiting the town.
For some, like dancer-turned-presenter Johannes Radebe, it was Strictly that made the Blackpool dream come true.
"Blackpool is the home of ballroom," he said in 2024.
"It's always special to dance at Blackpool and Strictly gave me the opportunity [as] when I was competing, we couldn't afford to travel to the UK."
He added that going to Blackpool was "like a school trip".
"Everyone wants to get to Blackpool so the excitement is off the scale," he said.
"As the dance floor is bigger we have extra dancers so it just feels bigger - and costumes and make-up are always fantastic."
It is hard to speak for a whole town, but in general, Blackpool loves Strictly almost as much as Strictly loves Blackpool.
Visit Blackpool, the town's tourism body, describes the town as "the spiritual home of ballroom dancing" and the show's annual visit as "the most dazzling dance event of the year".
Alongside celebrating the "magnificent" Blackpool Tower Ballroom, it also points visitors to waxwork gallery Madame Tussauds' replica Glitterball trophy and judges' desk.
This includes effigies of judge Craig Revel Horwood and former presenters Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.
The entertainment museum Showtown, which has a "dazzling dance gallery which will take you on a journey through Blackpool's history of dance".

Speaking to North West Tonight from the Tower Ballroom, Strictly pro Carlos Gu said he had "been dreaming of coming to Blackpool" since he was a child while Canadian pro Mark Karmalita said he had "goosebumps" when he first stepped into the ballroom.
Fellow pro Lauren Oakley said she had been coming to the seaside resort before she could dance to watch her mum and her cousins compete here.
"I can't even count how many times I've been here and it holds so many memories and it's so nice to be here with Strictly as well," she said.
Samantha Bell-Docherty, pictured with Aishley Bell-Docherty, said it was "great to see the gorgeous ballroom on national TV"
Samantha Bell, artistic director of Blackpool dance company House of Wingz, said Strictly's visit was "really great publicity for the town".
"It really shows what a special welcoming and warm place Blackpool is and all that is had to offer," she said.
"There's a real buzz about the town and you can feel it in the air.
"We are the world capital of [ballroom] dance and so it's really great that all the pros and that excitement comes to the town."

items.title: Rings of Power filming allows Morfydd Clark to see 'secret bits' of Wales
paragraphs: Morfydd Clark plays the elf Galadriel, portrayed by Cate Blanchett in Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings film trilogy
Actress Morfydd Clark has described how filming The Rings of Power allowed her to see "all these secret bits" of Wales she had not visited before.
The fantasy adventure is set thousands of years before the events of JRR Tolkien's The Hobbit and Lord of the Rings in the fictional Middle Earth.
Clark, who is from Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, was able to see parts of her own country she had not explored before while filming the third series of the Amazon Prime Video programme.
The star is reprising her leading role as the fierce elf commander Galadriel - and has also admitted how she slipped some Welsh words into her role.
Clark said her mother used to wait for the credits to see the interesting places where programmes had been shot.
It is reported The Rings of Power was filmed at Neath Abbey and Trefil Quarry, Blaenau Gwent, among other places.
Last autumn, the cast was also spotted in Devon, shooting along the coast.
"Look at the credits," Clark said, urging fans to do the same as her mum to find out where it was filmed.
It is not only the scenery that may be familiar to people from Wales, but Tolkien's invented Elvish language has been described as having Celtic influences.
Clark, a fluent Welsh speaker, admitted slipping some words in, including the command "cer" to her horse – the Welsh word for "go".
During series one, Galadriel was seen shouting the command "cer" to her horse, the Welsh word for "go"
The actress, who has also starred in Dracula and His Dark Materials, warned fans that all is not well for the protagonists in the upcoming series, joking: "It's going terribly."
Referring to the evil sorcerer who is trying to take over the fictional Middle Earth, Clark said: "Sauron is back and powerful and evil.
"They're just desperately trying to stem the tide."
Series three is set five years after the events of series two, and hope is dim in Middle Earth as Sauron's armies have conquered almost all in their path.
A few pockets of resistance remain, including Galadriel and her fellow elves, but Sauron works day and night to harness the power of the One Ring to crush them.
In the series, the "sorcerer of dreadful power" Sauron is played by Charlie Vickers, who starred in Netflix historical drama Medici
Despite this, Clark says the series will also look back on Galadriel's happier days, where the audience will see the serious commander dance and be cheerful.
Clark enjoyed the chance to "go back in time" and explore this new side of her character, adding: "It felt really exciting to go and find a different part of who she was."
In Jackson's Lord of the Rings film trilogy, Galadriel is serene and wise yet immensely powerful.
Meanwhile, the Prime Video prequel depicts the character in her youth, wilful and rebellious.
"It's wonderful to play someone brave and unapologetic, and also not afraid of social consequences," Clark said.
"I like to try and push myself to be a bit more like her at times."
Clark is joined in series three by Stranger Things actor Jamie Campbell Bower, who plays Galadriel's long-lost husband Celeborn
The Lord of the Rings franchise is globally beloved, so taking on such a recognised role as Galadriel comes with a lot of pressure, believes Clark.
However, given that an actor's job is to "make a career out of emotions", she feels a similar responsibility in all her acting pursuits.
"I've just resigned myself to the fact the neurosis will always be there, whether I'm doing a speech at Christmas or filming this," she said.
Series three of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is available to watch now.

items.title: How Westside Cowboy went from student gigs to rising stars in two years
paragraphs: Westside Cowboy formed while three of the band were students

In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.
What started as jamming for fun in a student bedroom has become the latest revolution in British indie known as "Britainicana".
Now the quartet have been named the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year for 2026.
Westside Cowboy join a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan and several other now household names that have won the award.
But how did they get there, and so quickly?
It is 3 December 2024 and I am finally about to see Westside Cowboy.
A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.
Wolstenholme, pictured with Murphy and Bradbury, has championed the band since the start
It was the launch night of their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You).
It is a sub-three-minute explosion of some of the finest pop rock you could ever hope to hear.
They had released the single on 7 November 2024 and uploaded it to the BBC Introducing website on the same day.
I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.
It was soon played by Emily Pilbeam on BBC Radio 6Music.
Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.
By the time their second single Shells was released in April 2025, Westside Cowboy had been selected by BBC Introducing to play on their illustrious stage at Glastonbury festival.
The song also went straight on to the coveted 6Music playlist.
Every other single the band have released since has received the same treatment and more.
This YouTube post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on YouTube

Paddy Murphy, Reuben Haycocks and Aoife Anson O'Connell met in autumn 2021 at the Royal Northern College of Music on Oxford Road.
One day, Murphy and Haycocks walked down Oxford Road to Johnny Roadhouse, a music shop fronted with an array of hanging brass instruments and full of Manchester folklore.
It has served the city's musicians since 1955.
They ran into guitar repairer, Jimmy Bradbury, who asked Murphy and Haycocks if they fancied starting a band called Westside Cowboy.
Be grateful that the answer was yes - with O'Connell joining later that evening.
Murphy and Bradbury had been in a band together before, a surf-rock trio called Katz, and Murphy and Haycocks both played in another trio, DieKaiDie.
Drummer Murphy played guitar for another band too, Holly Head, however O'Connell had not even played a guitar before she picked up the bass for Westside Cowboy. She was a cellist.
It is safe to say that this new band had plenty of competition for their time, but nevertheless it was soon to be their top priority.
Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.
Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.
On 1 February 2025 I introduced them on stage.
Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.
It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.
Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.
Westside Cowboy then also won Glastonbury's prestigious Emerging Talent Competition to perform on the Woodsies Stage alongside Blossoms and Scissor Sisters.
Westside Cowboy reminisced about the early days on BBC Radio Manchester
Loyal listeners to BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria followed every step of the band's progress through 2025.
Their claim to the show came courtesy of drummer Murphy, who grew up in the market town of Longridge, Lancashire, which sits a few miles north of Preston.
Imitations of his "Westsiiide Cowboooy!" scream became a regular feature, recognised as the only way to introduce the band's music on the radio.
The high point of 2025 for the band was the release of their first EP, which was recorded by Lewis Whiting, the guitarist from English Teacher.
Its title This Better Be Something Great wryly proclaimed the general astonishment at just how fast this little student band was blowing up.

The EP was used for the students' coursework at RNCM, and secured the band a contract with Island Records – the same label as Ariana Grande, Sabrina Carpenter, Florence + The Machine and English Teacher.
The band have performed on Later… with Jools Holland on BBC Two

They were soon jetting off to New York to record their next EP with Loren Humphrey, whose reputation was soaring after the success of Heavy Metal - the debut solo album from Cameron Winter, the lead singer of Geese.
Westside Cowboy then headed to Paris for a 15-date European tour supporting their heroes, Black Country, New Road.
Their second EP was released in January 2026 titled So Much Country 'Till We Get There.
In the months that followed, Westside Cowboy were back touring Europe, this time opening for Geese, who had a decent claim for being the most exciting indie band in the world.
This was possibly the hottest support slot on the planet, and these four Manchester students had it.
They soon announced their own debut album It Goes On, which charted at No. 5 in the Official Album Charts.
William Wolstenholme shares the best local musical talent.

After a performance on Later… with Jools Holland on BBC Two, Westside Cowboy were off to America again to make their US television debut on The Tonight Show starring Jimmy Fallon, one of the most recognisable TV shows in the world.
It was still under two years since their first headline show.

In a world where artists fiddle frustratingly at algorithms trying to get their music to an audience on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and Spotify, this is an old school meteoric rise the likes of which the music industry must have thought no longer possible.
It has been achieved by four seemingly ordinary students regularly seen wandering down Oxford Road in Manchester.
Together the have been named the outstanding emerging act of the year by the BBC Introducing.
