items.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
paragraphs: Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.
Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.
It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".
The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.
The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform £12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.
But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year.
It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.
The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".
In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".
The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than £354,000.
Nine of those , externalincluded a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".
Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review, external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".
Five months later, the investigation has not begun.
In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.
The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.
The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI, external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.
Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".
Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.
But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."
Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.
"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.
She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".
"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.
"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

items.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
paragraphs: Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

“You will see robots and humans working in harmony,” she declares as we move between different stations of the warehouse. Everything is designed to maximise what humans are good at, she continues, and what robots are good at – “working without getting tired”.

Almost every judgment call here seems to be made by a computer – not just where to stow items when they arrive at the warehouse (the system shines a light on to the spot on the specific shelf where the worker should place each item) but also which size box to pack something in once it’s been ordered, and even precisely how much tape to use to seal that box. The human beings are here to provide the hands, not the brains.

So far, at least, there is no hardware or software to rival a human hand. Humanoid robots – often called “embodied AI” – have made great strides over the past decade (literally, as evidenced in China’s recent five-day robot Olympics). But producing a robot that can pack a shelf, tighten a bolt and also pick a raspberry – actions that would make them useful rather than simply entertaining, actions most of us perform without any conscious effort – has proved surprisingly difficult. Replicating the breadth of function of the human hand is one of the biggest remaining challenges in robotics. Until robots are dexterous, human workers will always be necessary.

But investors are now gambling on humanoid robots soon becoming as much a part of everyday life as AI-powered large language models are for many of us today. The Chinese government has pledged to invest more than £100bn in robotics and high-tech industries over the next two decades. Earlier this year, Tesla halted production of its Model X and Model S cars so that factories could focus instead on producing Optimus humanoid robots. “Human hands have evolved to be this incredibly sophisticated machine. Your hand is actually a remarkable thing,” Tesla chief executive Elon Musk told a conference last year. “In order to create a robot that can be a generalised humanoid, you must solve the hands problem.”

Amazon employs more than 1.5 million people worldwide today. But from what I can see on the warehouse floor, it seems that if a task could be done more efficiently by a machine, Amazon would rather leave it to a robot. What will happen to these workers when the “hands problem” is solved?

And what will happen to the rest of us? Artificial dexterity combined with artificial intelligence will be hugely consequential for humanity. Forget retraining as a plumber in the age of AI – if engineers manage to replicate human hands, then potentially no job will be future-proof.

Dexterous robots that can rival a human hand are not here yet, but they are coming. What makes hands so difficult to reproduce in hardware and software? How close are robotics engineers to getting it right? And what will happen to the world of work when they do?

“The hand is our conduit between the brain and the world,” says Alistair Hunter, a hand and wrist surgeon at University College London hospitals. “The hand is our way of turning thought into action.” Hunter has spent most of his professional life seeking to understand how hands work, and how to return them to normal function when they don’t. “Hands are special because they are very complicated anatomically,” he tells me over coffee in north London. “There are 27 bones in the hand; there are nerves and muscles that control it. But behind all that is the brain, which is interacting millisecond by millisecond to understand what the hand is sensing, adjusting to that, and then providing action.”

We might assume that we owe our evolutionary advantage to our intelligence, but Hunter argues it’s actually the combination of our cognitive power and our dexterity that has given us the edge. Over the millions of years that the frontal cortex of our brains was developing, the hand evolved to differentiate itself from limbs, allowing for the development of fingers that could grasp branches and climb trees. Thumbs came next. All the great apes might have them, but ours are larger. “The joint at the bottom of the thumb – the trapeziometacarpal joint – is one of the main advances in evolution to allow us to do very fine pincer grip, very fine dexterous control between thumb, index and middle finger, but also incredible power, incredible grasp. That allowed us to manipulate things like stones and rocks, so three million years ago we started to develop tools.”

The brain is constantly coordinating the interaction between larger muscles in the forearm, which allow for power and strong grip, and smaller muscles in the hand itself that give us fine control. It also receives huge amounts of data from the hand. “The density of nerve fibres and sensory endings in the hand is enormous,” Hunter continues. As well as the nerve endings, the hand has specialist receptors that can tell our brains about very fine details: different corpuscle cells to detect vibration, roughness and smoothness, or how our fingers and hands stretch and conform around objects. “It’s that interplay between the sensory side, the motor side and the brain that makes the hand wonderful – and so difficult to replicate.”

When you pick a raspberry, your fingers sense how soft it is, whether it’s slippery, how the skin in your fingertips conforms around it. Your brain compares this information against what it expected to experience, and then recalibrates accordingly, slowing down the compression force if it feels as if the raspberry is being crushed. “That feedback loop takes about a tenth of a second,” Hunter tells me. “We’re also able to predict what that raspberry feels like – that’s called feed forward. Even before I’ve grasped it, my fingers and my hand know what pressure to put on it to pick it and not to squash it. That’s partly why you see a baby making a mess before they’ve learned that feed forward mechanism. Their hand is clumsy because it hasn’t got that predictive model.”

From striking a match to throwing a spear to playing piano, the range of tasks hands can perform is enormous. We can use them to catch, or cup them to turn them into a drinking receptacle. And they allow us to communicate – with gestures, with pens, with our thumbs over pocket-sized screens. Our hands are constantly adapting to our ever-changing needs.

It’s this breadth of function combined with adaptability that Hunter says would be such a challenge for any engineer seeking to replicate human dexterity in a robotic hand: being able to feedback and feed forward at the same time, using a model learned from years of experience and interaction with the world. That’s why robot engineers previously focused on creating task-based robots, able to perform a specific function, he adds, rather than trying to emulate everything a human hand can do.

“I think at some point they’ll be able to do it. We’ve got many, many years ahead of us, and you can see that already robots are able to walk and run. But building a computer that is able to predict the outside world and also deliver the right amount of sensory information back – that’s going to be difficult.”

If there ever was a symbol of dystopian tech, it is the robotic hand left clutching at Sarah Connor’s throat in the final scenes of the original Terminator movie. That’s the first thing I think of when I walk into the HQ of Shadow Robot, Europe’s premier manufacturer of dexterous hands, and see one of its prototypes – skeletal and grasping – mounted on a high shelf a few metres from the entrance. Then one of the office dogs bounds up to me, and I remember that I am in a cheery workspace a minute away from London’s Hampstead Heath.

Shadow Robot began in the 1980s as a collective of hobbyists and robot enthusiasts who met up in a north London attic to tinker around with scavenged materials, hoping to one day build a full humanoid. The company was founded after they received their first commercial order – for a leg – in 1997. For the last decade or so, their exclusive focus has been on hands.

In the demo room, the Shadow Dexterous Hands they have set up for me to see look almost friendly. Mounted on two outstretched motorised arms, their palms are open with their fingers curled slightly inwards, as if waiting to give me a hug, but we begin by shaking hands instead. Its right hand moves slowly towards mine, the fingers splayed, the wrist cocked in anticipation. Its grip is gentle – natural, even – but I don’t want to shake it too hard for fear of crushing it: it’s made of MDF and nylon, with textured magnetic sensors on its fingertips, and it feels very delicate. The starting price – without any kind of software or operating system – is £20,000 per hand; the full system costs £100,000. But my instinct to be gentle is mostly because it seems so human: it moves in an expressive way, as if it were animated by some sort of soul.

And it kind of is. It’s being operated by Liem Tran, robotics deployment and support manager at Shadow Robot, who is wearing gloves with sensors that track his movements, which the robot hands copy in real time. This teleoperation is a way of training the robot, showing the hands what to do, giving them a reference point on what constitutes a successful motion for any given task. Through machine learning, the hand will ultimately be able to replicate that movement without human help. The Shadow Robot company builds the hardware and basic systems; their customers – in industry, manufacturing and academic research – typically develop their own software to get what they want from the hands.

It’s a great time to be a hand roboticist, Tran says. “We don’t have anything that’s industry standardised, or anything that’s fully developed and ready for use. It’s exciting, because we’re essentially dictating what happens next with the tech. I like the idea of replicating a human in machine form and seeing where it takes us … Do you want a grape?”

The left robot hand reaches down to a brown paper bag on the table in front of us and pulls out a bunch of white grapes, holding the stalk with a delicate pincer movement between thumb and index finger. The right hand deftly plucks a lone grape and drops it into my palm. Each hand weighs roughly 4.5kg, Tran tells me, but the grape is resolutely unsquashed. I eat it. It passes me another.

This is only the first of several party tricks Shadow’s robot hands have up their sleeves. Tran shows me how they can stack plastic cups in a pyramid, gently positioning each one. They can hold a small wooden cube in one hand and build a tower seven blocks high on top of it with the other, keeping everything perfectly balanced. They can sort shapes, placing stars, cylinders and triangles into their appropriate slots in a bright plastic kids’ toy.

In one respect, it’s totally remarkable, but in another, completely mundane: these are hands, doing what hands do. And they are also doing it at the level of a small child. When Tran successfully manages to get the robot hands to put one of the shapes into the shape sorter, I find myself declaring, “Well done!” as if I were encouraging a toddler.

While these Shadow Dexterous Hands might look lifelike, they can’t generate anything like the amount of sensory data that the human hand can produce, and their learning model depends on a human showing them what to do. But Shadow has another model that’s got everyone here very excited – and it doesn’t look much like a human hand at all.

The DEX-EE hand, created for Google DeepMind and first unveiled in 2024, has only three digits and no wrist; the digits function like thumbs, making the DEX-EE look like a claw, with optical sensors on each fingertip. Much bulkier than the Dexterous Hands, it can’t handle very fine objects, but you can smack the DEX-EE with a baseball bat. Tran invites me to give it a try. I whack it a few times, but I don’t put my back into it: this model costs £60,000 per hand.

“It can take a beating,” Tran assures me. “That’s its whole purpose: it can go through hours and hours of collisions with the work surface.” The DEX-EE was designed to withstand hours of machine learning, making repeated mistakes that it can learn from. “It’s the same way that a baby learns to use their hands and fingers.” After experimentation with DEX-EE, DeepMind has been able to develop robots that can tie shoelaces, put a shirt on a hanger, and perform repairs on other robots.

Even though some of the most powerful tech companies in the world are working with hands that can learn on their own, manual labour looks to me as if it’s going to be safe, for now: these hands seem years away from being smart enough, robust enough or dexterous enough to deal with the variability workers in a fulfilment centre encounter every day.

But Tran quietly disagrees. “Around the world, so many companies are now making all these dexterous hands. There’s a huge race for the smoothest and most human-like. They’re getting quite impressive. The price point is becoming a lot more attractive: some hands in China are less than £2,000, which is very cheap; you don’t have to worry about repair, just buy another hand,” he says. “I don’t think we’re too far off.”

Shadow Robot never set out to compete in the high-stakes fight for global domination of the hands market. When they were a collection of amateur enthusiasts, their original aim was to build a useful humanoid, a kind of robot butler. “We built this biped – it’s now in the Science Museum, which is kind of nice,” Rich Walker, director at Shadow, tells me. Then Honda unveiled its P1 humanoid. Shadow’s biped could stand and right itself if it was shoved, but the P1 could actually walk. “As far as we can tell, Honda had spent in the order of $100m on the programme of development that led to them having a biped,” Walker continues. “We were kind of put back by that.” They decided to change tack. “We thought, what would we need a robot to do or to have in order to be useful? They’d need to be able to pick things up and interact with the same objects that I can interact with. So we decided to try building some hands.”

Walker was on the dole when he first started collaborating with the Shadow hobbyists in the 1980s. With bright blue eyes behind his varifocals and a wispy grey half ponytail that struggles to contain several thick dreadlocks, he looks part wizard, part cyberpunk, and nothing like an entrepreneur. “We never set up this organisation to make money out of building robots. It was much more, ‘Let’s build robots! How do we do that?’” he says, throwing his hands up in the air again. “Making some money on the way turns out to be a good way to make sure that you can build the robots.”

When they began developing their first prototypes, Walker tells me, their aim was to build a lifelike hand, but they soon realised what a massive task that would be. They pored over anatomy textbooks, envious of the natural hardware in the human body. “If we had those materials, it would be great,” he grins. “Self-lubricating joints. Skin that regrows. We don’t have those, so we have to use other mechanisms and solutions.”

Over the years it became clear that the most commercial proposition would be for the company to focus on hands that could fulfil specific tasks. They began to move away from the hobbyist drive to build the best thing possible, and towards a business imperative to build something that companies might want to buy in large quantities. “We’re working with a wide range of people, everything from applications in nuclear decommissioning through to medical technology and care robotics and production line stuff. A really wide range of areas where people have said, ‘Could we use a robot here?’ or, ‘Could we improve our robots with things like human hands?’”

I ask Walker what he wants his robots to be used for, and he pauses for several seconds. “We want to build robots for good. At the moment, we’re looking at robots that can do tedious things that get in the way of doing something else.” He gives the example of cleaning up the workbench of a highly skilled engineer. There are clients – and specific jobs – the company has turned down, he adds. They won’t work for arms manufacturers. After some discussion, the team decided not to lend their expertise to a project that would debone carcasses, and another that involved filling sausage casings with meat. “It’s just the ick factor sometimes.” (Walker is vegan).

But when the Shadow Robot company says no, there are now many competitors that customers can go to instead. “Ten years ago, there were four or maybe five companies making robot hands, and you knew all of them, and you knew everything about all of them. And now it’s just …” Walker throws his hands up again. “I had a Chinese analyst firm contact me a year and a half ago, and they were like, ‘We have 110 robot hands on our list.’”

It’s not just China. San Diego-based Psyonic specialises in making prosthetic hands for amputees, but has branched out into robot hands, billing its products as the “future of automation” with “human-level stability”. Sharpa, based in Singapore, boasts that its model has “human-like dexterity” and can handle complex tasks such as “screwing, clipping [and] fastening”. Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid is not yet on the market, but it can use nail guns and drills (deftly changing a fine drill bit in a demonstration video). Yet most of the momentum seems to be driven by Chinese companies: state media valued the domestic dexterous hand industry last year as worth more than 50bn yuan (£5.6bn).

Walker doesn’t like to use the word “competition” when talking about these companies. Ever the robot enthusiast, he sees them as working towards a common good. “There will be breakthroughs that suddenly just move everything forward. That might be a better motor, it might be a polymer that makes a skin that is better, it might be a way of sensing the world that lets the robot understand things in a way that we haven’t been able to do before at scale in a cheap robot.” He pauses. “It’s exciting.”

“Shadow is in a difficult position,” Nathan Lepora, professor of robotics and AI at the University of Bristol, tells me in a video call. “The Shadow Hand was best in class for 20 years, but it’s the price of a Lamborghini. Now there are a lot of very capable hands for the price of a Vauxhall. China is going through a massive expansion of hand development, and at the beginning of this decade you would never have predicted the level of dexterity that we’re seeing today.”

When I ask Lepora how close he thinks we are to developing a robot hand that can rival a human’s, he tells me that’s not the point. “We don’t necessarily need the robots to do all that hands can do. We want them to be able to pick up and manipulate objects and tools.” The current crop of robot hands might not be at that point yet, but they’re close, he says. “We’ve got a good chance of seeing general tool use by the end of this decade.”

I tell Lepora about the Amazon workers I saw in the fulfilment centre, who aren’t required to use any tools – they just have to be able to stow, pick and pack a wide variety of objects. “Their days are numbered,” he says, simply. “They are the last bits that haven’t yet been automated.” Amazon must already be working on replacing them, he adds. “I’m sure they are close to it.” Production lines without any human workers are part of manufacturing today: China has fully automated “dark factories” – so called because they can operate with the lights off – that run 24/7.

If the future looks bleak for Amazon workers, what about manual labourers in general? When I mention retraining as a plumber for job security in the age of AI, Lepora shoots me a look as if to say, don’t be naive. “Maybe for 10 or 15 years. Plumbing’s not going to be done by a robot this decade, that’s for sure. But after then?”

In Shadow Robot HQ, Walker argues that plumbers are here to stay for the foreseeable future. They have to apply themselves – and the available tools – to such a wide variety of unusual spaces and problems, after all; their skill comes from being adaptable, not from knowing the correct way to perform a procedure, he says. A dexterous hand alone will not take their job. “If you’ve ever seen a plumber get under your bath and do something to the tap at the back, you’ll realise that’s going to be a job for a humanoid robot at best.”

But on its website, the company say it is “working towards robotics for a safer world by allowing robots to enter extreme environments where it would be too risky for a human to go. This includes jobs that are too dull, dirty, difficult, dexterous, dangerous, and/or dear.” Walker and his team might be determined to build “robots for good”, but if they manage to get everything on that list right, they will eliminate much of human manual labour.
When I put this to him, he stiffens. He’d clearly much rather be talking about motors and tendon load sensors than the social and economic implications of where his hands might reach.

“If we solved all of the things on that list then that would be amazing, but I think that that’s several hundred years’ work for several hundred organisations and several hundred major breakthroughs will have to happen for that to happen,” he says. “Is what we’re doing likely to lead to the doom of humanity? That sounds like a marketing campaign. If I wanted to increase my share value, I’d probably say, yes, we’re going to lead to the doom of humanity – invest in us.”

No one likes to think that their job could be taken by a robot – not fulfilment centre workers, nor plumbers, nor journalists. What about Alistair Hunter, the hand surgeon? It’s hard to think of a profession that demands as much of a combination of knowledge and dexterity – brain plus hand – than his.

“When I’m operating, there are times where I’m at the very limit of my manual dexterity and my understanding. Is it possible for a robot to learn that amount of experience that I’ve developed over many years and then action it autonomously? I think that would be very difficult,” Hunter replies. “I don’t think you can ever say ‘impossible’, because 50 years ago I wouldn’t have anticipated anything of what’s possible now. But knowing what I do about the hand, and knowing what I do about surgery, I think that would be a very difficult thing to do.”

It’s easy to imagine that, in a world of embodied AI, it would be a safer bet to become a robotics engineer than a surgeon. But the nature of our work is changing so rapidly, and no career is necessarily safe.

Ultimately, Lepora says, robot hands will be making robot hands. “I don’t think any company is at that pivot point yet, but that’s where we’re ending up.” If and when that happens, robot hands will be cheaper than ever – and advancing at an extraordinary pace. “You could produce them at scale, but you could also automate the improvement of them as well,” he tells me, leaning forward with excitement. “Once they can build them themselves, you iterate it. That is the possible tipping point for when the hands will become really, really capable.” It’s also the point where robot engineers themselves might be out of a job.

items.title: From You Can See Everything to Take That: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
paragraphs: You Can See Everything Out now “Masterpiece” – it’s an overused word, but sometimes, it’s the only word. This funny, tragic, gripping, three-hour sensation (and, yes, masterpiece) arrives in the UK after a record-busting run in the States, where Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s portrait of their time immersed in the world of Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has gripped US audiences.

Josephine Out now Winner of the Audience and Grand Jury prizes at Sundance, this drama sees eight-year-old Josephine become witness to a horrific assault on a jogger in San Francisco’s Golden Gate park. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan star as the girl’s parents.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Out now Mahershala Ali stars as a former military hitman dealing with multiple crises. These range from orders to assassinate a Muslim porn studio head honcho’s charismatic Christian enemy, to finding fresh breast milk for his baby daughter, whose mother has recently passed, and who can’t digest formula.

Filipiñana Out now Seventeen-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) works at an elite golf course in the Philippines as a “tee-girl” – setting golf tees in the ground so that wealthy golfers don’t have to suffer the indignity of bending down themselves to do it. An examination of national identity as well as a personal drama, it marks the debut of director Rafael Manuel. Catherine Bray

Jungle to 28 November; tour starts Leeds With a Brit win, a Mercury nod and five Top 10 albums, dance-pop trio Jungle have quietly (and, let’s be honest, pretty anonymously) become one of Britain’s biggest bands. Their stealthy rise is cemented via this arena tour in support of August’s Sunshine album. Michael Cragg

Knats Future Yard, Birkenhead, 21 November; Waiting Room, Stockton-on-Tees 22 November This jazz, rock and dance trio’s punky “geordie jazz” started making waves in 2025. Their latest release, A Great Day in Newcastle, reveals hard-hitting poetry, humour, and a rebellious energy sure to take them far. John Fordham

Manchester Collective Lakeside Arts, Nottingham, 25 November; touring to 6 December The latest programme from this boundary-storming contemporary music ensemble mixes an experimental work by Icelandic soundtrack queen Hildur Guðnadottir with Bach chorales and movements from James Tenney’s 1980s electroacoustic classic Glissade. At its centre lies Black Gold, Luke Mombrea’s powerfully atmospheric audiovisual piece inspired by an oil well fire. Flora Willson

Action All Areas Roundhouse, London, 26 November Self Esteem, James Bay and Jade Bird are the musical performers at this one-off night of “intimate and unplugged” music and activism in aid of Greenpeace. It’s hosted by comedian and writer Sophie Duker. MC

Barbara Hepworth and Greece Pallant House, Chichester, to 2 May Arguably Britain’s most important modernist, Barbara Hepworth found inspiration for her elegant, curving sculptural forms everywhere. But a journey through Greece in 1954 changed everything for her, and this exhibition shows us the gorgeous results. Nan Goldin Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November to 14 March Get ready to feel a lot of feelings. American photographer Nan Goldin has spent her career documenting queer subcultures, personal relationships and addiction, often to devastating effect.

Ragnar Kjartansson Goodwood Art Foundation, Chichester, 26 November to 12 April This playfully melancholic Icelandic conceptualist was last on these shores with a hugely popular Barbican show 10 years ago, and now he’s bringing his signature blend of humour and discomfort to Chichester.

Peggy Guggenheim in London Royal Academy of Art, London, to 14 March Peggy Guggenheim became one of the biggest and most important art collectors of the 20th century, and it all started on Cork Street in London. This exhibition looks at Guggenheim’s first gallery venture in 1938, and the way it shocked conservative British tastes. Eddy Frankel

Birmingham Royal Ballet: The Nutcracker Birmingham Hippodrome, to 12 December One of the best Nutcrackers you’ll see in the UK, Birmingham Royal Ballet’s production was presented as a gift to the company by former director Peter Wright back in 1990 and has been a hit ever since. It ticks all the Christmas boxes: giant tree, falling (and dancing) snowflakes, and a full orchestra playing Tchaikovsky’s magical music. Lyndsey Winship

Eurotrash Young Vic, London, to 9 January A stellar double act – Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter – lead this stage adaptation of Christian Kracht’s darkly comic novel. It’s about a formidable mother and son who embark on a road trip across the Swiss mountains, intent on giving away the (slightly dodgy) family money, stashed in a plastic bag. Miriam Gillinson

My Fair Lady Pitlochry Festival theatre, to 31 December Alan Cumming stars alongside Verity Power in a chamber production of My Fair Lady, the final show of Cumming’s opening season as artistic director. It’s directed by Maria Friedman, whose work always has such grace and wit. MG

Sam Campbell Touring to 1 December Four years after winning Edinburgh’s best show prize, the Aussie eccentric has infiltrated the comedy mainstream; first as a contestant on Last One Laughing: UK, then via his surreal Channel 4 series Make That Movie. His new standup show Kid Giblet promises plenty more absurd flights of fancy. Rachel Aroesti

Sweetpea NOW & Sky Atlantic, 26 November, 9pm Fallout’s Ella Purnell is back as the wispily fringed Rhiannon, a meek outsider who finds her niche in vigilante serial killing in this smart and gruesome drama that reflects wryly on female empowerment and the concept of embracing your flaws. Will she continue to get away with murder in series two?

The Witch Farm iPlayer & BBC One, 22 November, 9pm King of the contemporary ghost story Danny Robins has adapted his Radio 4 drama about a couple who (unintentionally) move to a haunted farm in south Wales in the late 1980s into a goosebump-inducing TV thriller. Black Doves’ Gabrielle Creevy and This Is England’s Michael Socha co-star.

Oobah: Scams For A Better Tomorrow HBO Max, 22 November Fraudsters, grifters, conmen: to be alive today is to be besieged by bad actors – and Oobah Butler wants a piece of their pie. That’s the droll setup of his new series, which will really see the prankster documentarian highlight swindles in areas including wine, wellness and dating.

Blade Runner 2099 Prime Video, 25 November This sequel to the 1982 and 2017 films picks up the action a half-century later, when lab-grown humanoids rule over LA’s actual human inhabitants. Our protagonists are replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and human-pretending-to-be-a-replicant Cora (Hunter Schafer) who team up to track down a bunch of their awol peers. RA

Appulse PC, out 26 November An ingenious combination of pinball machine and top-down shooter, Appulse has you blasting enemy spaceships while rebounding between flippers and bumpers earning special upgrades. Surely, a veteran gamer’s dream.

Am I Nima? PC, out 27 November Locked in a basement and suffering from amnesia, you must convince your mum that you are in fact her daughter. Created by Vancouver studio Ho! Games, this is a psychological horror game with a truly interesting and unnerving premise. Keith Stuart

Lambchop – Demoed Out now In August Kurt Wagner shared his 17th album as Lambchop, a folk freakout titled Punching The Clown. This followup EP finds guest artists singing over a handful of that album’s demos. Vocalists include MJ Lenderman, Lauren Auder and Flock of Dimes.

Take That – Dreamers Out now Gary, Mark and Howard return with the 10th Take That album and their fourth as a trio. Eschewing the soft-rock sound of 2023’s musty This Life, songs such as the Stuart Price co-produced You’re a Superstar and the loved-up Sweet July are stadium-shaped pop stompers.

Bodywash – Laughing at Noise Out now Inspired by EVOL-era Sonic Youth and the harsh reality of city life, Montreal duo Rosie Long Decter and Chris Steward’s third album feels rougher around the edges than 2023’s shoegazey I Held the Shape While I Could. Single La Renommée carries a ragged but hushed sense of urgency.

REM – Reveal 25th Anniversary Edition Out now Hailed as a return to form in 2001 after the experimental Up, the 12th album by REM gets a 25th-anniversary rerelease. As well as the original 12-track album, led by the excellent Imitation of Life, the package features a previously unreleased 17-song live set.MC

Arkivism.com Online This ingenious archive collates the collections and catalogues made available by museums and institutions around the world and presents them on one, easily searchable website. Explore paintings from Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum and images from the British Library.

World of Secrets: Dr Skin Podcast The BBC’s investigations series returns with a gripping five-part deep dive into how one of the founders of modern dermatology, Dr Albert Kligman, conducted experiments on prison inmates, often leaving them with lasting health consequences.

One Last Order Netflix, 24 November A surprisingly moving and quietly intimate film following Floridian fast-food worker Sighle Williams on her last day of service. Her bosses announce every cent earned will go to Williams and joyous community spirit ensues. Ammar Kalia

items.title: This week we launched a series celebrating the top architects and designers of the next 20 years
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen, we kicked off our 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler, to celebrate 20 years of Dezeen.

Over the next month, we will reveal the architects and designers who will have the biggest impacts over the next 20 years, as selected by some of the biggest names in architecture and design from the past 20 years.

We started the series with an interview with Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Bjarke Ingels. We then interviewed Lanza Atelier, Freya Tangelder and Swedish Girls, who were selected by Frida Escobedo, Nendo and Sabine Marcelis, respectively.
In a big week for Dezeen, we also announced the winners of the 2026 Dezeen Awards winners at a ceremony in London.
We we revealed the architecture, design and interior project winners, including the Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi (pictured), along with the six designers of the year.
In architecture news, recently revealed images of the White House ballroom drew attention to the huge scale of the project, which many said “dwarfs” the central residence.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Hilary Clinton on X.
A group of Harvard GSD students also aimed to draw attention to another Donald Trump-backed scheme in Washington DC, by proposing alternative designs to his planned arch.
The two proposals for the planned site of the arch replaced the proposed structure with an expansive pool of water.
Also in the US, plans by SHoP Architects for a supertall skyscraper in Miami, which is backed by Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic, were revealed.
The 320-metre-tall skyscraper will have a ribbed design and include amenity facilities developed by the tennis player.
In less serious news, American fast-food chain Chipotle launched a range of hoodies all with a hidden, insulated pocket for sneaking burritos into cinemas.
The tongue-in-cheek clothing was designed to keep concealed burritos warm to allow for illicit snacking at the movies.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a “surreal” house in rural China, a pink commercial building in Mexico and a Cotswolds barn renovation.
This week on Dezeen is our regular roundup of the week’s top news stories. Subscribe to our newsletters to be sure you don’t miss anything.

items.title: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges
paragraphs: Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

items.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
paragraphs: When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).

The fee, in place since February, has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025.

“The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero. The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects.
Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket.
The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections.

Eric and Patty, a young couple from New York, said they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies.
Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”.
“I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” said Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.”

A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson said the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad.
Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception.

The initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year.

A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He said people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.”

The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

items.title: Teenager allegedly organised arsons and kidnapping on Signal during Melbourne hospitality wars
paragraphs: Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.
The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.
He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.

In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.
The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.
It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.

Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.
It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.
On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.
“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.
“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.
“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

items.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
paragraphs: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

items.title: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.
The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”
The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013.
It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.
The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.
The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.
Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.
Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.
Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.
Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.
While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.
The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.
“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”
With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

items.title: Villagers to vote on 'leaving UK' over plans to house migrants at RAF base
paragraphs: Residents in Barnham are deciding whether to remain part of the UK
Villagers will head to the polls on Saturday to decide whether or not to symbolically leave the UK over plans to house migrants at a former military base.
RAF Barnham, between Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, and Thetford, Norfolk, has been earmarked by the government as a potential base for up to 931 migrants.
The proposals have not gone down well with locals and far-right groups alike, sparking several anti-asylum demonstrations since the summer.
One way or another, residents are now poised to make their voices heard by taking part in a referendum to decide whether to symbolically secede from the country or remain.
Here is everything you need to know about the controversy that has thrust a tiny, otherwise unassuming village into the national spotlight.
The Home Office first floated the idea of using three Ministry of Defence (MoD) sites to house thousands of asylum seekers in June.
Facilities in Bicester in Oxfordshire, Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire, and Barnham in Suffolk were identified to help move people out of hotels.
As of March this year, 20,885 (21%) asylum seekers were living in hotels, while 72,768 (75%) were in other accommodation as they awaited decisions.
The Home Office initially sought to house 1,250 migrants at RAF Barnham, but that number has since been reduced to just shy of 1,000.
According to the government, they would be "single adult males" aged between 18 and 65 years old who could be permitted to leave the site.
Pictures released by the Home Office earlier this year showed some of the existing accommodation at RAF Barnham
If planning permission is granted and the proposals go ahead, "a specialist and experienced provider of security services" would be "permanently on site 24/7".
It is also hoped that there will be enough "essential services" to reduce "the need for asylum seekers to leave the site".
The Home Office, which could use a fast-track planning route to bypass local council permission, is said to have awarded a £3.4m contract for the project to Kier.
The construction giant has been hired to design the camp at the former nuclear weapons store, which has most recently been used for police training.
The site is located just over a mile away from its namesake village, nearly two miles from Thetford, and close to four miles from Elveden by road.
The plans have been met with strong opposition from local councillors and residents, such as Kim Dines, who has lived in the village for 13 years.
She previously said she had been "lying awake at night" wondering what may result from migrants being housed "so close".
"We're a village of roughly 600 people; we shouldn't be living in fear, we shouldn't be worried about what's going to be on our doorstep [and] who's around us," she said.
Resident Ann Houston does not like the sound of the plans, but says the government is stuck between a rock and a hard place
Ann Houston said the presence of migrants nearby might alter "the atmosphere in the village".
"Barnham is a place where you can leave your doors open at the moment, and that might change," she said.
Concerns have also been raised about the government's commitment to spend £3.4m on drawing up the scheme before a final decision has been made.
Helen Beck, chairwoman of the Barnham Residents Association, said: "At the moment they don't even know whether it can legally go ahead - hugely disappointing."
Parish council chairman John Bauer believes RAF Barnham is "vastly unsuitable"
John Bauer, chairman of Barnham Parish Council, said leading the campaign against the plans was ruining his retirement.
"I retired at the end of last year with the expectation I would be able to do a lot of the things that I had been looking forward to doing for a while," he said.
"Unfortunately, that hasn't happened. It is demanding and exhausting, and it is not necessarily what I would have chosen to do in [my retirement]."
In many respects, voting to break away from the UK would very much act as a symbolic gesture and a way for the village to demonstrate its strength of feeling.
That is because there is no legal mechanism allowing the likes of Barnham to declare independence from the UK.
RAF Barnham is used to train Suffolk and Norfolk police officers
Yes, quite recently, in fact – and for similar reasons.
In September, villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, in Oxfordshire voted to become independent of the UK.
Like in Barnham, it was held in protest against plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.
On that occasion, out of 312 votes cast, 285 people voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.
Piddington locals voted to become an independent state in a referendum earlier this year
Voting is taking place at Barnham Village Hall from 10:00 GMT to 16:00, before counting gets underway and the result is announced between 17:00 and 18:00.
The council cannot be completely sure how many people will be eligible to vote, due to being unable to use the electoral register, but believes up to 500 could take part.
In the interests of accessibility, some sealed votes will be collected by the council, which has also taken note of those who require help getting to the polling station.
An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.
The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.
About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites.
The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.
More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.
A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.
Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.
The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.
It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.
In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.
As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.
Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear.
Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.
About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.
The Home Office said it was "listening carefully to the concerns" of residents and that no decision had yet been taken.
A spokesperson said: "The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.
"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.
"We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised."
