items.title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
paragraphs: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

items.title: In a Sydney gallery, Philippe Parreno’s art is powered by a desert 17,000km away
paragraphs: I’m standing in a massive white-cube space, staring at a perplexing assortment of objects. There are several expensive looking lamps; a massive industrial fan; a couple of speakers; marquee-style lights; a glowing assemblage of power adapters. At the back of the gallery, a silvery light slides up and down a pole. The bulbs are flickering erratically, and there’s a low hum of machine noise, overlaid with bird song and distant barking.
As an installation, taken by itself, it’s deceptively underwhelming – a spectacle without a story.

This will be visitors’ first encounter with the Museum of Contemporary Art’s summer blockbuster exhibition, Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons, named for the five lunar cycles of the show’s duration. It’s the first major Australian exhibition by the acclaimed French contemporary artist, renowned for taking over museums and galleries – including Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall and the Palais de Tokyo in Paris – with discombobulating and delightful kinetic arrangements of objects, screen works, sound and lighting.
Parreno’s medium of choice is the exhibition itself; he creates holistic, unpredictable environments for the visitor to navigate.
At the MCA, Parreno has created a series of connected environments across the museum’s three levels, featuring works made over his four-decade career.

Upstairs, there’s an orange-carpeted gallery populated by floating, helium-filled, fish-shaped balloons in citrus tones, in which a grand piano plays an enigmatic score. On another floor, a giant luminescent cuttlefish gazes out impassively from a screen, its fins and arms gently undulating, as ambient electronic noise emanates from large swiveling speaker banks.
These spaces feel like haunted houses; machines operated by ghosts or powered by supernatural energy.

In fact, they’re powered by nature: real-time data – including wind speed, humidity and temperature – captured on sensors on an abandoned almond farm in the Tabernas desert in south-eastern Spain, a region best known internationally as the backdrop to spaghetti westerns such as The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and Once Upon a Time in the West.
Data from the farm has been reconfigured into an algorithm that influences the sound, air flow and lighting 17,000km away in Sydney. The land is improvising a score, and the museum is playing it.

In a darkened gallery on the museum’s third floor, a massive screen is showing an 11-hour film composed of footage shot on the abandoned almond farm. Visitors can, if they choose, sit and watch a night pass under the Spanish moon.

Live sound from this terrain is also played in the gallery, making for an uncanny mix: during my visit, nocturnal insect noises from Spain are punctuated by the toot of an ocean liner docked outside in Sydney Harbour.

“What I normally try to do for exhibition is to try to create sort of a milieu, or an ecosystem, where things are responding to each other,” says Parreno, whose family migrated from the same region of Spain hundreds of years ago, to Algeria, where he was born.
Backstory is important for Parreno’s art: without it, his ecosystems risk seeming frustratingly opaque or worse, inane.

Some parts of the MCA exhibition stand alone, without narrative, thanks to their aesthetic or mise en scene. Some are more tenuous: a white-walled area in which a layer of helium filled speech-bubble balloons covers the ceiling, while a series of coloured lights flash. When you learn the lighting pattern is a morse code translation of a mystical adventure by French writer René Daumal, it suddenly feels more substantial.

Parreno’s most famous artwork, his 2016 takeover of the Tate’s Turbine Hall, delighted some and frustrated others. But his backstory, involving a jar of yeast in a hidden lab whose biodata was influencing the whole thing, was almost irresistibly intriguing.
“Lots of the things I do require people to endorse a fiction,” Parreno commented at the time.

His interest in fiction is more than a gimmick, it’s deeply philosophical, and 5 Moons is underpinned by ideas of how our perceptions of a thing change it; how the way we imagine land, by knock on effect, influences and transforms it.

When Parreno showed an earlier iteration of the 5 Moons film at Munich’s Haus der Kunst in 2024, he said the work was designed to feel as if the land was “speaking to you”. “With the ways climate change is changing the world, how do we address the landscape? Are we going to keep transforming it? Or is it maybe the other way around – that the land is looking at us.”
When he started out making exhibitions in the late 80s and 90s, Parreno had revolutionary ideals. “You want to change the world. You want to produce a new reality,” he tells me.

And now? “I want to create that thing that you don’t see much [these days],” he says. “In the system we live in, you are always obliged to respond to a signal. Here you are not. You just float with your own attention, and you spend the time you want.”
Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons is on at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney, until 26 April 2027

items.title: 'I was exhausted': Two days in the shoes of a tradwife
paragraphs: Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.
As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.

The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.

While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.

For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife.
On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life.
"I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.
During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.
She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress.

"What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."
The tradwife phenomenon has been popularised on social media which has been a major driving force in its expansion.
Some US creators have millions of followers - Hannah Neeleman, widely seen as one of the world's leading tradwife influencers, has 10.3 million users following her Instagram account, Ballerina Farm.

However, another popular American influencer, Nara Smith, has rejected the label. Smith married young, has four children and her content centres on cooking food (or even making toothpaste) from scratch, but insists she's no tradwife.

"They kind of used me as the poster child of the tradwife movement, which was very bizarre to me," Smith said on the Call Her Daddy podcast. "Sure, do I love cooking... but that's a passion of mine, it's a hobby - it's not something that I need to be doing."

The tradwife trend has also made its way into popular culture, with author Caro Claire Burke's satirical novel Yesteryear selling more than 1.4 million copies and Hollywood actress Anne Hathaway has signed up to produce and star in a film adaptation.

Jay tells BBC News she saw how much work Molly did which had "parallels" with her upbringing in a conservative Muslim family, which included her entering an arranged marriage when she was 19. She and her husband divorced about five years later.

"I've helped raise my siblings, I know my way around a kitchen, I can cook, I tutored my siblings," Jay said. "Other than the chicken coop, it's not unfamiliar territory. But I think doing it for two days - I know this sounds ridiculous... it's just the relentless pace of her life."
While Molly manages the house, her husband Aaron is a full-time theologian who shares his views on religion and anti-feminism on social media.

When speaking to Jay, Aaron explained the reason the household work was down to his wife: "Molly's obviously omni-competent and brilliant but submission is still really hard," he says, "and when I say something that Molly disagrees with, that's when the submission really matters."
While Molly says her social media does not make money, some tradwives do look to turn a profit through their posts.
West Sussex couple Megan and Joseph Landreth-Smith have three children and have an Instagram account with nearly 6,000 followers.

Megan often gets brand deals to share products on her Instagram, which she says helps with some extra income and "feels like a really natural fit" around what they are doing already - producing content while being with their children.
Just like many influencers, trolls can be a problem, but they also help to bring in some money.

With her husband Zion, Yorkshire-based life coach Laura Zachary promotes a course called the Academy of Biblical Wifery, based on their born-again Christian beliefs, to more than 32,000 Instagram followers.
"The more disagreement on a comments section, the more people that come to it and the more you get paid".
The "appeal" which Jay identifies goes much broader - a report published by King's College London, external found 79% of women surveyed were drawn to the relaxed, calm lifestyle it portrays.
But its co-author, Prof Heejung Chung, who specialises in researching the tradwife phenomenon, said that it can be the tip of a political change.

The content might begin with "nice dresses", said Chung, but can "draw them towards more extremist, far-right, or nationalist ideologies, which ultimately seek to curtail women's autonomy and reinforce patriarchal authority".
However, her report concludes most young women and men surveyed showed "largely progressive views on gender roles".
For those who liked the content, it was down to its "lifestyle imagery", rather than "the traditional gender division of labour or power".
But this does not mean the tradwife movement poses no risk to gender equality, the report says, and its "growing popularity... should not be dismissed or trivialised".

items.title: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
paragraphs: The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.
Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.
“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.
But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.
McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.
“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.
Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.
“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.
“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”
On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.
Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.
The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.
Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

items.title: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember them
paragraphs: Phoebe Bridgers' concerts have inspired some fans to explore their artistic talent
Phoebe Bridgers has drawn in fans over the years with her raw, vulnerable lyrics and indie sound that can make even the messiest emotions feel less lonely.
The US artist's third album Lost Weekend, released this summer after a six-year wait, delves into falling in and out of love, grappling with change and the confusing feelings that come with grief.
On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy - a move that's had an unexpected side effect.
Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.
Massive Bridgers fan Olivia MacDonald, from Massachusetts, attended the singer's show in Boston last month.
She was initially "shocked" by the no-phone rule, as employed by artists including Bob Dylan and Jack White, but became a convert.
Without the distraction of phones, she says, fans chatted, danced and sang along with each other.
"Once I got to the concert, I realised this is such a unique way to connect and bring everybody together," she says.
Fans have used a range of mediums to recreate moments from The Lost Tour
MacDonald, a pen and ink artist, brought her sketchbook along to the show after spotting fellow fans' interpretations on social media.
She relived the gig by drawing standout moments such as Bridgers' dripping, electric blue eye make-up and her guitar, originally owned by the late American musician Elliott Smith.
"Everybody takes away something different," says 28-year-old MacDonald.
"That's the beauty of it, that everybody can have a different interpretation."
Sharing her designs on social media helped her connect with other fans, who reached out to discuss their experiences of the show.
"I feel like with photos or videos, you capture a moment in time, and with drawings, you really capture a feeling and people can connect to that feeling," she says.
Fan Olivia MacDonald has been converted by the no-phone rule
Bridgers has navigated an emotional whirlwind since she was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged and critically acclaimed album Punisher in 2020.
The 32-year-old Californian has toured and won three Grammys with supergroup Boygenius, lived out a high-profile romance and breakup with Irish actor Paul Mescal, and lost her dad in 2023.
Fans believe she explores some of these experiences in her latest album.
MacDonald says Bridgers explained to the Boston crowd that the no-phone rule would allow her to talk openly with her audience like friends, without the worry of those moments ending up online.
Some fans expressed worries the policy could exclude people with disabilities or those who might need to contact someone in an emergency.
MacDonald says she shared the reservations, but points out fans were able to keep their phones on them and access the sealed pouches they were stored in at special designated areas inside the venue.
Phoebe Bridgers was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged album Punisher in 2020

Fan Anna Meyer, who attended the New York show, agrees the device-free aspect made the show a better experience for artist and audience, and allowed the special lighting effects to be fully appreciated without being distorted by phone lights.
The graphic designer, 35, chose to capture this element afterwards - focusing on a poignant moment when a kneeling Bridgers played piano in the glow of a spotlight.
"It was so cathartic to feel so inspired," she says.
"And I do wonder, if I did have my phone, would I have felt this need to sit down and immediately draw something from the show?"
Meyer feels the trend is particularly special as it's put a focus on techniques, such as pen and paper, in an age when traditional art feels under threat.
"We're now in an era of AI where they want us to believe if you want to create something visual, you have to use a computer and AI programme," she says.
"We all have the ability to create, and our own creations that come from our own mind and hand are far better than anything that a computer can create.
"And sometimes even far better than anything that a camera can capture."
Phoebe Bridgers fan Anna Meyer's time-lapse of her artwork inspired by the singer's gig had a positive response online
Followers of the new trend argue it also helps to guard against gig spoilers, where big moments go viral on social media before crowds get to see them in-person.
Lillie Collins, a fan from Michigan, feels artwork offers "a little teaser" rather than giving everything away.
The 20-year-old painted her own interpretation after seeing Bridgers' show in Detroit and her videos revealing the piece blew up on TikTok.
She says the wave of positive responses was "very exciting" as she'd never had that reaction before, and it's now made her consider that creating art could be a successful career route.
Bridgers herself appears to approve too, as her team has shared several posts praising the artworks, external.
MacDonald and Meyer were among those who got shout-outs on the official Lost Tour Instagram page, as was Collins, who says the idea Bridgers may have seen her artwork had her "screaming".
"I really appreciate how she was able to bring this level of creativity and humanity into her performances," she says.
Lillie Collins got a shout-out on the official Lost Tour Instagram page
Bridgers will kick off her UK run of shows at Manchester's Co-op Live on Thursday, followed by dates in Glasgow, Birmingham and London.
Ayanoh Nakamoto was one of the fans who attended a special intimate show at Union Chapel, London, where Bridgers tested the no-phone policy.
She will be back in the crowd for the first London show next month, and says the "excitement has built up so much because we haven't been able to see what is really happening in the US right now".
"It's just so cool to have an experience where it feels like it isn't spoilt for you," she says.
Despite Nakamoto running a TikTok page where she shares her concert video content, she admits it feels liberating to put her phone away and be in the moment.
She jokes she doesn't have an "artistic bone" in her body, but thinks this might be her chance to try her hand at drawing, even if it is a stick-figure sketch.
"I wonder if this is going to be a stepping stone for artists to maybe have this at more concerts and just feel that connection back to the audience in the future."
Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

items.title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
paragraphs: Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

items.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?
paragraphs: After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?
What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.

He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they also go for an equally big name for a "Bond girl", or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.
Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".
Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."
And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?
No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya, whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.
The duo have already shared three films together this year, and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.
Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".
But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.
Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".
Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)
Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said, external.
Other names that have been floated include Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley, Marisa Abela, Emily Blunt, Lily James, Chase Infiniti, Inde Navarrette, Simone Ashley, Deva Cassel and Ambika Mod.
And it could easily be someone totally different. Producers have previously chosen a Bond girl who isn't particularly famous yet - or is on the cusp of stardom.
But then there’s the wider question of whether the whole idea of a “Bond girl” is now somewhat outdated.
Historically, the character had little agency and existed primarily as Bond's romantic interest - and the term "girl" itself is also criticised for infantilising women.

Monica Bellucci rejected the label. She told the Guardian, external ahead of her appearance in Sceptre in 2015: "I can't say I'm a Bond girl because I'm too mature to be a Bond girl. I say Bond lady; Bond woman."
The way the films have treated Bond girls "hasn't always aged well", says Rose.
Some scenes from 1960s Bond films are "basically rape", and "wouldn't fly today", said No Time To Die director Cary Fukunaga in 2021, external - referring to Thunderball and Goldfinger.
In reality, we have come a long way since then.
Over the years, producers have taken steps to usher the franchise into the modern era.
These days, the women of Bond are now much more likely to be sharp, capable equals to 007 - and what's defined as "attractive" has also evolved.
Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).
We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.
Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.
"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".
Many people say, however, there is still further to go.
Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."
"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," says Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”
Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.
“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and film-maker.
"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."
More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.
“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”
None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.
"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.
But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.

“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.
Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.
But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."

There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit".
"Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

items.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
paragraphs: A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."
Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.
According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.
They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."
To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.
For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.
Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.
After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.
"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"
Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.
Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.
She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.
"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.
"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"
Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.
But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

items.title: Price beats Kotaskova to become undisputed champion
paragraphs: Price won every round from every judge in front of a partisan Cardiff crowd, producing an unrelenting pace that punished her opponent at every opportunity.
Although Price could not force a stoppage, there was never any doubt she had done enough against an opponent full of stamina and stubbornness.
Kotaskova, beaten only once, but never stopped in her career, showed real heart but had no answer to Price's expertise.
The Tokyo gold medal winner could celebrate even before the final bell sounded, climbing the corner ropes and into the record books.
It was lapped up by a sell-out Utilita Arena crowd who excitedly acknowledged the achievement and the moment.
Wales has produced 14 world champions, some of them genuine greats.
They include, of course, Joe Calzaghe who so often graced this venue with successful defence after successful defence of his super-middleweight crown.
He never reached undisputed status, though he was able to cross the capital city to go from arena to stadium champion.

That is the next challenge for Price, claiming before she left the ring that more is to come while talk immediately turned to five-weight world champion Claressa Shields as a stadium fight next summer.
That is for the future, but this was a night for history - with the calibre of some of the former boxers in the stands a nod to that.
Champions know champions. Five Welsh world title winners were in the capital to watch their compatriot do something never been done before.
From Cinderella Man Steve Robinson and Barry Jones, to the more recent Joe Cordina, who may still be eyeing a stadium return of his own in the coming weeks.
All have been proud to fly the flag, but perhaps none have worn it quite as much on their sleeve - or shorts - as Price has done.
Here, entering to the strains of a Welsh male voice choir, the atmosphere moved from Friday night in a city centre to full-blooded patriotism.
The anthem stirred so much Kotaskova couldn't help but raise an eyebrow before stepping out of her corner.
From then, she had no time to savour the moment let alone consider become an opportunity the Czech Republic's first world champion.
She felt flurries of punches from the first moments and struggled with the unrelenting pace set by the champion.
Steely-eyed, Price refused to allow a breath and, while Kotaskova continued to try and come onto the front foot, she was met by angry, but calculated attacks.
Kotaskova's problems only increased when she was cut in the fifth round, the hooks from the home fighter providing no let up.
At one point in the seventh, Kotaskova took a shot so fierce she almost turned her back to say no more, but still she came and still Price went hunting with hooks.
She could not find the decisive blow, finally letting the tempo slip, and even enjoying the final seconds as she accepted she had done more than enough to win and win a place in boxing history.
Price was not the only Welsh winner on the night as Rhys Edwards secured a significant victory over Lee McGregor, taking an unanimous decision to claim the WBA Continental featherweight championship.
McGregor, 29, had stepped back down to featherweight after two defeats in his last three bouts and had made it clear he knew his chances of returning to world-challenging level was on the line.
His determination to keep coming forward showed what it meant, soaking up several clean shots, but Edwards proved too quick and too sharp.
The 26-year-old from Penygraig also had something to prove after a disappointing draw with Gully Powar last time out.

Then he faded in the latter round, but here Edwards managed to take McGregor's punches and maintain his own pace. It ensured what is perhaps the biggest win of his career, and to leave McGregor contemplating his options.

Elsewhere on the undercard, Willy Gilheaney's unbeaten record was taken away by the experience of Argentinean Alberto Igancio Palmetta, the former Olympic boxer showing plenty of know-how to overcome the Swansea fighter's guts and early control to take an unanimous points win.

Earlier in the night, Doncaster's Jake Goodwin took the decision in a game middleweight bout with Liverpool fighter Sean Arkwright. Goodwin – who had former world featherweight champion Josh Warrington in his corner – had only accepted the fight on two weeks' notice, accepting before he was even granted time off work.
And there were wins for Welsh fighters Brandon Scott and Kane Shepherd, while Cardigan's Josh Mellor and Newport's Lewis Howells fought to a draw.

items.title: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
paragraphs: A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.
It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."
Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.
Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.
One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.
"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."
In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.
"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.
"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.
Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.
There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.
"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."
The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.
As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."
These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.
When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.
"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.
One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.
But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.
The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".
Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."
Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."

In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."

Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.
"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.
But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.
Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".
The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.
Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.
One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".
"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.
Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.
"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.
"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.
"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."
Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.
Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.
"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling. "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."
Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."
She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."
With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

items.title: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation
paragraphs: The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.
At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas. Minns has rejected the idea the legislation goes around the high court decision.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.
“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”
She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.
“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.
The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.
She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.
The Law Society of NSW said on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

items.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
paragraphs: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

items.title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
paragraphs: Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.

Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.

Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

items.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
paragraphs: Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.
The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.
The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.
She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”
The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”
He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”
Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”
Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.
Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

items.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
paragraphs: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption

NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market.
