Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

items.title: Trump, Takaichi discuss Indo-Pacific security as Japanese leader reaffirms Taiwan policy
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original Mandarin article.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says she spoke to President Donald Trump on Thursday, discussing regional and international issues following Trump's meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Speaking to the press afterward, Takaichi said the two leaders also discussed the Indo-Pacific and the war in Ukraine during the roughly 20-minute call. “I will further elevate Japan’s relationship with the United States to a higher level,” Takaichi told reporters.

But Takaichi acknowledged differences with Washington over the International Criminal Court, which the U.S., China and Russia criticized in a joint declaration in Shenzhen. She said Japan has consistently supported the court and that Trump is aware of Japan’s position.
Earlier Thursday in Shenzhen, Takaichi told reporters there was “absolutely no change” in Japan’s position on Taiwan, as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communique.
Takaichi added that Japan would continue close communication with Washington to strengthen the bilateral alliance and consult on a range of international issues.
VOA reached out to the White House for comment on the call but didn't receive a response at the time of publication.

Yu-Hua Chen, an associate professor in the Global Studies Program at Akita International University (AIU) in Japan, told VOA that U.S.-Japan relations under Takaichi have been particularly close. Tokyo has been using multiple institutional channels to maintain the relationship, with post-summit phone calls serving as one example.
Trump also spoke with Takaichi by phone after meeting Xi in Beijing in May.

Akita International University's Chen said Takaichi's latest remarks were considerably more moderate than her earlier comments in November 2025. This time, she returned to Japan's traditional approach of strategic ambiguity on Taiwan, he added.
"Takaichi's aim was probably to prevent tensions between Japan and China from escalating further," Chen said.

In November 2025, Takaichi told parliament that the use of military force by China on Taiwan, such as a naval blockade, would likely constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that would force Japan to respond.

Her remarks triggered strong protests from Beijing and contributed to a prolonged deterioration in bilateral relations. China subsequently increased pressure on Japan through measures including restrictions on exports to Tokyo, warnings against travel to Japan and tighter controls on strategic materials such as rare earths.

Takaichi's appearance at the APEC summit also underscored the difficult state of Japan-China relations. According to Japan's Kyodo News, Xi and Takaichi had a brief encounter at the summit's opening ceremony. Takaichi approached Xi, but he did not respond.

China also sent retired former ambassador to Greece, Zhang Qiyue, to receive Takaichi at the airport, rather than having a senior leader greet her. The reception contrasted with Xi's personal welcome for Trump and senior Communist Party official Cai Qi's reception of Putin.
Takaichi's visit had been viewed in Japan as an opportunity to restart high-level dialogue with Beijing. However, Xi did not hold any formal meetings with her.
Chen said the Japanese government had likely anticipated the relatively cool reception, but that Takaichi chose to attend the summit, nonetheless.

"This shows that Takaichi's approach to foreign policy is considerably more flexible than many observers expected," Chen said. "It also shows that Takaichi as prime minister can be very different from Takaichi as a member of parliament."

Takaichi has nevertheless reiterated her willingness to maintain communication with Beijing, saying before returning to Japan that she was not concerned that Trump's meetings with the Chinese and Russian leaders would undermine Japanese interests.

items.title: Iran’s Supreme Court Upholds Death Sentences of two protesters
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Human rights sources this week reported that the death sentences of Navid Najjaran and Milad Armoon had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court, and that the cases of the two young protesters had been referred to the sentence enforcement branch.

The case dates to the 2022 nationwide protests, when Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij militia, was killed in Tehran’s Ekbatan neighborhood. A criminal court first sentenced Armoon, Najjaran and four other defendants to death for murder, but the Supreme Court overturned those sentences. In a retrial, Armoon was sentenced to prison and ordered to pay blood money, while Najjaran was acquitted for lack of evidence.

Earlier this year, Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court, presided over by Abolghassem Salavati, sentenced Armoon and Najjaran, along with two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, to death on a separate charge of “moharebeh,” or “enmity against God.”
Rights groups say the convictions relied on forced confessions.

The Dadban Legal Training Center reported Thursday that the Supreme Court had upheld the death sentences of Armoon and Najjaran, and that their cases had been sent for enforcement. Citing an informed source, Dadban said the court overturned the death sentences of Imani and Hosseini and sent their cases to another branch of the Revolutionary Court for retrial.
The United States sanctioned Salavati in 2019 for imposing harsh sentences, including death sentences, on political prisoners and peaceful protesters.

The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights also reported that Shamim Ettehadi, a Baha’i resident of Yazd, was arrested after intelligence agents raided his parents’ home and searched the property. He was taken to an undisclosed location.

The Baha’i faith is Iran’s largest non-Muslim religious minority, with an estimated 300,000 followers, but it is not recognized under the Islamic Republic’s constitution, and its members have faced arrests, property seizures and bans on higher education since the 1979 revolution.

According to Hengaw, government forces searched the home during the raid and confiscated several books and other items related to the Baha’i faith, along with electronic devices belonging to family members. Ettehadi had previously faced arrest and judicial action because of his religious beliefs and related activities. Authorities have not disclosed the reason for his arrest or his whereabouts.

The U.S. State Department has also documented the persecution of Baha’is in Iran, reporting that government forces have raided their homes, arrested them, and seized their personal belongings and electronic devices. The department says Baha’is face charges such as “propaganda against the state,” national security offenses, imprisonment, and other government-imposed restrictions because of their religious beliefs and activities.

items.title: Shevchenko lying about drugs test claims - Mudryk
paragraphs: Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.
Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.
In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".
Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.
"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk.

"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong."
Mudryk also said the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.
BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

items.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
paragraphs: Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

items.title: MLK's handwritten draft of iconic speech on display for the first time
paragraphs: ATLANTA, GA - THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 2026 - Exterior of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights where King's draft of the speech is displayed. Lynsey Weatherspoon for NPR hide caption

ATLANTA – The only known draft of one of the most famous speeches in American history is on public display for the first time: The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s remarks at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963. And it's written in his own hand.

"Just for a few days we have this incredible artifact here, which is Doctor King's handwritten, final draft of what became known as the 'I Have a Dream' speech," said Jill Savitt, CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, King's hometown.
"Nothing has given me chills like this handwritten document, where you see him crafting one of the most iconic speeches in U.S. history."
It's written in cursive, blue ink on yellow legal paper. King scratched through entire sections and reworked them, or changed a particular word or phrase.
"You see him on the page wrestling with the words," Savitt said. "He's struggling with: How do you make this case to America that we're not living up to our own ideals?"

The seven-page document, which will be on exhibit here through Sunday, is enclosed in a glass case in a gallery dedicated to the March on Washington. Above the display, footage plays of speeches and the crowd of 250,000 gathered on the National Mall on Aug. 28, 1963.
Savitt said King originally titled the speech "Normalcy Never Again." Notably, the manuscript does not include what became the most famous lines from that day, "I Have a Dream."
"Doctor King improvised that," she said. "The preacher in him connected with a crowd in a particular way. And when you watch footage, you can almost see this electric charge go through him."
His rousing words that day on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial included:
"I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream today."
Savitt says King sent the draft to be typed up in the pre-dawn hours from the Willard Hotel in Washington, DC, on the day he was to deliver it.

The handwritten copy of King's speech was discovered by Xernona Clayton, an Atlanta civil rights leader who worked closely with King and his wife, Coretta Scott King. Her late husband, Edward Clayton, was one of King's speechwriters.
Now 96, she said in an interview with NPR Thursday she found the papers tucked in a manilla envelope while cleaning out his old desk.

"I knew Doctor King's handwriting very well, and I said, 'Oh, this can't be the speech,'" she recalled. "Then when I started reading it, I knew that it was and then I got scared. Like, what do I do now?"
That was in the late 1990s, and she tucked it back into the desk. She rediscovered it a couple years ago, and it took her back to 1963.
"As I went through the speech, I was reading his words and hearing them in my head," she said. "Martin Luther King spoke to the world through that speech."

She decided it was time to share the document with the world. Clayton's charitable trust is offering it for auction through Christie's in New York in January, where the auction house says bids could top $10 million. Prior to that, the manuscript also will be on display in Chicago.
Clayton said she wanted it available to the public with the hope that people will find inspiration in King's words today.

"He used to tell me all the time how much he hated that we as a people can't live together," she recalled. "That was his preachment. All of the time he was preoccupied with what can we do to get people to love each other."
For former Atlanta Mayor Shirley Franklin, who visited the center last week, seeing the document was personal.
"Do you see me?" she asked, pointing to a photograph on display of the crowd at the March on Washington. "I'm sitting right there by the reflecting pool."
Franklin was Atlanta's mayor from 2002-2010, the first Black woman elected to lead a city in the Deep South.
"It's amazing that 60 years later this document has survived," she said.
Looking at King's writings, Franklin said she was struck by how thoughtful he was about each and every word.
"As brilliant as he was, as clear as he was about what he was trying to accomplish, it required enhancement and refinement," she said. "He was making this speech as good as it could be."
Yet even with all the reviewing and refining, what stuck from that speech never made it on the paper.
"What we remember is the part that came from his heart," Franklin said. "Gives me the chills."
Franklin is a living witness to the change wrought by the work of King and others civil rights pioneers, but she said seeing the speech is a reminder that the work is ongoing.
"Sixty years later, we've made some progress," she said. "Much of what he says is relevant today, because we've not really fulfilled the full promise of a free and a loving community."
Franklin helped found the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta. She said it's fitting such a foundational document got its public debut here.
"This is one of my favorite rooms," she said, as the famous ending of King's speech played on the screen overhead:
"In the words of the old Negro spiritual, 'Free at last, free at last. Thank God almighty we are free at last.'"

items.title: Iraqis cautiously optimistic as government forces enter Iran-backed militia stronghold
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Iraqis expressed cautious optimism Friday after government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar for the first time in 12 years. There were no reported clashes.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi described the entry as a return to state control over a strategic town long dominated by an Iran-backed militia.

The deployment, carried out under al-Zaidi’s direct supervision, followed days of tension and threats of confrontation with Kataib Hezbollah, the powerful militia that has controlled the area since 2014.
The operation involved federal police, two brigades of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), energy police and counterterrorism units.
For some residents, the peaceful deployment offered hope that years of insecurity and displacement might finally be coming to an end.

“So far, everything is good. The situation is calm,” resident Wissam Daghiri told VOA. “The security forces have arrived; they understand the situation and have adapted to it. Our relationship is good. There is no sound of gunfire, thank God, and that is exactly what we want.”
Daghiri said residents also hoped the operation would pave the way for displaced families to return to their homes and communities.
Another resident, Mazen Mahmoud, welcomed the security forces' arrival.

“We thank our security forces. They have been very cooperative and friendly with us, and there have been no disagreements between us,” Mahmoud told VOA. “We hope, God willing, that peace will return.”
Iraqi officials portrayed the deployment as a significant step toward restoring government authority over territory controlled by armed groups operating outside the state's effective command.

“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi army proves that it is the protector of the country and its security,” said Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for Iraq's commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
He described the operation as an ongoing replacement and redeployment of personnel, adding that a new phase focused on public services would follow.
In a video statement after the deployment, al-Zaidi declared that “no force should remain outside the state.”
Jurf al-Sakhar, southwest of Baghdad, has been under the control of Kataib Hezbollah since Iraqi forces and allied militias recaptured the area from Islamic State militants in 2014.
Its status has become a test of Baghdad's ability to assert authority over powerful Iran-aligned armed factions, some of which operate within Iraq's official security structures.

The government has also been investigating allegations of illegal oil trafficking throughout the area. Iraqi officials have reported identifying suspected oil-smuggling operations using satellite imagery, although the full extent of the alleged activities remains unclear.

Despite the peaceful entry of government forces, some observers question whether the arrangement represents a genuine transfer of authority or merely a reorganization of armed factions under official command structures.
The agreement reportedly involved Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, and an influential figure within the PMF.

Critics fear that militia-linked networks could retain influence through PMF units or their connections within the federal police, allowing the same armed groups to maintain effective control under a different administrative arrangement.
The United States has also called on Baghdad to confront Iran-aligned militias.

“The United States expects Prime Minister Al-Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable for engaging in violent and destabilizing activities throughout Iraq and the entire region,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA earlier this week.
The spokesperson accused the militias of undermining Iraq's sovereignty, weakening its economy and diverting Iraqi resources through corruption for their own benefit and that of Tehran.
Beyond the immediate security arrangements, the future of Jurf al-Sakhar's displaced population remains a major unresolved issue.

Thousands of residents have been unable to return since 2014. Estimates of the displaced population vary, with some local accounts citing 120,000 people and other assessments placing the figure substantially higher.
Elizabeth Tsurkov, a researcher on Iraqi affairs who was abducted by Kataib Hezbollah in 2023, told VOA that Jurf al-Sakhar's problems extend far beyond allegations of oil smuggling.
She pointed to allegations of sectarian targeting, enforced disappearances and other serious human rights violations against its Sunni population by the Shiite militia.

Tsurkov called for genuine government control, investigations into suspected mass graves and weapons-storage facilities, and the return of displaced residents, whose number she estimated at between 120,000 and 180,000.

items.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
paragraphs: The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.
The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.

The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.
Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

items.title: Dmitri Kasterine obituary
paragraphs: In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.”

Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance.

These lessons supplemented his photographic craft, honed since the beginning of the 1960s, creating a style that led to Kasterine, who has died aged 94, becoming one of the most significant portrait photographers of the 70s and 80s. He photographed James Baldwin, Michael Caine, Patricia Highsmith, Martin and Kingsley Amis, Tom Stoppard and Queen Elizabeth II for Harpers & Queen, Vogue, the BBC’s Radio Times and the Daily Telegraph magazine.

In his work, Kasterine wanted to “avoid the conventional” and prevent the sitter from “putting on a polite face”. He utilised his gentlemanly charm and elegance, putting the subject at ease before turning away, pretending to adjust his equipment, ignoring the sitter – attempting to catch them off guard, thus revealing something of themselves. This approach unveiled vulnerability in Dirk Bogarde, discomfort in Samuel Beckett and boredom in Muriel Spark.

In an interview with the reporter Bradley Towle, Kasterine said: “I look for something that gives me a shock. I look for something that has unusual elements. It could be what they’re wearing; it could be the background. It could be just an expression. I don’t really look for it, it comes to me.”

As well as his acclaimed portraits of the literati, he took great pride in a personal project undertaken between 1996 and 2018 in his adopted home of New York state. He had become fascinated with the city of Newburgh on the Hudson River, which, from being awarded the title of All American City by Look magazine in 1952, had become, by the 1990s, blighted by recession, corruption and racism. He set about to capture the decaying splendour of the city and, more importantly, the dignity of the overlooked, predominantly Black community that called it home.

In the introduction to his 2012 book, Newburgh: Portrait of a City, Kasterine wrote: “This is a record of uncelebrated and ignored people … But in the ruins of the buildings and in the faces of the people I see warmth and beauty, and in some of the faces a determination to change things.” Three years later, Kasterine filmed a documentary, Newburgh: Beauty and Tragedy. The city embraced his work, and 44 of his Newburgh portraits were mounted on the exterior of its Ritz theatre, from 2012 to 2026.
His photographs are held by the Royal Collection Trust and the National Portrait Gallery in London, and the Smithsonian Institution’s National Portrait Gallery in Washington DC.

Dmitri’s father, Nicolas Kasterine, had served in the Russian Imperial Guard and was the aide-de-camp to the Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich, who was involved in the assassination of Grigori Rasputin. Having fought the Bolsheviks in the 1917 revolution, Nicolas escaped Russia via Finland, bringing with him a large, uncut diamond, which, when in London, he sold to buy a suit and a sports car. There, Nicolas married Katherine White, the daughter of an insurance broker, and the young couple socialised with other Russian émigrés in Paris, Monte Carlo (where Dmitri’s elder sister, Irina, was born), and London.

The young family then settled in the village of Kemsing, near Sevenoaks, Kent, where Dmitri was born, named after his godfather, the grand duke. Kasterine’s parents divorced in 1935, and Katherine took her two children to live outside the village of Westerham, also in Kent. Nicolas died in a car crash the following year.

The second world war was a frightening experience for the sensitive Dmitri. Being close to Biggin Hill aerodrome, Westerham was frequently bombed by the Luftwaffe, and on his eighth birthday, bombs fell so close that the house was badly damaged.

When the air raids stopped, Katherine put up a bird table outside the kitchen window. Dmitri wanted to photograph the birds, so his mother bought him a camera. He built a dark room and excitedly developed the film. When he saw that the birds were pinpricks in the frame, he burst into tears. Undeterred, he moved on to cows in the fields, with excellent results.

After the war, Dmitri was sent to board at Radley college in Oxfordshire, where he remained until 1950. It was while at school that he learned of his mother’s death in a riding accident in 1948. He was just 15.

After leaving Radley and working briefly as a wine merchant and then for Lloyd’s of London, Kasterine, who had inherited a love of fast cars from his father, took up motor racing. In 1956, he suffered a life-threatening injury when the Lotus-Bristol racing car he was driving at the Aintree International meeting overturned and crashed through the safety barrier. A friend visited while he was recovering in hospital and suggested he take up flying. He did, and for a while he worked as a commercial pilot flying to Australia.
On a stopover in Karachi, Kasterine photographed the breaking-in of a young thoroughbred. Pleased with the result, and frightened of flying, Kasterine decided to take up photography professionally.

In London from 1961, Kasterine shared a studio with the photographer Michael Wallis, who mentored both Kasterine and their dark-room assistant, Patrick Lichfield. Dmitri hustled for work from magazines and sought out public figures to request a sitting, and his career took off.

In 1981 his first book, England and the English, was published. This gentle collection of portraits, daily life and landscapes was a swansong to the bucolic ideal of his native land. He needed a new challenge.

He had been to the US once, to photograph Mick Jagger in Los Angeles in 1975, and had visited New York City on the way home. He liked it, and moved there in 1984. There, he shot celebrated portraits of art-world luminaries such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Roy Lichtenstein and Cindy Sherman, and commissions for the Sunday New York Times.

In his later years Kasterine moved to Garrison, in the wilds of New York state, with his second wife, Caroline (nee Cristofalo), whom he had married in 1988. There he took pictures of farmers and people who loved horses, and in 2021 he published a collection of his work, Who How When Where. After seven decades taking photographs, he was, he told Towle, still “… always on the lookout … It’s very difficult to explain exactly why and wherefore I take a picture, but it’s a silence; it’s a tap on the shoulder.”

He is survived by Caroline and their son, Nicholas; his children, Alexander and Cathy, from his 1963 marriage to Elizabeth Dickson, which ended in divorce, a daughter, Lucie, from a relationship with Frances Pemberton, and six grandchildren.

items.title: We’ve tried everything to get off our phones. These 11 things work (and make great gifts)
paragraphs: Logging off is en vogue. From touting analog bags to playing vinyl records, many of us are tired of living life behind a screen.

So 2026 may be the ideal year to gift some low-tech entertainment instead of the newest iPhone. These days, we’re all trying to connect with the “real world” more, and the latest string of tech outages has been a good nudge to buy stuff that won’t glitch.
We’ve experimented with screen alternatives such as MP3 players and “dating cards” throughout the year, sharing the ups – and some downs – in our series Do not disturb.
Here are 11 picks that would make perfect gifts, from the beautiful (displayable board games) to the practical (daily planners).

Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for obsessively vetted gift ideas, or get inspired by our full array of guides, including a gift guide for the person who has everything and a guide to cozy gifts.

If someone in your life always looks for the worst, brighten up their spirits with Papier’s gratitude cards. I recently tried them with my friends over Chinese food in Brooklyn, delighting in questions including, “What are you proud of quietly?” and “Who made you feel seen recently?”. They also make a great hosting gift that (gently) forces your guests to get off their phones.

Stationery brand No Particular Order’s guided journal is the ideal companion for self-discovery. It has 200 journal prompts for your recipient to fill out, including “Who’s in your circle?” and “Who or what do you hope to be in a future life?”. I used this the summer after finishing my undergraduate degree to stave off feelings of existential dread.

Last winter, I tried No Particular Order’s dating app alternative, acquaintance cards. Inspired by Victorian-era calling cards, you fill out your information and hand it to someone who catches your eye. These cards helped me get someone’s phone number at a bar – yes, in 2026! Instead of asking your giftee when you can expect a grandchild, hand them these.

This solid wood chess set is too pretty to hide in a dusty cabinet. Its colorful mosaic box and squiggly board are built to be shown off; the Filter’s commissioning editor, Karen Yuan, has it displayed on her living room coffee table. “Do I play chess? Not in years. Will I leave the box out just for compliments? Yes, shamelessly.” Gift this to the former captain of their school’s chess team or someone who’s always wanted to learn.

I love watercoloring, but that doesn’t mean I’m producing paintings worthy of an art gallery. But I enjoyed the guided watercolor book from Emily Lex Studio, which has lightly outlined pencil drawings and simple instructions for painting over them. This is the present for someone who needs a winter evening activity that doesn’t involve scrolling on social media. While I tried the holiday theme, the Woodland and Animals workbook looks delightful too.

It turns out I do have the patience for a 1,000-piece puzzle, as long as it looks as pretty as the eclectic ones from Piecework. This past summer, I waxed poetic about the brand’s Happy Camper puzzle: “Whenever I worked on it, I lost track of time.” The brand has plenty of festive options, including Tinseltown and Peppermint Parade. It has also branched out to other tabletop games, including Scrabble and Yahtzee.

Last winter, I asked experts who study digital detoxing about how to reduce screen time. One of their tips? Leave your phone outside your bedroom. Catherine Price, the author of How to Break Up with Your Phone, says her husband uses this clock from Arne Jacobsen. And, like your iPhone, you can snooze the alarm as many times as you’d like.

Whether gifting for a stressed student or workaholic loved one, you can’t go wrong with a planner. Like most things at Papier, this version marries function with an aesthetically pleasing design that they’ll want to show off on their desk. I wrote about how I use mine to stay organized – including reminding me to send a mega-important email I had forgotten about that day.

I’ve owned my secondhand Olympus film camera for four years and use it to snap candids of friends and family. It’s always fun to get photos developed, even if the older adults in my life can’t fathom why I would opt for it over the convenience of my iPhone’s camera. Gift this for someone who loves snapping photos and insists that everything looks better on film.
You can grab one secondhand at Mercari, eBay or Etsy.

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
paragraphs: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

items.title: Gérard Depardieu and French author investigated over sexual allegations
paragraphs: Warning: this story contains graphic content
French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.
The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.
Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.

The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.
She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".
French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

items.title: NYU Launches a Ukrainian Studies Initiative
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
New York University has launched a Ukrainian Studies program, making it the latest college to join this fast-growing international network of universities studying Ukraine.
Since its founding two years ago, the Global Coalition of Ukrainian Studies, backed by the Ukrainian government, has expanded to more than 100 institutions in 28 countries.

Universities join the coalition by signing a memorandum of understanding. Each school runs its own programs, while the coalition, fronted by First Lady Olena Zelenska, connects them with Ukrainian scholars, conferences and shared resources.

Anastasiia Vlasenko, head of the Ukrainian Studies initiative at NYU, says students have been among the main advocates for the program. “We have a very large Ukrainian student association... They were the ones who wrote the largest number of letters to the university administration calling for Ukrainian Studies to be established,” Vlasenko told VOA.

At NYU, Vlasenko teaches a new course, “Governance and Politics of Ukraine”, which covers "a vast part of Ukrainian history, which is known for its democratic movements... We also look at Ukraine’s political situation, protests, corruption and anti-corruption efforts, and the various scandals that are a constant feature of Ukrainian political life,” Vlasenko notes.

Some students admit that they knew little about Ukraine before taking the course. “I've seen a lot about the war in the news, and I don't really know much about it. So I chose this class just to learn,” says NYU student Raihan Alam.

Atticus Sambar Landa studies economics at NYU and is especially interested in the transition from communism to a capitalist society. “We just talked about corruption today, and I think the transition of specifically state-owned enterprises into the private sector are very fascinating and how that's played out for the people, for the oligarchy,” the student says.

Some students, like Daria Kalinichenko, were born in Ukraine and want to learn more about their homeland. “This is the first semester that NYU has offered this particular course, and it’s a great opportunity to learn a little more about Ukraine in the context of America and international politics," Kalinchenko said.

Anna Ivanenko attends the Stern School of Business and says, “I hadn’t planned to take anything related to politics, but when I saw that Ukrainian politics was being offered as an elective this semester, I thought it would be great to take a course related to Ukraine.”

Vlasenko believes the knowledge students gain in the classroom may prove useful after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends. “Ukraine’s reconstruction will create investment opportunities for major American businesses and will be important for U.S. policymakers. NYU can help provide them with the expertise and perspective they need...,” she said.

items.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
paragraphs: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

paragraphs: GTA VI is finally here, and it’s already a huge hit.
GTA VI is finally here, and it’s already a huge hit.

GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales, which set “a new record for entertainment across any medium,” according to an announcement from Rockstar Games. The game also sold 32.5 million in pre-orders.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder. said in a statement “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.” Rockstar claims that the game’s release, which happened Thursday, was “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

The news follows leaks, delays, and a huge amount of interest ahead of GTA VI’s launch. (Many other games steered clear of GTA VI to get their time in the sun.) But even with the weight of anticipation placed upon GTA VI, it actually lived up to the hype, my colleague Andrew Webster said in his review.

items.title: Afghanistan marks 80 years at U.N. as Taliban are denied country’s seat
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
As Afghanistan marks 80 years as a member of the United Nations, the country’s seat in the world body remains in limbo, with no clear path for the Taliban to gain recognition.
Afghanistan’s permanent representative to the U.N., Nasir Ahmad Faiq, appointed by the former Afghan government, told VOA that the U.N. has rejected the Taliban’s bid to take over Afghanistan’s seat.
“This shows that the international community is not ready to recognize or normalize relations with the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan,” he said.
No country except Russia has recognized the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, although several countries maintain working relations with the group.

In the five years since the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan, the U.N. has declined to hand over Afghanistan’s seat to the group, while the representative appointed by the former government has continued to serve.
Faiq said his mission is to amplify the voices of Afghans, particularly Afghan women and girls.

“Our message is clear: The Afghan people should not be forgotten. The rights of girls to education and work, the rights and freedoms of all citizens and their participation in determining the country’s future should be at the center of international efforts," he told VOA.
The Taliban, however, called the U.N.'s refusal to hand over Afghanistan’s seat to their representative ‘injustice’ and urged the world body to recognize them as the country’s government.
Shinkai Karokhail, a former Afghan ambassador to Canada, told VOA that the Taliban failed in their pursuit of both domestic and international legitimacy.
The international community has linked the Taliban government’s recognition to respect for human rights, the establishment of an inclusive government and efforts to combat terrorism.

Karokhail said that Afghanistan is a signatory to various conventions and has endorsed numerous declarations and resolutions, adding that “the Taliban should have upheld those international commitments but instead defied them.”

Afghanistan joined the U.N. in November of 1947, a year after the world body was formed. The country was one of the first Muslim-majority states to vote for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. In the years that followed, Afghanistan signed a number of international treaties that required governments to respect human rights and uphold certain international legal standards.

“Eight decades later, Afghanistan remains a member of the United Nations and has made significant contributions to multilateralism, but its people have gone through decades of war, foreign intervention, instability, displacement and serious human rights violations,” said Richard Bennett, U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Afghanistan.

Bennett told VOA that the U.N. has played a vital role in Afghanistan through humanitarian assistance, development programs, efforts to document human rights abuses and work to promote dialogue and peace initiatives.
He added that the anniversary is also an opportunity to reflect on the U.N.’s shortcomings and the opportunities it missed in Afghanistan over the years.

“Despite decades of international engagement, Afghanistan has serious human rights violations. One of the most painful examples is the situation of Afghan women and girls. After two decades of progress, they have lost many of their hard-won rights and freedoms while the international community has struggled to respond effectively,” Bennett told VOA.
Shukria Barakzai, former Afghan parliamentarian and Afghanistan’s ambassador to Norway, told VOA that the Taliban’s policies made Afghanistan an isolated country in the world.
She said that the engagement that should exist between Afghanistan and the international community is lacking.
“The country remains isolated, and, unfortunately, the will of its people in determining the political system is being disregarded,” she said.

items.title: Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
paragraphs: The robot vacuum / mop hybrid is our top pick for smaller homes and apartments, offering flagship features for less.
The robot vacuum / mop hybrid is our top pick for smaller homes and apartments, offering flagship features for less.
Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge
writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. Eufy’s Omni C28 robot vacuum / mop hybrid can help, and thanks to an early Black Friday deal, you can pick it up at a new low price of $379.99 ($420 off its original price) at Amazon, Best Buy, or directly from Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1). While this model has dropped to around $499.99 a few times before, it commonly sells for a lot more, making now a great time to consider buying one.

The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops. She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. It offers features typically found in pricier flagship models, including a multifunction dock that automatically washes the mop roller with hot water and dries it with hot air, yet it doesn’t take up too much space. The robot itself is also relatively narrow and maneuvers easily around furniture and into tight spaces. It boasts excellent navigation, and had no trouble climbing over the legs of Jen’s lounger, which have tripped up many of the more expensive models she’s tested.

The Omni C28 also does a great job cleaning with its mops, particularly on hardwood floors. Surprisingly, it’s powerful enough to lift up dried oatmeal. Unlike most other robot vacuums Jen’s tested, this one lacks a camera, making it a good option if you’re concerned about privacy. Unfortunately, the trade-off is mediocre obstacle detection, so you’ll want to pick up socks and cables before running it.

items.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
paragraphs: While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.

is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:

Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.

We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.

So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.
