items.title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
paragraphs: In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.
The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.
“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

items.title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
paragraphs: President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week. John McDonnell/AP hide caption
A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.
Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.

The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."

The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.

"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.

On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.

That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.
Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.
And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.

She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.
"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.

Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.

The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

items.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
paragraphs: Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”
This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”
For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.
More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.
While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.
Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

items.title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
paragraphs: SSD costs are still sky-high, but at least there are decent deals on microSD Express cards.
SSD costs are still sky-high, but at least there are decent deals on microSD Express cards.
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards, while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk, if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason.

For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon. That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be.

I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

items.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
paragraphs: The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026, but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it, even given their extravagant headgear.

A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in time.

“While standing in front of a painting by Jan van Eyck we … believe he succeeded in rendering the inexhaustible wealth of detail that belongs to the visible world,” the art historian Ernst Gombrich wrote in Art and Illusion (1960). An exact replica is unachievable to a painter “however patiently he worked with a magnifying glass” – artistic virtuosos are only human too. From 15th-century Netherlandish paintings to 19th-century Victorian novels to the hyper-realism of Grand Theft Auto VI, mimetic art, at its best, immerses us in artificial worlds so absolutely we forget the hands that created them.

“Jan van Eyck was here, 1434” the artist playfully reminds the viewer in an inscription on The Arnolfini Portrait, a treasure of the National Gallery’s permanent collection. Despite centuries of speculation it remains a mystery. Is the woman pregnant? Who are the figures glimpsed in the mirror? Might it be a self-portrait of Van Eyck and his wife, as a catalogue essay suggests? Or is that the artist under swathes of vermilion cloth in another portrait? What is truth and what is fiction, these pictures ask.

It is no wonder that single portraits have inspired whole novels. Maggie O’Farrell’s The Marriage Portrait (2022), partly based on a painting of a 16th-century Italian duchess, explores this slippery relationship between art and artifice. Vermeer’s masterpiece Girl with a Pearl Earring sparked Tracy Chevalier’s bestseller and an acclaimed film. We long for such luminous figures to step out of their canvases and tell their stories.

With their mottled skin and sideways glances, Van Eyck’s faces are as revealing as Lucian Freud’s unflinching portraits or Jenny Saville’s colossal nudes. If, as Oscar Wilde observed, “Every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist and not of the sitter,” it is also a portrait of the viewer. These strangers confront us with our own humanity and mortality: “Look, we were once flesh and blood like you!”

The Cambridge dictionary editors had something more 21st century in mind when they defined “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”. To come face to face with Van Eyck’s portraits, often barely the size of a laptop, is a timely reminder of human creativity. This is what “human” means, warts and all.

items.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
paragraphs: Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting.

While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida. GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments.

From the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia to the painstaking world-building of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictional take on Florida, players have shared their wide-ranging experiences with the Guardian, revealing what has surprised and challenged them about this long-awaited release – and what this all means for the series’ evolution.

Pete Langhelt, 39, from Colchester, pre-ordered GTA VI “as soon as I could”, and has been looking forward to its release for a long time. “Out of my group of friends I’m probably the only one really nerding out about it,” he says.

While Pete hasn’t been able to take time from work in the civil service, he’s still clocked “about 10 hours” of gameplay already. “The core of the missions themselves are pretty similar,” he says. “You turn up somewhere, shoot a load of people and escape. But the development of the characters has changed an awful lot. I have enjoyed the dynamic between Jason and Lucia. I never thought you could make comfortable domesticity into an enjoyable side activity in a video game.”

Pete has played all the installments of GTA franchise from the first, when he was “probably too young to be playing”. “I think Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favourite Rockstar game going into this, and it seems to have developed the things that I really liked about Red Dead.”

The game encourages exploration, he says. “The day and night cycle seems a lot less intense than GTA V, meaning you don’t feel rushed to get things done. I can let Jason take a slow start to the day before taking a slow drive or boat ride to whatever criminal activity needs completing.”
His partner is less keen. “She’ll have to put up with me being on the Xbox for the next few weeks,” he says.

A 59-year-old MBA retiree from Venice, Florida, was also struck by just how much of the experience revolves around everyday life. He described it as the “most beautiful, real, open-world game that’s ever existed”.

“I was surprised that, with about 10-plus hours of play, most of my time has been spent performing mundane tasks like home repair, grocery shopping, personal grooming and trying to open a bank account. The realism is incredible, but perhaps too real,” he said.
“It’s as fully realized as a game world could be. I never expected to see anything more fully developed,” he added.

Rob Smeraldo, 28, from Dundee, took the day off work yesterday to play the game on his PlayStation 5. “I made sure I had loads of snacks and Domino’s,” he says. And already, Rob believes that “GTA VI must be the greatest game ever made”.

“I think the realism and just the detail put into it is absolutely astounding. The shadows, the way the hair moves when people move around … They took their time, but it’s definitely been worth it,” he says.

Rob is a longtime GTA fan and wore a GTA VI T-shirt and drank from a GTA mug to mark the occasion. “I purchased the physical copy [of the game] as soon as it became purchasable – I just wanted the memorabilia, you know?”

Ella Delancey, 35, of Berkshire has been playing GTA since she was a child. “GTA III is a huge core memory for me. My brother and I were much too young to be playing it and I definitely wouldn’t let my daughter play it now, but at the time we were obsessed.”

So far, the social and brand director has been surprised by how much there is to do aside from pushing the story forward. “I’m not very far into it yet, but I’m already struck by the graphics and the sheer depth of what you can do. It’s very violent, obviously, but I play by the rules, which probably makes me a bit boring. I’ve been birdwatching and exploring, and there’s so much to do outside the main story.”

There is one thing she is struggling with, however, and that’s Lucia, one of the main protagonists, leaving her child in a cafe and going to prison, only to come out and start committing more crimes. “As a mother, that doesn’t sit comfortably with me. I know it’s a game and you have to suspend your morals to a degree, but that part has given me pause,” she says.

“I do think it’s a step forward that you can no longer hire sex workers as in previous games. GTA still has a complicated relationship with misogyny – and it’s far from perfect, but that change feels significant.”

While Ella hasn’t taken any time off work to play, she has set aside time on Friday to play or watch her partner play. “It’s so immersive that it doesn’t feel like a chore, and I can see it replacing our usual after-work TV downtime for a little while,” she says.

Clint, 36, who works in the music industry in Chicago, describes the game as “truly one of one”, pointing to its unexpectedly domestic moments and the relationship between Jason and Lucia as some of its biggest draws.

“The story is just downright cute. I just had my character build an Ikea table with his girlfriend, and loved it. I typically skip some cutscenes, but now I’m rewatching them when I miss something,” he says.
Clint says Jason and Lucia’s relationship is particularly significant, describing it as an example of healthy masculinity that could resonate with younger players.

“The main character’s relationship is healthy (at least so far, at six hours in – and ‘healthy’ for a GTA game), which I see as such a positive. Positive both because I can relate to caring for one’s partner and because I love that real, healthy masculinity is being portrayed. I love that you are incentivized to complete menial tasks to make Lucia happy in between the wild and chaotic portions of the storyline. I’d like to hope that this might show young and/or disaffected men that misogyny is super lame and unmanly, at least in some small way,” he says.
Beyond the relationship dynamics, Clint praises the game’s approach to world building, which he says “feels so deep and textured”.

“Also refreshing are the built-in guardrails that make the game feel so lifelike … The player cannot just go steal a car or engage in indiscriminate violence without consequence. Every fight comes with police scrutiny, even speeding got me chased until I slowed down. It moderates what was a free-for-all melee atmosphere in the previous titles. This both enhances a sense of realism and immersion and makes me wonder if that doesn’t have some, albeit minor, benefit towards the ‘video games breed violence’ crowd,” he says.
The Guardian’s own team is also getting in on the action. The US’s deputy sport editor, Bryan Graham, says “it’s been a strange 24 hours” since the game dropped.

“Maybe we’ve been starved of genuine monocultural events for so long that we’ve forgotten how to handle them. The first sign the discourse might be getting a little carried away came when the New York Times invoked Jean Baudrillard, Jorge Luis Borges and bell hooks in their suite of GTA 6 think pieces (a dream blunt rotation I’d be sure to remember later),” he said. “Meanwhile, the day’s sanest take came from Glenn Beck, of all people, who went viral for pushing back on the strange spectacle of gen Xers scolding younger generations for getting excited about a video game.”

Graham continued: “Then came midnight. Really, it should be called Florida: The Game. With apologies to Sean Baker, I’m not sure there’s ever been a piece of media that is more of a love letter to America’s weirdest state, or more affectionate in its ridicule.

“Having played only a couple of hours before passing out, I’ve mostly been poking its version of the Florida Keys, where shimmering waterways give way to sun-bleached houses, shabby strip malls and alligators in the reeds. But that small sampling has been enough to see that Rockstar has created something both exquisitely observed and gloriously unhinged, a funhouse mirror held up to an America that increasingly resembles its own parody. Make no mistake: this is art!”

Tom Johnson, the Guardian’s vice-president of audience and strategy, says he was “probably lying to myself when I fired up my PS5 at six thirty this morning to ‘make sure the game installed properly’.
“I blinked and nearly an hour had passed and I had to remind myself I did not in fact have the GTA flu and needed to start getting ready for work,” he quips.
Of the game, Johnson said “the stunning graphics and well-paced storyline sucks you in immediately by allowing you to play as both characters, drive a car, captain a boat and even fly a small plane.
“Even the more mundane side quests are enthralling – I spent a few minutes doing a kettlebell workout and painting a room before wondering if I was just playing a sexier version of The Sims.

“I grew up in Miami, far away from the more glamorous parts of the beach, and I can’t wait for this workday to end so I can head west towards Kendall in search of my childhood home. At this point, given the game’s commitment to realism, it wouldn’t surprise me if an accurate replica of my parents’ car will be there waiting for me, parked in the driveway.”

items.title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.

The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.

The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.

Gemini for Home was announced last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

items.title: Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
paragraphs: From AirPods to Apple Watches, many Apple devices are already seeing notable discounts ahead of November 27th.
From AirPods to Apple Watches, many Apple devices are already seeing notable discounts ahead of November 27th.
Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge
writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, which have dropped to new lows.

Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of.

The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.

Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.

The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.

The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

The Baseus PicoGo AM52 is a 10,000mAh magnetic power bank that supports fast 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging and up to 45W wired charging via its built-in USB-C cable. It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batteries.

The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

Designed to pair with a Mac, the latest Apple Studio Display features a sharp 5K Retina display, a great 12-megapixel Center Stage camera that keeps you in frame during video calls, and a good six-speaker sound system with spatial audio. Sadly, it only offers two Thunderbolt 5 ports in addition to a pair of USB-C ports. Read our review.

items.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
paragraphs: At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable.

It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.”

Featuring more than 50 works, The Circus is a dazzling exploration of one of the 20th century’s most distinctive artists, delving into the way this magical arena and its cast of intriguing characters captured Chagall’s imagination, dancing across his canvases for more than 60 years. For Chagall, the circus is a mesmerising space beyond reality where it is possible to find childhood memories, artistic inspiration, spiritual enlightenment and both radiant light and deepest darkness.

The show includes his theatrical collaborations, paintings he produced in a box at the Cirque d’Hiver, pieces he made after his return to Paris after the second world war, and autobiographical works relating to Vitebsk, Russia, where he grew up. But shimmering at the heart of this exhibition is Cirque, an art book, large suite of lithographs and essay (newly translated into English for The Circus).

An entire, windowless space in a deep red is the setting for Cirque, which is presented here in its entirety. With the colourful lithographs popping off the walls, it feels as though I have disappeared into a big top. This is enhanced further by the decision to record Chagall’s Cirque essay, which is read by a French actor to give the language the artist’s accent. I pop on the headphones and for 24 minutes I am no longer in misty Wakefield but in the rafters of a tent watching hoops spin – or centre stage beside a ferocious lion.

The language in Cirque is as important as the visuals; as with Chagall’s art, where bodies float and animals shapeshift, so the text moves from a memory of street performers in Vitebsk, to the tail of a circus horse, to the story of Noah, to the greed of humanity. While I listen, I observe the vivid, swirling colours of a red leotard, a clown’s painted face and a bouquet of flowers. In many of the lithographs reality melts away – a moon bursts through the big top, a fish plays a drum, a Janus-faced figure plays music and weeps at the same time. For all their sparkling joy, each work features a looming audience, their round faces in rows, indistinguishable but heavily present, judging and reminding us of the outside world. Chagall’s words play through the headphones: “Alas, in life I have seen a ridiculous circus: someone thundered to terrify the world, and a thunder of applause answered him.” The circus is not all fun and games, on either side of the canvas.

The clever thing about placing Cirque at the start of the show is that it is then possible to follow these motifs through the rest of Chagall’s work, both before and after Cirque’s creation. The Four Heads – one of 19 paintings Chagall created from a box at the Cirque d’Hiver – was made in 1927 and, featuring a clown atop a many-headed creature, captures an early interest in the momentary spectacle of circus. Much later pieces from 1980 of his home in Vitebsk also include acrobats, lovers dancing and instrumentalists, indicating that these performing artists had inhabited his mind since childhood.

It is clear that for Chagall, performance and circus are inseparable. His work for Mozart’s The Magic Flute at the Metropolitan Opera in New York in 1967 involved set and costume design. The archival design pieces presented here again find flying figures, animals and instrumentalists – and that oppressive audience, sitting just beyond the performance, passing judgment on the art.

The challenge for any curator is to create a space that does justice to the spirit of the art on display. This is particularly hard when the subject is a supernatural display of magic, movement and artistry. But The Circus more than rises to the challenge, with thoughtful interventions that elevate the entire experience. From the ceiling fall two large, patchwork curtains by German artist Ulla von Brandenburg, which are pinned back with rope as if we are entering a circus tent and everyday life can surrender to the wonder of performance. In the centre of the gallery, a small inner room plays archive footage from the Cirque d’Hiver, encapsulating the stunning skills of the performers in real life.

Early on in his Cirque writing, Chagall asks: “These clowns, these bareback riders, these acrobats have taken up residence in my visions. Why?” We will never know the full answer, but certainly they imbued his art with the sensation that the world may be more than it first appears, and that can be a glorious thing.

items.title: The best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, tested
paragraphs: You don’t have to live in the American deep south to feel the effects of humidity. At home, just breathing makes the air more humid, let alone cooking or showering.

And when it gets too humid, it’s bad for our health as well as our homes. In fact, the two are connected: humidity lets mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.

Dehumidifiers can make your indoor environment more comfortable by reducing the amount of moisture in the air. Because of this, they’re also a great laundry-drying hack. I use mine to dry clothes fast, and for a fraction of the cost of tumble drying.

Not sure if you need one? You can buy a hygrometer cheaply – the one I used for testing cost less than £10 – to check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision. Should you opt to buy one, do your research at reputable sources (like, hint, the Filter). Researching this piece, I was shocked to learn that customers had been duped into buying very basic dehumidifiers for well over the odds.
This Black Friday we’ve found the Ebac 4650e, our favourite dehumidifier, for its lowest ever price.
The VonHaus smart dehumidifier has a large capacity and is our favourite budget-friendly pick. It’s currently as cheap as it’s ever been.
The Duux Bora Smart dehumidifier is discounted by £100.
Best budget dehumidifierVonHaus Smart dehumidifier with laundry mode
Best combined dehumidifier and air purifierDevola Platinum hybrid DVHA20L
Best dehumidifier for drying laundryDuux Bora Smart
Best quiet dehumidifierMeacoDry Arete Two

I’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist with decades of experience testing electrical appliances; I’ve been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with a lovely number of children and far too many pets, so there’s lots of laundry: I use a dehumidifier to dry clothes. I’ve also been known to use one for speedy DIY, drying plaster and paint faster.

I selected 14 dehumidifiers from leading brands to test, then set them up and used them, each for several days. I used a power meter to measure how much electricity (and therefore money and carbon) they use. Using the Sound Meter app, I measured the noise from 1m away in decibels (dB) on multiple occasions – the figures featured here are all the ones that I measured at home, in consistent conditions, so they often differ from manufacturers’ official figures, which are measured in lab conditions but in inconsistent ways. More subjectively, I paid attention to the quality of the sound – was it annoying, gurgly, hard to ignore, easy to fall asleep to? And I measured each dehumidifier’s size.

To measure the room’s humidity while testing, I used a digital hygrometer held 1m away (though humidity would be roughly the same elsewhere in the room), and a thermometer to check the temperature. Dehumidifiers fill a tank with water they have extracted from the air, so one measure of how good a job they’ve done is to measure how much water is in there – which I did, using a jug.

Because conditions vary from moment to moment and room to room, it was impossible to test each one in precisely the same conditions. As such, I’ve only mentioned the results of these not-so-scientific tests when they stood out.

After testing, any dehumidifiers that weren’t collected by manufacturers were donated to Furnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes the empty social housing in which women and children are placed after surviving domestic abuse.
What we loveBritish-made, long warranty, and great performance
What we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank is

This is the priciest dehumidifier on test, but it’s worth the money. It’s large but luggable, with a single deep handle on the rear that makes it easy to carry and an integrated cable tidy on the back that’s great when you want to store it.
Why we love it I like the design. For example, a flap at the front opens to reveal a black water tank that’s easy to empty, with water coming out of just one hole (most water tanks are messier).

The small display is colourful, and there’s a good range of modes, including laundry. A smart control feature remembers your home’s humidity levels and kicks in only when the levels start to rise: in a home that doesn’t have major damp problems, this will save a lot of electricity. It can be controlled via an app, and it also comes with an activated carbon filter for removing unwanted smells.

Performance was good, bringing relative humidity down by 4% in a short time, and its capacity and smart controls make it a great all-rounder. You can simply leave it switched on and trust it to manage your home’s humidity levels without wasting electricity. The Ebac’s sound was inoffensive, too: I could definitely sleep with it on. It’s pretty energy efficient, and it’s made in north-east England, so its carbon footprint is lower than some other models. It also comes with a four-year warranty if bought directly from the brand.
It’s a shame that … there’s no window to inspect the fill level.

Dimensions: 34 x 27 x 54cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 18l Tank capacity: 3.5l Peak power use on test: 180W Average noise level on top setting: 10dB Target humidity range: 35-80% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 5p/hour
What we loveBritish-made, long warranty, and great performance
What we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank is
What we loveGreat value, quiet and app control
What we don’t loveThe air filtration is basic
At the time of writing, a discount brings this dehumidifier’s price down to less than £150. Even at full price, though, it’s a bargain.

Why we love it Alongside a laundry mode, a sleep mode brings down volume levels from an already quiet 15dB to 10dB by slowing the fan speed, and it turns off the screen so the lights won’t disturb you.

Other modes include auto, which turns the machine off when it reaches the target relative humidity, and continuous, which means it won’t turn off until the tank is full. An app lets you control it from your phone or with Google Home or Amazon Alexa. Simple coloured lights on the front give a visual indicator of what mode it’s in.

It’s a great all-rounder for the price. On test, it started cutting humidity levels within minutes, and over a couple of hours, it brought relative humidity down by at least 5%, pulling 450ml of water out of the air. It’s good for drying laundry and tackling damp – the only corner cut, when compared with pricier models, is Hepa air filtration.
If you’re not sure whether or not to invest in a dehumidifier, this is a good buy for the price.
It’s a shame that … it only has a washable dust filter, not Hepa air purification, even though there looks to be enough room for a larger filter.

Dimensions: 31 x 24 x 49cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 20l Tank capacity: 4.5l Peak power use on test: 290W Average noise level on top setting: 15dB Target humidity range: 30-80% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 8p/hour
What we loveGreat value, quiet and app control
What we don’t loveThe air filtration is basic
What we loveGood value for a model that features Hepa air filtration
What we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filters

Kill two birds with one stone with this new hybrid model that promises cleaner as well as drier air. It comes with a Hepa filter (for filtering the air), an ioniser (for pulling dust out of the air) and an ultraviolet lamp (for killing germs).

Why we love it Several models on test come with Hepa filters, but what sets this model apart is that it measures air quality too: simply press a button to get a traffic light measure of PM2.5 particles (green, blue or red light, depending on your air quality). Air pollution is a silent killer, and indoor air quality can be worse than outdoor, so filtering these fine particles is a brilliant idea if you don’t already have an air purifier.
Dehumidifier modes include laundry and night (quieter at 20dB), and the flap on the top is motorised, so it opens automatically and can be set to “swing” to circulate air.

It was great being able to see the air quality improve, as well as the humidity. I found the Devola to be well designed, too: the water tank is accessed from the side and its handle doubles as a visual level indicator. And I found the tank easy to empty without making a mess.
It’s a shame that … it’s not quieter. Hepa filters will need replacing periodically, too (Devola suggests every six months, so budget about £15 a year).

Dimensions: 36 x 27 x 57cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 20l Tank capacity: 2.9l Peak power use on test: 330W Average noise level on top setting: 30dB Target humidity range: 40-80% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 9p/hour
What we loveGood value for a model that features Hepa air filtration
What we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filters
For more, read our guide to the best air purifiers
What we loveQuiet and uses an eco-friendly refrigerant
What we don’t loveNo Hepa air purification

This is a good-looking dehumidifier, with clean lines. The water drawer at the front has a useful visual indicator, so you can see at a glance how full it is. It features wifi and app control so that you can set schedules, and an activated carbon filter works to remove odours, gases and smoke.

Why we love it I loved the four-hour laundry mode: it reduced relative humidity by 5% in the first five minutes, swiftly drying clothes. And you’ll be able to sleep nearby, since the Duux is Quiet Mark certified for its ultra-quiet operation. The night mode turns off the lights, although I had to turn down the fan speed myself – and in my tests it then reached an impressively low average of below 10dB, much quieter than the manufacturer’s claims. It sounds like a fan with a little bit of fridge sound thrown in, but quieter.

I also like that it uses the environmentally friendly R290 refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential (GWP). In fact, its GWP is only triple that of carbon dioxide, while some refrigerants have a GWP that’s hundreds of times that of CO2 (and some refrigerants now banned from sale have GWPs of thousands).
It’s a shame that … it doesn’t offer Hepa air purification at this price.

Dimensions: 32 x 24 x 51cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 20l Tank capacity: 4l Peak power use on test: 270W Average noise level on top setting: 20dB Target humidity range: 30-80% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 7p/hour
What we loveQuiet and uses an eco-friendly refrigerant
What we don’t loveNo Hepa air purification
What we loveImpressively quiet, Hepa filtration, app and a long warranty
What we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filters

You’d expect the successor to the popular Arete One to be impressive, and this doesn’t disappoint. It’s not just a dehumidifier – it also purifies the air, thanks to the included dust and medical-grade H13 Hepa filters.

Why we love it The Arete Two can be controlled via a smartphone app or voice control via Google Home or Amazon Alexa. Modes include continuous, smart (which aims for a middle-of-the-road 55% humidity) and laundry. The louvre on top opens manually and can be directed at your washing.

Its display is slightly unusual: rather than a number, it shows a sliding scale of humidity levels, giving you a clear visual indication of the current humidity and your target. The interface is intuitive, however, and there aren’t too many buttons.

The five-year warranty is the longest I’ve seen for a dehumidifier. But most of all, I was impressed by the quiet. The average noise was just 5dB, and this dropped to 4dB (considerably quieter than the manufacturer’s claimed noise level) in night mode. You can honestly forget that it’s on.
It also has some thoughtful features. For example, if you leave it plugged in but not switched on, it will say “wet” on screen to alert you when it detects a relative humidity of 70% plus.

You can also choose your type of air filtration when you buy refills (£39.99 for a pack of three). Replace the Hepa filter if you have allergies or pets; swap for an activated charcoal filter if you’d prefer to remove cooking smells, smoke and VOCs (chemicals that come off new furniture, paint, carpets and so on).
It’s a shame that … the louvre isn’t motorised, considering the price.

Dimensions: 37 x 27 x 62cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 20l Tank capacity: 4.8l Peak power use on test: 230W Average noise level on top setting: 5dB Target humidity range: 40-70% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 6p/hour
What we loveImpressively quiet, Hepa filtration, app and a long warranty
What we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filters
What we loveQuiet, compact and impressive performance
What we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank is

When compared with the other smaller (12-litre capacity) models on test, this extracted the most water from the air. It removed 200ml, reducing relative humidity by 5% in a short time. It also looks good.

Why we love it Performance is impressive for a small dehumidifier. And it’s especially impressive considering it comes with a Hepa filter for air purification, which is bound to slow airflow for dehumidification.
It was pretty quiet and sounded like a fan. I could definitely sleep through its 5dB on low fan mode.

Got enough space for a larger model? For only a little more, you can buy the larger Devola DVHA20L above, which features a built-in PM2.5 air quality monitor, so you can see the impact it’s having on air quality.
It’s a shame that … the rear tank doesn’t have a visual indicator, so you can’t tell how full it is without pulling it out.

Dimensions: 30 x 23 x 47cm (WDH) Daily extraction rate: 12l Tank capacity: 2.7l Peak power use on test: 180W Average noise level on top setting: 10dB Target humidity range: 30-80% Laundry setting? Yes Running costs: 5p/hour
What we loveQuiet, compact and impressive performance
What we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank is
What we don’t loveThere’s no laundry mode
The Swan’s design is as elegant as its feathery namesake. It’s also a contender for best bargain when reduced.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the powerful upwards fan and motorised flap make it great for drying laundry, but there’s no laundry mode, and the minimum target for relative humidity is 40% (many models go down to 30%, and laundry mode is invariably 35% with a timer).
You can still dry laundry by choosing 40% and setting a timer, but it seems like an oversight.

Dimensions: 33 x 22 x 57cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 20l; tank capacity: 4l; peak power use on test: 330W; average noise level on top setting: 30dB; target humidity range: 40-80%; laundry setting? No; running costs: 9p/hour
What we don’t loveThere’s no laundry mode
What we loveA desiccant dehumidifier suitable for spaces as low as 1C
What we don’t loveUses twice as much electricity as a condenser dehumidifier

This is a desiccant dehumidifier, rather than a condenser dehumidifier like the others here (see the guide below for more information on the different types). As such, it uses more electricity but can be used in colder spaces, operating as low as 1C: perfect for a garage or shed. This one features an ioniser that helps cut airborne dust, and it’s compact, light and easy to carry. On test, it performed well, cutting relative humidity by 10% but raising the temperature slightly.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s good for garages, but since it uses twice as much electricity as condenser dehumidifiers, I wouldn’t use it in the home. It doesn’t display the humidity level, either.

Dimensions: 36 x 20 x 55cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 8l; tank capacity: 2l; peak power use on test: 690W; average noise level on top setting: 40dB; target humidity range: 40-60%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 18p/hour
What we loveA desiccant dehumidifier suitable for spaces as low as 1C
What we don’t loveUses twice as much electricity as a condenser dehumidifier
Dehumidifier with max extraction and laundry mode

At the time of this page update, the ProBreeze website had a discount code that brought this dehumidifier’s price down by £40, making it a bargain for such a workhorse. In my tests, it extracted moisture powerfully, bringing relative humidity down by more than 10% in a couple of hours. For £50 extra, you can get a version with smart app control.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it uses quite a lot of electricity, even on low power mode. And although it was fairly quiet (15dB on low fan mode), there was an annoying low hum as well as the fan noise.

Dimensions: 32 x 20 x 58cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 20l; tank capacity: 5.5l; peak power use on test: 360W; average noise level on top setting: 20dB; target humidity range: 30-80%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 9p/hour
Dehumidifier with max extraction and laundry mode
What we loveThe coloured humidity indicator on the front
What we don’t loveThe next model up, with Hepa air filtration, is better

I liked the way this affordable dehumidifier looked, and loved the little notch at the top of the rear water tank. It means that, when dry, you can stow the power cable in there, making this an easy machine to store.
A light-up ring on the front indicates relative humidity at a glance: green for good, red for too humid, blue for too dry.
It didn’t make the final cut because … I preferred the newer Devola DVH12L, which also has a Hepa filter for air purification.

Dimensions: 26 x 22 x 47cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 12l; tank capacity: 2l; peak power use on test: 180W; average noise level on top setting: 25dB; target humidity range: 30-80%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 5p/hour
What we loveThe coloured humidity indicator on the front
What we don’t loveThe next model up, with Hepa air filtration, is better
What we loveIt’s compact and uses an eco-friendly refrigerant
What we don’t loveDehumidification performance wasn’t great on test

This was the smallest on test, so it could be worth considering if you only want to use it occasionally and need to stow it away most of the time. The dust filter is washable, and while there’s no true sleep mode (there’s one that dims the lights, but it doesn’t reduce noise), most of the lights turn off after a minute, and it’s not too loud.

The comfort mode targets a relative humidity based on the temperature, and its front water drawer gives a visual indication. I also like that it uses the environmentally friendly R290 refrigerant, which has a low GWP.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it didn’t reduce humidity as much as some, collecting just 150ml overnight. Also, unusually, I spilled some water when carrying it after testing.

Dimensions: 28 x 24 x 39cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 12l; tank capacity: 2.5l; peak power use on test: 180W; average noise level on top setting: 20dB; target humidity range: 30-90%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 5p/hour
What we loveIt’s compact and uses an eco-friendly refrigerant
What we don’t loveDehumidification performance wasn’t great on test
What we loveCompact, and you can add a Hepa filter for air purification
What we don’t loveI prefer models that measure air quality too

This has excellent features, including top-notch air filtration and a three-year warranty from some retailers. Like its big sibling, the MeacoDry Arete Two (above), it purifies the air thanks to an included medical-grade H13 Hepa filter and dust filter. The Hepa filter is optional, and it will need replacing (about every three months) if you want to use it. Budget £40 a year for refills.

It didn’t make the final cut because … you can’t see whether the air purification is working. For only a little more, you can buy the larger Devola DVHA20L, which features a built-in PM2.5 air quality monitor. I also didn’t like the looks, finding the green and white a bit clinical.

Dimensions: 32 x 24 x 49cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 12l; tank capacity: 2.5l; peak power use on test: 200W; average noise level on top setting: 20dB; target humidity range: 30-80%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 5p/hour
What we loveCompact, and you can add a Hepa filter for air purification
What we don’t loveI prefer models that measure air quality too
What we loveIt’s easy to carry around the house
What we don’t loveIt’s a smaller model with no sleep function

This has a daily extraction rate of 16 litres, which isn’t the weediest but is one of the smaller models on test. It has a simple handle across the full width that’s well balanced. If you find it difficult to carry heavy items up and down stairs, choose a smaller model like this.
I liked the display, with relative humidity and temperature shown inside a cartoon house. And there’s a fan swing function that helps with drying laundry.
It didn’t make the final cut because … there’s no sleep function, although it’s fairly quiet.

Dimensions: 30 x 19 x 47cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 16l; tank capacity: 2.4l; peak power use on test: 230W; average noise level on top setting: 20dB; target humidity range: 50-70%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 6p/hour
What we loveIt’s easy to carry around the house
What we don’t loveIt’s a smaller model with no sleep function
What we loveIt displays the precise humidity, and it has app control
What we don’t loveHigher running costs and loud at times

I liked the Black+Decker’s design, from the coloured light at the top that indicates humidity (red for high, green for good, blue for low) to the large, white digits on its front that tell you the precise relative humidity.

These quick-glance displays work well when it’s paired with the app, so you can control it from afar. You can even add Google Home and Amazon Alexa voice controls. I could use my phone as a remote control from anywhere in the home to check on progress – rare for a dehumidifier at this price.
It didn’t make the final cut because … the machine was loud at times (although the sleep setting averaged 17dB).

Dimensions: 34 x 24 x 57cm (WDH); daily extraction rate: 20l; tank capacity: 6.5l; peak power use on test: 395W; average noise level on top setting: 20dB; target humidity range: 30-80%; laundry setting? Yes; running costs: 10p/hour
What we loveIt displays the precise humidity, and it has app control
What we don’t loveHigher running costs and loud at times
Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapour in the air compared with the maximum that the air can hold.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. So if the amount of water in the air stays the same but the temperature drops, relative humidity increases.
When relative humidity hits 100%, the air is fully saturated, and water condenses on surfaces, like how dew condenses on cool morning grass.
All the dehumidifiers tested here measure the relative humidity (a percentage) and let you set a target.
If the air is too humid, it feels muggy, and it’s hard for sweat to cool you on a hot day. If the air is too dry, it can lead to problems such as dry eyes and throats.
For your health and your home, the ideal relative humidity is 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter.
You may benefit from a dehumidifier if you have damp and mould problems. Humidity helps mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.

Another benefit is drying laundry fast. Use a dehumidifier to pull moisture out of the air, then clothes in the room dry much faster and without causing damp problems such as condensation on windows or walls.
Dehumidifiers are also good for specific uses, such as drying paint or plaster faster, or helping a room dry out after flooding.
If in doubt, use a cheap hygrometer to check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision.

Most of the dehumidifiers tested here are compressor dehumidifiers, so they work a bit like a fridge, compressing and then expanding a refrigerant to cool a metal coil. Water from the air then condenses on the coil and drains off into a water tank. These are usually the best style of dehumidifier for the home.

Don’t throw away the plastic tube if you find one in the box. Some models come with a drain hose – so you can constantly dry rather than stopping when the tank is full. Other models let you add a hose if you need it (but most people don’t use them, which is why they’re not always included).

I tested one desiccant dehumidifier. These excel in cold environments, such as garages, cellars and outbuildings. This is because they work by using moisture-absorbing materials that don’t rely on temperature to remove humidity. However, they use more electricity to do so. They don’t require refills (none of the units featured here needs refills for dehumidification – the only ongoing cost apart from electricity is that some have Hepa air filters that need replacing every three to six months).
Peltier dehumidifiers are small and quiet, but they’re not very effective, and they use more energy, so we haven’t featured any in this roundup.
The larger (20l a day) models tested here are good for larger homes and open-plan spaces. You can put them somewhere central to tackle humidity in the whole home.
The smaller (12l a day) models are very popular and better for smaller homes or single tasks, such as drying laundry. However, if you have persistent damp problems, then it could be worth sizing up.
You can add a hose to most dehumidifiers if you want to keep them in constant use without having to empty the tank.

I measured each dehumidifier’s power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). For example, if you’re running a 200W dehumidifier for four hours, it would use 800Wh or 0.8kWh.
The energy price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is 26.32p a kWh. Multiply this by the last figure, and you’ll discover it costs about 21p to run the dehumidifier for four hours.

This compares favourably with a tumble dryer. One load in a traditional model uses about 4.5kWh (£1.18), although an energy-saving heat pump model uses half that. Either way, it’s much cheaper to run a dehumidifier than either type of tumble dryer.
Many dehumidifiers have a laundry mode that aims for a low relative humidity of 35%, with a timer that turns off automatically, typically after six hours.

To dry laundry effectively, hang it in a room, turn on the dehumidifier and close the doors. That way, it’s drying the air (and speeding the laundry drying) without having to dry moist air that comes in from the outside world.

Empty the water tank after each use, or when it’s full. Regular cleaning mainly involves dusting the unit and cleaning the air filters. Dust filters can usually be vacuumed and washed, while paper Hepa filters need replacing. How often depends on use: about three months for continuous use, six months for average use, or annually if you only run it occasionally. Smart models should track usage and alert you when the filter needs changing.
If you use your dehumidifier mainly in the winter, then give it a thorough clean before storing it away.

Start by running the unit on fan-only mode to dry the interior; if it doesn’t have one, set it to its highest humidity setting. Clean the unit and filters, then wash and disinfect the tank with a 50/50 mix of white vinegar and water to help prevent mould. Finally, leave everything to air-dry for at least 24 hours, ensuring it’s completely dry before reassembling and packing it away for the summer.

A dehumidifier will stop working when its water tank is full, usually signalled by a flashing light, beep or app alert. But it’s good practice to empty the tank regularly rather than wait for this to happen.

I mainly use a dehumidifier to dry laundry, which takes two to three hours and costs far less than tumble drying (see “How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?”). I simply turn it off when the clothes feel dry and empty the tank, or set the timer if I’m going out. Some models also have a dedicated laundry mode that switches off automatically.

If you run a dehumidifier continuously, don’t aim for the driest air possible. Ideally, indoor relative humidity should be 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter. How often you need to empty the tank depends on the humidity, how much you use it, and tank capacity. A larger tank means you’ll have to empty it less often.

No. If anything, a dehumidifier makes a room a little bit warmer while it’s running. However, humid air makes sweat evaporate less effectively, so reducing humidity can help you feel cooler on a warm day.

This isn’t the case on a cold day, when high humidity can make you feel colder. That is because water vapour conducts heat away from the skin more efficiently than dry air. So getting the relative humidity right year-round improves comfort.
For more, read the Filter’s guides: The best heated airers, tested The best electric heaters The best electric blankets to keep you toasty for less

Caramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotment

items.title: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
paragraphs: is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”

The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp.

Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.

If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.
