items.title: From the Reeboks of a retired raver to a nude swim in a Monster Energy drink: four free exhibitions to see
paragraphs: Desire is a quiet, private, lonely thing in Malaysian painter Zearo’s world. In a single monumental image that spans almost the entire gallery, Zearo depicts men in a park at night, waiting, hoping, longing for companionship and love, but it feels like it might never come.

The park in the centre of the painting is a cruising spot, a place for men to express their sexuality in a society where that isn’t an acceptable thing to do. The men smoke languidly, leaning against trees, or lie impatiently on the grass. Some have found each other, they embrace or talk, but most are isolated, alone despite being in one of the only places where they don’t have to be.

The painting is called The Curfew. Read from left to right, it’s a journey from daytime through the early hours and on to dawn, when desire has to be hidden again. This is a painting of a window of opportunity – a chance to be free – that won’t stay open for long.

Upstairs, the paintings are smaller, depicting interior scenes in bedrooms and living rooms, but no less lonely and dreamlike. It seems to be perpetually dusk in Zearo’s world, like life is always on the precipice of transformation that never comes.

Zearo makes hazy, fuzzy, melancholy paintings filled with intricate details and symbolism. Like Salman Toor at the Courtauld and the recent Louis Fratino show at David Zwirner, queerness here is presented in elegiac, quiet, nostalgic ways, with this gentle 90s colour palette. It’s something permitted but barely accepted, suffused with loss and angst.
The Sunday Painter, London, until 19 December

Richie Culver has encased history in resin, just like that mosquito preserved in amber in Jurassic Park. But this isn’t the ancient, prehistoric, geological past. This is personal memories, hazy nostalgia, the lost joys of youth preserved in thick, gloopy, oozing toxic plastic.

A pair of white Reeboks – signifiers of a youth spent at raves, every filthy scuff earned through hypnotic movement in some field or club long ago – is frozen in yellowed resin. Behind it, a cap has been pinned to a sheet of timber and framed against gluey, sticky cardboard, another marker of the past saved for the present.

But this is more than just rave-culture nostalgia, it’s Culver reckoning with what’s happened since those heady party days. Another Reebok has been bent and glued into a twisted, awkward shape. On its sole there’s now a photo of Culver’s stepfather in the final days before he died. Pictures of old clothes have been pasted on cardboard around the gallery, a sheet of wood is covered in staples and ripped fragments of images. On the wall, a mirror is grubby and opaque with glue, making your reflection opaque and fuzzy. It’s like Culver is trying to sift through the past, through what he was, trying to understand who he is now that it’s gone, but the answer is too out of focus to decipher.

I like Culver’s art, a lot. I want to see more of his post-rave minimalism, somewhere bigger. But shown here, in the basement of someone’s flat (you have to book an appointment via the website), the domesticity amps up the introspection, the queasy, uneasy nostalgia, the feeling that the past is a distant world that you will never ever be able to grasp again.

When he was a student, David Micheaud got a job operating the Bournemouth Eye, a tethered hot air balloon tourist attraction that floats over the coastal city. They offered him the job full-time. He could see his life’s path laid out before him: four decades of balloon tethering, retirement, death.

He said no and became an artist instead, but that big old balloon seems to have haunted him ever since. There’s one in the middle of this small show, drooping bulbously from the ceiling. And the orb appears in every work on the wall – his first foray into pastels after a body of quiet, austere paintings. It’s a red buoy with a boat tethered to it, it’s a paper Ikea ceiling lamp, it’s the knob on top of a banister, a ball on a table. All these orbs are weird, ghostly presences – he draws precisely but foggily, everything is hazy, uncomfortable, all the shadows are harsh, all the lighting is dramatic. They’re awesome images, strange and discomfiting. It’s like he escaped a fate that just keeps coming back to pester him, leaving the traces of what could have been dotted throughout his life for him to notice.
In one image, a huge orb has crushed a man, based on a still from 60s TV show The Prisoner. Life can crush you, or you can dodge the ball of fate and make your own way.
The phrase “green energy” promises natural, ecological optimism. But it’s something a lot more toxic in Amélie Mckee’s debut UK exhibition, a few doors down from David Micheaud’s show.

Two ionic columns in the centre of the space have been turned into Tesla towers, most of the stone replaced with metal. In the middle of each, vintage 1930s dinner plates glow a sickly green because they’re made of uranium. The same stuff we use to build nuclear weapons used to be fine china for dinner parties. Mckee is making the line between caloric energy and industrial power feel pretty blurry.
On a plinth, more gross glow: a can of Monster Energy drink has been poured into a 1928 pin tray with the figure of a nude woman now seeming to swim in the yellow sludge.

The gallery text is some of the most incomprehensible semi-English bullshit I’ve read for a long while, which makes figuring the work out a little tricky, but I think I get it. This is about authority and energy, about fuel on an industrial and personal level, about how toxic our relationship with power (who controls it, who consumes it, the greed and evil of it all) has become. It’s all framed in a semi-retro, toxic sludge aesthetic. Power corrupts, but energy is monstrous.
Plicnik Space Initiative, London, until 19 December

items.title: CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house
paragraphs: Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House-Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.
Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.
Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.
Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.
“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.
“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.
The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.
“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” said Barnes.
“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.
“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.
Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.
Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.
Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

“It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” said Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”
Inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-plan kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.
Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.
Above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.
The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

Interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.
Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.
A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.
CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.
“We think it’s important to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.
“These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”
CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

items.title: My all-time favourite pro headphones got a £100 price cut for Black Friday
paragraphs: I test out the very best audiophile wired headphones for a living and out of all of them, the best open-back option is hands down the HEDDphone D1. And even at its original price of £599, it's worth every penny.
But thanks to this early Black Friday headphone deal, the HEDDphone D1 is now down from £599 to £499 over at Peter Tyson.

Open-back headphones are the holy grail for audiophiles craving a spacious soundstage, but they usually offer some unique hurdles to achieve true tonal accuracy. When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I said that the German audio company had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

At 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.
This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
paragraphs: They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.
In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, launched to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a big impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.
For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.
Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.
“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”
The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all users.
“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a company after that.”
The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.
“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”
As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.
Arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.
“The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.
That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.
“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.
When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.
But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

“I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”
“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”
For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.
“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”

Lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.
Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.
“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” said Abascal.
“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”
Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

“Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a big issue and will be forever for these big cities.”

There is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

items.title: How Blackpool gets ready for Strictly Come Dancing
paragraphs: The Strictly Come Dancing stage takes shape inside the historic Blackpool Tower Ballroom ahead of this weekend's live show
Long before the sequins start to sparkle under the lights and the judges prepare to lift their paddles to deliver their scores, Blackpool Tower Ballroom is a hive of activity.
I have arrived here before Strictly Come Dancing returns to our screens from the famous ballroom.
While instantly recognisable, the venue is very different from what BBC One viewers will see on Saturday night.
Instead of dancers taking to the floor, a team of production crew is taking over with a different kind of choreography.
Standing beneath the lighting rig, I find myself looking up rather than down at the famous dance floor. Above me are hundreds of lights, hoisted into position days before anyone steps on to the set.

It is only when I sit in the balcony that the scale of the operation becomes clear. Camera tracks snake across the room, crews move between rehearsals, and every few minutes somebody is testing a new cue.
Dozens of cameras, lighting rigs and crew members transform the ballroom into a live television studio ahead of the weekend's show
Blackpool week has become one of the most eagerly anticipated dates in the Strictly calendar.

Contestants spend weeks hoping they will survive long enough to perform beneath the ballroom's famous chandeliers, while fans look forward to the spectacular routines that the venue has become known for.
It's Olympic skeleton racing champion and Strictly contestant Tabby Stoecker's first time in Blackpool.
"Everyone has been describing the ballroom but I can't believe I get to dance in here," she says.
"I don't have words for this - it's so ornate and beautiful."
Fellow contestant Graeme Hall, also known as The Dog Father, says he has been "thinking of all the dancers who have been on this iconic floor, and now that'll be us on Saturday night".
Mirror balls hang from the ceiling of the Blackpool Tower Ballroom, ready to sparkle under the studio lights
While the spotlight is often on the celebrities and their journeys, Blackpool holds a special place in the hearts of the professional dancers.
Many of them hit the pinnacle of their competitive careers on this very floor.
Last year's Glitterball winner Carlos Gu says he "dreamt of coming to Blackpool every year since I was a kid in China - we heard about Blackpool before London".
He says: "Blackpool is the place where all dancers' dreams come true, it's a place that holds so many dance legends."
Fellow professional Lauren Oakley has an unusual claim to fame - she performed in Blackpool before she was born.
Oakley explains: "My mum won the British Championships in Blackpool when she was pregnant with me
"I can't count how many times I've been here - it holds so many memories and now it's nice to be here with Strictly."
Actor Jamie Winstone and professional dancer Carlos Gu pose backstage overlooking the Blackpool Tower Ballroom
The ballroom is a landmark in its own right, attracting visitors from around the world, but for one week each year it becomes the centre of one of the BBC's biggest shows.
By Saturday night, the cables will be hidden, the equipment will fade into the background and the focus will be firmly on the celebrities competing for a place in the next round.
But after seeing what is involved in bringing Strictly to Blackpool, it is very clear that the production off the dance floor is almost as impressive as what happens on it.
You can watch Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One from 18:35 GMT on Saturday

items.title: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
paragraphs: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.
Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
paragraphs: AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.
The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.

In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: How much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?

There are two new indices that rank countries and US states on brain capital, using about 60 indicators ranging from child poverty to the prevalence of Parkinson’s disease. Yet they both possess a flaw: neither measures whether people’s livelihoods are secure – whether income is predictable, debts are manageable or homes are safe. The World Health Organization counts safety and security among the foundations of brain health, but nobody building these indices asked people what drains their mental capacity.

I call this missing liability “cognitive taxation”. It is a tax no government voted for, levied on attention, memory and the capacity to learn, and collected through rents, debts and welfare paperwork. Worry over insecurity runs in the background like an app draining a phone battery, and over years, the chronic stress wears down the brain itself. And AI is raising the rate.

Livelihood pressures stack up to exceed what one mind can handle. Poverty manufactures its own interest payments. Imagine a week in which a worker’s rent goes up and she loses a shift at the last minute, something common for workers without guaranteed hours. She puts the shortfall on a credit card. Preoccupied with finding the rent, she returns a benefits form late and loses part of her benefits payment as a penalty. Three small setbacks leave her household poorer in money, headspace and health.

Financial scarcity measurably impairs how well people think, but the effect lifts when the pressure does too, according to a 2024 analysis of 112,000 people in the Journal of Economic Psychology. Low-paid workers in rural India who received their wages a few days early were 7% more productive and made fewer mistakes. When South Africa lowered the pension age for men from 65 to 60, those who became eligible earlier showed slower memory decline and were about five percentage points less likely to develop dementia.

Though AI is increasing the value of human judgment, it also increases cognitive taxation. Automation makes work less predictable, shifting and shortening schedules, long before it eliminates jobs, as Walmart staff dealing with AI-set schedules have found. Meanwhile, overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue, according to research by the Boston Consulting Group. Workers required to retrain for the AI economy will struggle to learn new skills if their minds are already occupied by worries over pay, housing and debt.

Britain shows what insecurity already costs before AI adds to it. About 2.7 million people there are out of work through long-term sickness. And my institute’s research found that people facing insecurity across several areas of life carry an earnings penalty as large as the gender pay gap, one that roughly doubles after seven years. Those findings suggest that worry erodes how well people work. Now the UK’s AI minister says the government must seriously consider that the tech could have “an unprecedented impact” on the jobs market. Worries abound and compound.

When Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would bring “universal high income”, he offered Silicon Valley’s favourite answer to job losses: cash. Yet a study funded by Sam Altman, giving low-income Americans $1,000 a month, found that mental health gains faded after the first year. Extra cash helps, but it cannot guarantee a place for your child at a nursery or a bus that gets you to work on time. These pressures already tax the minds of people in work, and no payment removes them.

The better answer to cognitive tax and job loss is universal basic services, providing childcare, housing, transport and digital access, free at the point of use. The principle is the one behind the UK’s National Health Service: people should be able to rely on essential support without facing a bill when they use it. Extending free childcare alone is expected to bring 60,000 non-working parents into jobs in the UK.

Every government should ask this question of every fiscal policy: How will this policy affect the cognitive load of the poorest people it touches? Britain, which takes over the G20 presidency after December’s summit in Miami, should put it to the world’s largest economies. This question belongs in every treasury’s fiscal plans, brain-capital indices and AI-powered public services before they launch.

Sixty years ago we learned to count the damage economies do to the air and water, and it has changed how we build infrastructure for the better. Now that AI is making our minds the most valuable thing we have, it is time we count the damage done to them.
Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.title: Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"
paragraphs: Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.
“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.
This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.
“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.
Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.
“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.
The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the issues that will dominate the next century”.
Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”
The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.
“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.
The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

items.title: GTA 6's environmental storytelling is hidden in the details you might never notice
paragraphs: The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

“The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

“Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he says. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger says, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”
It’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Percy Jackson returns as teen stars adapt to life in the limelight
paragraphs: Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.
As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.
The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.
Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.
"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."
Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.
His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.
In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, external, he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.
Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".
"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."
The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.
An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.
So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.
"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.
"So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."
Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.
"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.
"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."
It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".
The first series was hugely successful with the opening episode of it reaching 13.3 million viewers, according to entertainment data company Luminate.
That dipped to just over 11 million for the second series and the cast is hoping a fresh take on the story will keep fans interested.
"I personally really like seeing people theorise about what's going to make it," says Simhadri.
"People who have read the books like talking about how they think we're going to adapt it, I love reading those."
It's been a big year for Greek mythology adaptations, with Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey getting huge box office numbers and critical acclaim.
Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Athena's daughter Annabeth Chase, says its popularity could be down to how people connect the ancient stories to their own lives.
"There's stories for everyone," she says.
"You can have a family where the dad is obsessed with The Odyssey but the children are too young, so they can just watch Percy Jackson.
"I feel like there's probably a cooking show about Greek mythology at that point, I mean like there's so many connections no matter what you like."
Percy Jackson is released on Disney+ and Hulu on Friday 20 November.

items.title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller covers Christmas classic
paragraphs: The singer-songwriter from Pontprennau in Cardiff recently sang at the Carnaby Street Christmas lights switch-on in London
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.
In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.
The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.
While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."
His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.
Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.
Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).
Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.
The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.
Before Miller, the last Welsh solo male artist to top the singles chart was Shakin' Stevens with Merry Christmas Everyone
Regardless of the outcome of the Christmas charts, it is clear the success of Babydoll has had an enormous impact on the singer's life.
He previously shared with the BBC that "nothing feels normal" after the success of the track.
The star said Babydoll came after "a really, really hard few years in my personal life" and with almost 10 years of trying to make it in the industry, he had decided to give it one "last chance".
Miller praised his mum, Anne, when he appeared on the podcast The Person Who Believed in Me for her unwavering support.
He said that, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.
But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".
"She's just the best thing that's ever happened to me," Miller said.
Miller lives in Los Angeles and says, no matter the time difference, his mum Anne "will always be there on the end of a phone call"
He also credited Anne for helping him get out of the "dark headspace" he was in some years ago: "There was a point where I didn't want to be here anymore. Being in that mind-frame was really scary."

He said she flew to the United States where he was living to spend time with him, and her love for him, expressed in "going on beach walks, going to grab me a coffee, pulling me out of bed", was what "got him out".
Miller also disclosed that money was something he had worried about throughout his life, adding the moment he knew he had "made it" was when he earned enough to help his parents retire.
The singer said his mum had "served everybody else for so long" and talked excitedly about calling her to say: "By the way Mum, you never have to work again."
Miller said his mum was a cleaner who suffered from arthritis, and all he wanted to do was "take those products out of her hands and give her the life she deserves".
Perry Como's It's Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas currently has almost 600 million streams on Spotify, while Michael Bublé's cover has more than 1.3 billion
The artist, who describes his style as "future-vintage pop", will join a host of singers who have covered It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas, including Bing Crosby and Michael Bublé.
The song, first recorded by Perry Como and The Fontane Sisters, is a festive staple despite never reaching Christmas number one.
It remains to be seen whether Miller could change this, and the announcement of who has topped the Christmas chart will come on BBC Radio 1 Christmas Day.
Miller's cover of It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas is released on Friday. 20 November.
If you need support with mental health or feelings of despair, help and support is available via BBC Action Line.

items.title: "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"
paragraphs: Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong‘s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.
And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.
Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks
There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.
In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.
You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.
When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.
Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
paragraphs: Switching to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet the UK's net zero targets
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March.
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets.
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.

Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many.

The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.
Check if you are eligible for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, external
For low-income households and those in social housing, the government is providing an extra £5bn for the Warm Homes Local Grant, external and the Social Housing Fund, external.
Scotland, external and Northern Ireland, external have separate schemes to help make homes more efficient.
UK households can also apply for low and no interest loans of between £7,500 and £35,000 to install green technologies under the Warm Homes Loan Scheme, external.
The government has promised to keep funding for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at £400m in 2027-28 before increasing it in line with inflation.
However, this represents a significant cut compared to what was previously announced.

Some of the money the energy and environment departments have to spend on loans and investments is also being diverted towards the £4.7bn "Your First Home" scheme, which aims to help people purchase a property.
This could mean further cuts to the Warm Homes Scheme, but the government has said it "remains committed to heat-pump deployment".
Heat pump installations currently benefit from a 0% VAT rate, but this is set to rise to 5% in April 2027.

While the upfront costs remain substantial, heat pumps could become cheaper to run than gas boilers, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC), external, which advises the UK government on cutting emissions.
Savings depend on energy prices and how efficiently the heat pump works.
Electric heat pumps use around three to four times less energy than gas boilers, but electricity typically costs much more than gas.
At the moment the cost of electricity is mostly driven by gas prices in the UK and around the world, but the government expects this to change as renewable energy expands.
A modest reduction in prices is also expected from the scrapping of VAT on electricity bills.
Households who install solar panels can potentially save more by generating their own energy rather than relying on the grid.
The innovation charity Nesta estimates that the average home with a heat pump and solar panels could cut its annual energy bill by nearly £1,000.
For a typical household on dual fuel tariff
Previously, homeowners needed planning permission to install a heat pump within 1m (3ft) of a neighbour's property because of concerns about noise.
The rule was dropped to encourage uptake.
Newer devices are also quieter and must be below 42db, which is similar to the level of noise produced by a fridge.
Rules specifying the size and number of heat pumps which households can install have also been relaxed.
More gas boilers continue to be installed in the UK than heat pumps, which are found in fewer than 2% of homes.
Installation rates are also lower than in other major European countries, like France, Germany and Italy.
Sales have increased significantly in recent years though there are concerns progress is slowing.
Double the number of heat pumps were installed in the first half of 2026, external compared to the same period of 2021.
However, this is 22% fewer than were installed in the first half of 2025.
The CCC says sales need to rise to nearly 450,000 a year by 2030 and 1.5 million by 2035 to help meet climate targets.
It says around half of UK homes need to have heat pumps by 2040.
Significantly more trained heat pump installers are needed to achieve this.

items.title: The best designers in the world right now
