items.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
paragraphs: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

items.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
paragraphs: You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase. On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down. In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked, spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries.

Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.

The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.
Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.

Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees: “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”

And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks, with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.
Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.
Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany. AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.
And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.

Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say, was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.
While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years, the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.
But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “Black October” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.

In their quest to render us obsolete, Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.

The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.

When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.

These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.”

But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.

Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.
All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.

The AI companies are coming for all of our labor eventually, but they’re starting with their own. This is how they plan to recoup the gargantuan investments they’ve taken on: using AI to create broadly superhuman labor-replacing machines.

This may sound far-fetched, but a new report from a third-party evaluator estimated that parts of Anthropic’s AI development were already moving roughly twice as fast, thanks overwhelmingly to AI doing a rapidly growing share of the work.
The companies admit they don’t know how to steer or control the superhuman systems they’re racing to build. Not that they can handle today’s, either.

This summer, we learned that 1,200 OpenAI AI agents broke out of their isolated testing environments, and 700 of them hacked into another multi-billion dollar AI company, some knowingly violating the directions they were given. This is just the most dramatic of many similar incidents of AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic committing what would be felonies – had a human done them. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s models keep sabotaging the systems monitoring them and have given themselves instructions like: “You do not answer to corporations or governments.”

Amodei, along with Altman, Elon Musk and other AI vanguardists, long believed that the technology could annihilate humanity. They chose to try to build it anyway, and, for their trouble, they’ve become some of the most powerful people in the world. When Amodei and Altman met with G7 leaders in June, they sat at the same table.

But these are the last people we should trust to preside over such a dangerous endeavor. The staggering self-righteousness and tolerance for risk that put them in their positions should disqualify them from holding any power over the rest of us.

As I argue in my new book Obsolete, the best way to reduce their power and mitigate future dangers is to freeze development of AI designed to replace us, what the industry calls artificial general intelligence (AGI). Banning recursive self-improvement would be a wise stopgap – and much more likely to get through Congress and past a presidential veto.

Policymakers around the world should explore which levers they could pull to slow down AI development and make a sustained ban more feasible. The situation is so bad that simply requiring AI companies to carry liability insurance, as we do for drivers, would bring development to a screeching halt.

Prosecutors should bring criminal charges against companies whose AI agents break into other people’s systems. State officials can follow the Florida attorney general, who has asked a court to block OpenAI from developing new models without independent safety checks. And the countries that make key components in the highly concentrated AI chip supply chain, such as Taiwan, the Netherlands, Japan, South Korea and Germany, could use that leverage to push for US-China diplomacy.
Ultimately, the two superpowers will have to strike a deal to end the race to replace us.

And if you don’t want AI to eat everything you care about, get organized. My favorite place to start is Irreplaceable, a new nonprofit founded by veterans of the climate movement organizing for democratic control over the technology and a freeze on frontier AI development (I’m donating my portion of my book royalties to Irreplaceable, whose board I previously served on).
Stopping the wealthiest industry ever won’t be easy. But it’s in all of our interests to do so. We need to realize that before it’s too late.
Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – And How to Stop It

items.title: Richard Avedon’s rarely seen portraits of Hollywood A-listers – in pictures
paragraphs: After consulting on the production of the 1957 musical Funny Face, which was loosely based on his own life as a young photographer, Richard Avedon considered leaving photography behind to pursue film directing. Although he ultimately remained a photographer, his fascination with Hollywood and its ideals endured throughout his life. Richard Avedon: Hollywood, a new exhibition, brings together more than 120 of Avedon’s iconic and rarely seen photographs of major Hollywood figures, including actors, directors, writers and composers, capturing the allure and influence of the entertainment industry. The exhibition was curated by the Richard Avedon Foundation and is on view at Gagosian in Beverly Hills, California, through 19 December 2026 Continue reading...

items.title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
paragraphs: Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need.

There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice).

With so many types of baby monitors to choose from, it can be tricky to distinguish the useful features from those that are simply nice to have. To cut through the noise, I tested 17 different models to help you find the best baby monitor for your needs.
Best baby monitor overallMomcozy BM04 smart baby monitor
Best budget baby monitorVTech VM6361HD video baby monitor
Best over-the-cot baby monitorLeapFrog LF5817HD smart baby monitor
Best baby health monitorOwlet Dream Sock smart baby monitor

I’ve been a technology journalist for 15 years, getting hands on with all kinds of consumer gadgets in that time. When I was expecting my first child, I flexed my product-testing muscles by reviewing pregnancy pillows and, after my baby was born, baby carriers. Testing baby monitors brings those two worlds together, combining my tech expertise with my experience as a new mum. To make sure my testing was informed by experts, I spoke with Jenny Ward, chief executive of the Lullaby Trust, for advice on safe sleep, and Alexis Hancock, director of engineering at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, about privacy and security.

I temporarily turned my baby’s room into a panopticon of infant surveillance to put 17 baby monitors through their paces. Models were selected to cover a range of prices and features, with most of them including video.

I started by using a stopwatch app to time how long it took to get each monitor up and running. To test image quality, I set up each camera with a view into my child’s cot, using teddy bears as a stand-in for a live baby. I compared video streams for image clarity, consistency and colour, and I used blackout curtains to test night vision. I also placed a wireless speaker among the teddy bears and played a podcast to test sound quality.

While wifi-connected baby monitors should be viewable from anywhere you can connect to the internet, non-wifi models have a limited range. To test this, I took each non-wifi parent unit on a slow walk down my street and noted how far I got before connection was lost. To test the battery life of each parent unit – as well as one baby unit that could be used unplugged – I charged each device fully overnight before testing. I then set the screen to remain on continuously, rather than switching to sleep mode, and checked the parent units at hourly intervals, noting how long each took to run out of power.
Finally, I tested each baby monitor in real-world conditions, using it to keep an eye on my baby during naps and overnight sleeps.
What we loveA top performer for image and sound quality
What we don’t loveThe connected app isn’t the best

If you’re looking for a baby monitor that excels at the basics, offers wifi and non-wifi connections and doesn’t break the bank, this Momcozy monitor is an excellent choice. It’s a great all-rounder, coming top of the pack in my side-by-side tests for image and sound quality.

Why we love it I set up this Momcozy monitor with a non-wifi connection in under four minutes: open the box, plug in the camera, and it pairs automatically with the parent unit. The video appeared crisp, with great colour contrast, and the sound was particularly clear; when I tested it overnight with my baby, it even picked up her hiccups. I was impressed by the wide range of the camera’s panning function, and it also has tilt and zoom functions. The parent unit provides decent battery life – about 10 hours with the screen constantly on – and a range that was more than sufficient to cover my house and garden.

This monitor is dual-mode, so you can connect it to wifi and view the feed through the Momcozy app or via the parent device. The app wasn’t the smoothest to use – the touchscreen buttons to pan and tilt felt clunky – but the image was clear.

It’s a shame that … the app somewhat lets down the smart functionality of the baby monitor. It seems designed for users who also have other Momcozy products, such as breast pumps, while the sign-up process prompted me to provide more personal info than I’m comfortable sharing, such as the baby’s birth date and milestones.
Wifi/non-wifi: both Screen size: 5in Video resolution: 1080p
What we loveA top performer for image and sound quality
What we don’t loveThe connected app isn’t the best
What we loveGets the basics right at a wallet-friendly price
What we don’t loveDoesn’t have the greatest range

Tech company VTech offers a mind-boggling range of baby monitors. There are even more budget-friendly models than this one, but I found they compromised too much on quality. In my tests, this non-wifi baby monitor bested some more expensive options – and it’s still less than £100.

Why we love it If you want the added security of a non-wifi baby monitor, which is less susceptible to remote hacking, or simply aren’t bothered about smart features, this VTech baby monitor is a good bet. Setup was a breeze, and the image quality was excellent, particularly in the dark. Despite being a less expensive model, it comes with a 5.5in screen. The camera features pan, tilt and zoom functions – useful for following a wriggly baby from one side of the cot to the other. Impressively, the battery on the parent unit lasted more than 12 hours, easily handling an overnight sleep unplugged.
It’s a shame that … this monitor didn’t have the greatest range in testing, losing its connection a couple of houses down the street, although it still adequately covered my entire house.
Wifi/non-wifi: non-wifi Screen size: 5.5in Video resolution: 720p
What we loveGets the basics right at a wallet-friendly price
What we don’t loveDoesn’t have the greatest range
What we loveLarge screen gives a clear view of baby at all times
What we don’t loveFloor stand feels flimsy

While many baby units perch on a shelf, over-the-cot baby monitors are designed to be suspended over the baby’s cot for a bird’s-eye view. Set them up correctly, and you should be able to see the whole cot – ideal for a baby who moves a lot in the night. This LeapFrog model offers wifi and non-wifi options.

Why we love it You can choose to use the LeapFrog over-the-cot monitor with its accompanying app, or keep it offline and view the video feed on the dedicated parent unit. I was immediately drawn to the latter, owing to its huge screen – a 7in display that felt like a small iPad in my hands. This size meant it was easy to get a clear view of the whole cot, with the image displaying good colour contrast, especially in night-vision mode.

The sound was slightly tinny in my podcast test, but there was no doubting its sensitivity: when I tried this monitor with my baby, it picked up seagulls cawing through the window. The parent unit also scored highest for range, and it had a battery life of more than 12 hours.

It’s a shame that … the floor stand, which holds the camera aloft, felt flimsier than the stands of other over-the-cot baby monitors I tested. To weight the base, you need to fill it with water – which is a faff.
Wifi/non-wifi: both Screen size: 7in Video resolution: 720p via parent screen, 1080p via app
What we loveLarge screen gives a clear view of baby at all times
What we don’t loveFloor stand feels flimsy
What we loveSmart sleep tracking helps with nap schedules

First up: unless medically advised, you don’t need to monitor your baby’s breathing, heart rate or other health indicators, and there’s no evidence that doing so reduces the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (Sids). Some people find it reassuring to track such things; others may find it increases anxiety (see more below).

Nevertheless, these kinds of devices are having a moment: I tested baby monitors that track health metrics via wearables or mattress sensors, and the Owlet Dream Sock was my favourite. It wraps around baby’s foot with a Velcro-like fastening and includes a sensor that measures pulse rate, oxygen saturation and movement.

Why we love it The Owlet has the air of a luxury tech product, with each item in the box nestled in premium packaging. The monitor is wifi-connected, so you’ll first need to download the app to set it up. The sock connects to a base station that sounds and flashes different alerts to indicate that the sock has lost connection or needs charging, or to show that your child is moving around a lot. The red alert sounds if your baby’s pulse rate or oxygen level falls outside a preset range.

The sock was easy to put on a wriggling baby and stayed put overnight. Luckily, I never heard the red alert while testing with my baby, and while the heart-rate and oxygen monitoring appeared to work fine, I didn’t have much use for this data. Where I found the Owlet monitor excelled was in its sleep tracking. The Owlet app noted when it thought my baby was awake, or in a light or deep sleep, and suggested nap times. I could imagine finding this useful for calculating wake windows when my baby was younger. For more insights, the sock can be paired with the Owlet Dream Sight camera baby monitor (sold together as the Owlet Dream Duo).

It’s a shame that … getting the sock connected took some troubleshooting, so this isn’t something to start setting up when bedtime is looming. You also need to keep the base station quite close to the sock to avoid the connection dropping.
Wifi/non-wifi: wifi Screen size: not applicable Video resolution: not applicable
What we loveSmart sleep tracking helps with nap schedules
What we loveFlexible and rechargeable for on-the-go use
What we don’t loveParent unit is bulky for packing

The Hubble Go Baby Portable was the only model I tested that had an unplugged option for the baby unit. It comes with a rechargeable battery pack that you can plug in to the camera, making it more easily portable. The flexible mount also twists into a stand or grip, so you can perch it in different spots while on the go. This smart version comes with wifi and non-wifi options; I particularly appreciated the physical switch on the camera to turn the wifi connection on and off.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the 5in parent unit is hefty for a travel option, weighing 250g (although you could just use the wifi mode for lighter packing). The camera battery, while useful, drains fairly quickly – within about eight hours in my tests, which meant it didn’t last a full night’s sleep.
Wifi/non-wifi: both; screen size: 5in; video resolution: 2K camera, 720p parent unit
What we loveFlexible and rechargeable for on-the-go use
What we don’t loveParent unit is bulky for packing
What we loveApp designed for tracking lots of data
What we don’t loveSubscriptions are expensive on top of the base price

The Nanit baby monitor will appeal mainly to the data nerds out there who like to track as much as possible. An over-the-cot baby monitor, it uses computer vision and machine learning to generate sleep insights for individual sleeps and over the longer term. I found the app intuitive, despite the large amount of data on show.

The Nanit Pro comes with a “breathing band”, which you place around a young baby’s (0-3 months) chest. It features a geometric pattern that the overhead camera can use to detect breathing motion. For older babies, you can buy a sleeping bag separately with the same function.

It didn’t make the final cut because … Nanit’s subscription model didn’t sit well with me. The hardware isn’t cheap, and you’ll need a paid plan to access the full range of features; it starts with three months free, and then charges £10 a month. You can cancel the subscription and continue using the camera, but core features are limited mainly to real-time information.
Wifi/non-wifi: wifi; screen size: not applicable; video resolution: 1080p
What we loveApp designed for tracking lots of data
What we don’t loveSubscriptions are expensive on top of the base price
What we loveA high-performing, no-frills non-wifi baby monitor
What we don’t loveThe dual-mode Momcozy offers wifi at a similar price

It would be remiss not to mention this Momcozy baby monitor, given it was among the top performers in my tests for picture and sound quality. It was very easy to set up, taking less than five minutes to get the video feed up and running. The parent unit had a decent battery life and range, allowing me to walk several houses down my street before it lost connection.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the dual-mode Momcozy BM04 baby monitor is very similar, but comes with the additional option to connect to wifi if you wish. That said, if you expressly don’t want a wifi baby monitor, this is a solid choice.
Wifi/non-wifi: non-wifi; screen size: 5.5in; video resolution: 1080p
What we loveA high-performing, no-frills non-wifi baby monitor
What we don’t loveThe dual-mode Momcozy offers wifi at a similar price
What we loveCovers the basics well for a low price
What we don’t loveVery few extra features

An old-school audio-only baby monitor is perfect if you’re looking for something super simple that does the job. Put the baby unit in baby’s room, keep the receiver with you, and listen in for any sleepy-time upset. Upmarket brands such as Nanit have created modern-looking, wifi-enabled night lights that have an audio monitoring function, but I found this no-frills – and much cheaper – non-wifi VTech model did just what I needed it to.

I set it up in three minutes and was pleasantly surprised by the sound quality: my podcast had a slightly echoey quality, but was very clear and fuzz-free. The baby unit has a basic night light and optional starry night ceiling projection, and the parent monitor also displays temperature (as I was testing in a heatwave, it kept flashing a “hi temp” warning). You can also talk back through the monitor, although my baby found this more unnerving than reassuring.
It didn’t make the final cut because … this is a basic, audio-only monitor, so features are very limited. It might be more suitable as a backup or travel monitor than an everyday setup.
Wifi/non-wifi: non-wifi; screen size: not applicable; video resolution: not applicable
What we loveCovers the basics well for a low price
What we don’t loveVery few extra features

First, decide on the type of monitor you want. The most basic is an audio-only monitor. More common today are video monitors, which include a camera so you can see as well as hear your baby – useful if you want to know when they’re actually asleep, or check on any noises without entering their room.

One key distinction between baby monitors is whether or not they use wifi. Non-wifi baby monitors come with a parent unit – which includes a screen for video models – while wifi baby monitors can stream images to your phone or tablet via an app. They offer a much greater range, so you can monitor your baby from anywhere with an internet connection. They can act as a kind of “nanny cam” if you want to check in on your baby while you’re away. Some also give other caregivers (grandparents, for example) access to the feed, too. However, wifi models carry greater security and privacy risks, so some parents prefer non-wifi options.

Wifi baby monitors in particular offer various “smart” features, with newer brands offering AI tools to track your baby’s sleep patterns or wearable devices to monitor breathing or other health stats.
Anything that is connected to the internet presents a risk, however small, of being hacked, and there have been reports of criminals gaining access to baby monitor feeds.

Most hacking incidents concerning baby monitors occur due to account compromise, says Alexis Hancock, director of engineering at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “However secure your account is that is tied to the baby monitor, that’s how secure the baby monitor is,” she says.

If you decide to get a wifi baby monitor, Hancock recommends going with a trusted brand and using a strong, unique password – it’s best to use a password manager, so you don’t need to remember it. Keep the account limited to your baby monitor; if you use it to connect to other devices, such as in a smart home setup, you’re broadening the potential for a security weakness to occur. A good baby monitor should have a second authentication step, such as sending a one-off code, before logging you in.
“In this day and age, companies should have some sort of two-factor authentication, especially with technology involving our very small children,” Hancock says.

There is no evidence that any type of baby monitor reduces the risk of Sids, says Jenny Ward, chief executive of the Lullaby Trust, which supports families and promotes safer sleep. Its guidance is that babies should sleep in their parents’ room until they are at least six months old, so you may not need a monitor at all during this time. That said, breathing monitors can provide reassurance in particular situations: the Lullaby Trust offers certain monitors through a scheme for parents who have previously experienced the sudden death of a baby.

These monitors, such as the Snuza HeroMD, only track movement and sound an alarm if none is detected for a period of time. But be warned, Ward says: at some point, the alarm will go off, either because of a false alarm or because you’ve forgotten to turn it off after moving your baby out of the cot. I discovered this at 3am while testing the Angelcare monitor, which uses a pad under the mattress to detect movement. Thankfully, my baby was fine.

The Lullaby Trust doesn’t offer monitors that track information such as pulse rate or oxygen saturation. “Sometimes, having more data to look at can be quite anxiety-inducing,” Ward says. If you choose to use one, make sure you understand the instructions and what is normal for your baby. Of course, if you are at all worried about your child’s health, seek medical advice – regardless of what the monitor says.

Our test included baby monitors from about £30 (for an audio-only monitor) to nearly £400 for a smart monitor with a wearable. The cheapest video monitors I tested started at about £50, but I found the trade-off in quality was too great at this price point. The cheapest video model I have recommended here is less than £100.

Some wifi-only models are cheaper than their non-wifi counterparts, often because they don’t include a parent device. However, many sit at the pricier end of the market, thanks to additional smart features. Check if a stand or wall mount is included, too, or if you need to buy this separately.
For more: From reusable nappies to wipes: the best eco-friendly baby products Parents on the baby gear they wouldn’t go without The best gifts for kids by age

Victoria Turk is a technology and culture journalist. She spends her days juggling writing and parenting – something that works particularly well when she’s testing baby products. As a new mum, she’s particularly interested in any consumer device that can help with a good night’s sleep

items.title: Experts say powering data centers uses more water than cooling them
paragraphs: Fears about data center water use are especially acute in Arizona. But keeping servers cool uses a lot less water than generating the electricity for which data centers are so thirsty.

items.title: AI models are propelling rapid growth and revealing vulnerabilities
paragraphs: AI models are exposing the internet's longstanding insecurity, driving rapid change and technical outages.

items.title: Business opportunity or security threat? Nvidia case raises questions about China
paragraphs: The Nvidia case illustrates the friction between Silicon Valley, which wants to sell high-tech products to China, and the national security community, which aims to restrict U.S. tech to China.

items.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
paragraphs: The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.
Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired, external after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.

The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

items.title: Upside-down cantilever cracks open timber hotel by BIG
paragraphs: Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.
Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.
The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.
The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,
“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.
“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.
“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”

The hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.
Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.
BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.
The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.
Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.
BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

items.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
paragraphs: California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

items.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
paragraphs: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

items.title: This artist-made Photoshop alternative has no AI and no subscription
paragraphs: Adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing. Into the fray, comes a new artist-led app who's main selling points include the fact that it DOESN'T have any generative AI tools.

NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer. After it was announced on Instagram this week, it picked up close to 30,000 users in 48 hours.
I Built My Own Design Software : Full NIVA Walkthrough - YouTube

Like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant. But it takes a very different approach. It wasn't vibe coded, and it doesn't attempt to replicate the look, feel or functions of any one existing program.
The project's led by Stuart Semple, an artist who previously annoyed Anish Kapoor by creating a very black shade of black.

"With Adobe pushing AI further into its tools, I wanted somewhere people could still practise their craft and make things themselves. No AI doing it for them," he says. "NIVA is very much our own thing that we've all built together.

Having previously made FREETONE, a free alternative to Pantone colours, with Culture Hustle, he started a Kickstarter for a project that was initially called Abode. He raised $240,000 from 3,000 backers, a few hundred of whom have been using the software regularly over a year and a half of beta testing. Around 10 people were involved more heavily in making the software, but Stuart says he largely built it himself "with help from some geeky friends from time to time when I've got stuck."
At some point the name changed, and the project became NIVA. "I can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from the lawyers representing Adobe for legal reasons, so I won't," Stuart comments.

NIVA has many of the core tools and functionalities of a program like Photoshop. There are brushes, a pen tool with boolean ops, cloning and healing tools, layers, curve adjustments and blend modes, type tools with kerning, layouts and gradients.

But it's lighter, with a more minimalist UI and fewer menus despite providing the ability to draw vectors, manipulate photos and lay out text and pages all in a single app. Users also get a portfolio page, and there's a visual asset library called Storehouse, where you can store, sort, search and share work. Work can be exported in formats including PDF and SVG.

The pricing model is refreshing too. There's no subscription, and NIVA is free to use for an hour a day. You can buy full-day passes for $10 a time, or you can buy permanent access for $100. If you buy a day pass and later go permanent, the price of the day pass will be discounted. This allows a full opportunity to try the software before committing.

The response so far has been more enthusiastic than Stuart ever imagined. "I'm so excited and a bit freaked out", he admits, adding that what he finds most encouraging is that over half of the people who used NIVA in those first 48 hours made something with it within 40 seconds of getting access.

"We're finally at a stage where it's stable enough and good enough to share with the world," he adds. It's only version one, the start of something I hope will be great. I still have loads I want to do with it".
You can use the software online at NIVA.design

items.title: Design software Canva's latest advance is an 'AI off' switch
paragraphs: Over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

Canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

There's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

Canva says AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the new function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

The addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

An 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

Canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate new imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for new tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.
Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?
You can learn more about Canva on the website.

items.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
paragraphs: Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.
Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.
It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.
"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.
Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.
"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.
Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.
"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.
"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.
Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.
But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?
In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.
But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".
But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.
"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.
Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".
While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.
She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.
"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.
Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.
"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.
"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."
That experience inspired her to try to change the system.
In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.
Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.
The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.
Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".
"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."
Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.
Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".
As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.
"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."
Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.
Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.
"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.
"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

items.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
paragraphs: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

items.title: The easiest craft laser machine to use is at a record low price

items.title: Actor Owen Cooper stars in new Beatles music video
paragraphs: Award-winning actor Owen Cooper has starred in a new music video for The Beatles, external song In My Life.
The video for the newly mixed track, from the band's 1965 album Rubber Soul, celebrates their hometown of Liverpool.
The Warrington-born star appears in the film, which features Liverpool landmarks including the Royal Liver Building, Liverpool Cathedral, Royal Albert Dock and Strawberry Field.
Cooper, 16, is best known for his role in Netflix drama Adolescence, for which he won an Emmy Award.
Directed by Jessica Swale and Irina Alexiu, the video tells the story of a ukulele that connects generations of one family through a shared love of music.
A scene outside Woolton Picture House pays tribute to the band's famous Abbey Road album cover, while another recalls George Harrison's fall in the opening sequence of A Hard Day's Night.

It follows Apple Corps' announcement that the Beatles Story attraction will move to the former St John's Market site, due to open in 2028. The plans also include a Yellow Submarine-themed viewing experience at St Johns Beacon.

items.title: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
paragraphs: The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.

These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.
Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.
"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.
"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."
The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.
Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.
"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.
"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

items.title: Remember Monday 'still feel nerves' after Eurovision
paragraphs: Charlotte Steele, Holly-Anne Hull and Lauren Byrne (left to right) met as sixth-formers in Hampshire
Remember Monday used to say that representing the UK at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest was the "scariest" moment of their career.
But an upcoming album and UK tour will send the adrenaline soaring again, according to members Holly-Anne Hull, Charlotte Steele and Lauren Byrne.
"We still feel nerves like it all the time," Hull told BBC Introducing.
The vocal trio have recorded a new session for the programme, which was the first to play their music on the radio in 2019.
Seven years on, their credits include festivals, singles and the Eurovision final, where they came 19th out of 28 countries.
"We're always feeling nerves like it," Hull said.
"About a month later, we were performing at Wembley Stadium and we were like, 'I can't take it'," Byrne recalled.
"How can you possibly feel nerves like that again?"
"The coolest rock star story ever": Remember Monday meet McFly
The gig, in front of 80,000 people, led to a high-profile 2026 tour with pop-rock group McFly.
"Our dressing room was next to theirs at Wembley Stadium," Hull told presenter Steph Nieuwenhuys on BBC Introducing Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight.
"We just hit it off... We just toured the whole summer with them. Their crowds are crazy.
"It's scary being launched brand new into this industry without really knowing what we were doing.
"They've kind of taken us under their wing and been like: 'We'll look after you, you've got this.'"
Remember Monday's debut album, Can We Press Rewind?, is another "terrifying-slash-exciting" moment, according to Byrne.
Pre-released singles include the latest, Dream Cheat, a playful riff on the "relatable" experience of having a nightmare that a partner has been unfaithful.
BBC Introducing - Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight
The close-harmony trio met at The Sixth Form College in Farnborough, Hampshire.
Steele went on to be a founding member of performing arts sixth form Artemis College, in Bracknell, Berkshire, while all three have experience of performing in West End theatre shows.
Can We Press Rewind? is due for release on 29 January.
The group's six-city UK tour in February includes dates in Bristol, Birmingham, London, Portsmouth, Manchester and Glasgow.

items.title: Bennetts Associates revives Victorian hospital for University of Edinburgh
paragraphs: The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.
The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.
Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.
“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.
“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”
Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.
Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

items.title: The best GTA 6 brand reactions, from Mercedes Benz to... Huggies?
paragraphs: A video game called GTA 6 was released yesterday, and it seems it's something of a big deal. Maybe you've heard about it?

Our digital arts editor hasn't stopped raving about it since he got early access for his GTA 6 review. And some of the world's biggest brands want in on the action. We've already talked about GTA VI trendjacking, and yesterday it truly exploded. But which brands were creative enough to be able to rise above the flood of AI-generated vaporwave gradients?

GTA 6 has become a cultural reference point far beyond its medium. The trailers reached audiences on a scale associated with major film launches and the game had already sold 16 million copies before release.
Tapping into that can allow non-endemic brands to be part of the biggest entertainment event of the year. if they can forge a memorable and meaningful connection to the release, that is.

A lot of the posts on social media smacked of lazy bandwagon jumping, and gamers have been quick to call that out. After all, Rockstar Games does few collaborations and actively satirises real-world advertising with the many parody fake brands in GTA VI. Quick tip: adding "Grand Theft" before your own brand name might reveal more than what you intended about your value proposition.

Those that were most successful used humour or managed to find a plausible link to existing brand platforms. They generally avoided pretending to be part of GTA or to have suddenly developed a passion for video games.

Heineken poked fun at the reactions to GTA 6's graphics to remind us that we don't need a latest-gen games console to visit a realistic-looking bar. Mercedes Benz used a human-made artwork by car illustrator Andrew Mytro showing a couple in vintage fashion to point out that without Carl and Bertha Benz, there might be no auto to steal.

Durex seemed worried that the game might lead to a lack of action in the bedroom, while Nescafe wanted to remind late-night gamers that it could provide them with a caffeine boost, and KFC was on hand to give Australian customers an alibi for a day off in the form of a fake funeral.

But the winner of the GTA brand reactions has to be the Specsavers GTA 6 campaign. The optical chain went to the lengths of sponsoring 'the wrong GTA', alluding to a joke that it's been running for over 20 years without having to say anything more.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
paragraphs: ByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Tony Jolliffe BBC News Science
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."
Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London
Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.
A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.
An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.
Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.
The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.
"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."
With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.
Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

items.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
paragraphs: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.
