The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

items.title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music
paragraphs: Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles.

I had mentioned the two versions, a routine enough inquiry, but it quickly turns into a discussion about the potential replacement of car stereos with immersive sound systems, which then unexpectedly shifts into an explanation of the work of Michael Levin, an American professor of bioengineering who specialises in morphogenesis. “He’s found some bio-electric instructions that can make an eye grow on the leg of a frog, for example,” says Gabriel, and has apparently “created life forms that never existed before, which really challenges evolution.” Gabriel is interested in “sonifying” some of his data and using it in a subsequent mix of the album.

From there, we move on to software engineer Blaise Agüera y Arcas, whose experiments with an esoteric 90s programming language called Brainfuck have led him to “the radical idea that some constants in maths might actually have some form of life”. This leads us, via the “re-evaluation of what consciousness is and what intelligence is”, to the belief of internet pioneer Vint Cerf that attempting to communicate with other intelligent species might prepare us for the possibility of encountering aliens, and thus to Savage-Rumbaugh and Kanzi the bonobo.

“She used to allow the bonobos to watch videos, and to choose the videos they watched,” Gabriel says, laughing, “and their favourite, perhaps obviously, was Planet of the Apes, then Harry and the Hendersons, which is a film about a sasquatch who came to live with a family. The whole thing blew me away. I think we’re the most arrogant of all apes, and there’s just so much intelligence we’ve chosen to ignore and instead see the world as something that’s entirely available for our exploitation, and I think that’s cost us, as we are now learning.”

Morphogenisis, inter-species communication, the re-evaluation of consciousness: it should go without saying that you don’t usually end up discussing these things when you ask an august rock legend about his latest album. But, as it turns out, that’s what inevitably happens when you ask Gabriel a question. We meet in a pub not far from his home in Notting Hill. He says he’s here “to sell the new album”, but almost every query about it seems to lead him somewhere completely different: science, activism, the nature of consciousness, how language is “a fairly crude tool” for communication, the controversial 1970s self-improvement courses of Werner Erhard.

You can’t fault his diversity of interests, even if that diversity of interests is why it takes so long for him to make albums. o\i is essentially the second part of a project that began with 2023’s i/o, which was his first album of new material in 21 years. Like its predecessor, it contains songs that Gabriel has spent decades tinkering with: he started work on A Hard Lesson in 1989, when he was still a huge mainstream pop star thanks to 1986’s So, an album that shifted more than 5m copies in the US alone.

Yes, he concedes, it is a bit weird to find yourself, at the age of 76, still working on songs you started writing in your 30s: “I recognise that guy, but you’re bound to make different decisions having lived a little longer.” But that’s just the way it is. His friend Laurie Anderson once suggested that Gabriel’s problem was that he was more interested in the process of making something than in finishing it. He thinks the real issue is that he’s easily distracted.

“If you have some measure of success, you end up meeting all sorts of people and having fascinating conversations, which lead to detours, and you think, ‘Well, life is for living,’” he says. “If you get on that conveyor belt of album-tour-album, there’s not time to breathe or have any kind of life, and that always seems somewhat sad to me. I think the diversions feed the music. You know, if you want a better class of shit, you’ve got to eat a more varied diet.”

Hence the digressive nature of our interview. Gabriel seems to have developed a genuinely intriguing theory about virtually everything, from theme parks to funerals: he thinks people should “plant a tree over their dead body, or the dead body of their loved ones, so you’d get woods where there wouldn’t be any signage, but if you go and sit under your dad’s tree, your phone would have the GPS position and you would start seeing his videos, hearing his voice, all the digital data would be locked into that GPS point”.

Moreover, he has an incredibly engaging way of talking about all this stuff, evincing such enthusiasm and curiosity that you’re carried along with him: on the off-chance that you wanted to pitch the idea of growing eyeballs on the legs of frogs, you could do substantially worse than get Gabriel to act as your salesman. It probably helps his cause that Gabriel has a hugely impressive track record of thinking ahead of the curve.

At the height of his fame as the frontman of Genesis, he was sharp enough to realise that the genre of progressive rock they had helped invent was becoming too grandiloquent and remote for its own good – “prancing around in fairyland” as he once put it – and that the band he had formed might be more successful without him. The latter opinion wasn’t very popular with the rest of Genesis, but nevertheless proved to be spot on.

A few years later, he was the first British artist to realise that the future of pop lay in sampling: for some time in the early 80s, if you wanted to use a sampler on your new track you had to borrow Gabriel’s, because he was the first person in the country to own one; he then set up a company to import and distribute the new technology. Twenty years later, he cottoned on very quickly to the idea that music was going to primarily exist online, co-founding a streaming platform that might have become the industry standard had it not launched at exactly the same time as a competitor called Spotify.

If he was right about everything from sampling to streaming to the latter-day career of Genesis, perhaps he’s also right about AI. In a musical world filled with people decrying its malign influence, Gabriel is one of its few high-profile boosters: he recently suggested that ultimately “everything will be done better” by AI than by humans.

He says it again today, albeit with caveats. “The application of AI and robots in warfare is really scary. There’s the sense that we’re creating a species that is way, way more intelligent than we are. If we look around, there are not many good examples of intelligent species looking after less-intelligent species, except as pets.

“You can see the worry on [computer scientist and ‘Godfather of AI’] Geoffrey Hinton’s face,” he continues. “I think we need to slow it down a bit, we need some international agreement, for which there are precedents, like in air safety or the Start treaty for nuclear weapons. We need guard rails, like a seed of wisdom in every algorithm before it’s allowed to be released that could allow for monitoring and a measure of control and an ‘off’ button. But it interests me in the moment as a whole new set of tools that could encourage people to consider themselves film-makers, painters, musicians, to explore themselves in that way.”

With or without AI, Gabriel says he thinks that’s true anyway: “Being those things is just a matter of walking around and saying, ‘This is what I am’, then committing to learning about it. You can get accelerated learning through AI – even though you haven’t learned all the skills to get there, you can quickly access some of the joy of making really nice-sounding things or have the AI eliminate some of your worst moments. So in the long run, as a creative tool: absolutely extraordinary. It’s like you’ve been painting in black and white and someone suddenly throws a colour palette at you, saying: ‘What can you do with this?’”

Contrary to most, Gabriel genuinely seems to believe that AI is capable of creating great art. “It’s just down to better algorithms. So how do we deal with this as a species? I think long-term, if you can’t defeat it, you have to join it. I think we will become cyborgs, because we’ll have these brain-computer interfaces, where you insert something in your brain that allows you then to communicate to the computer … I don’t think there’s any reason why we shouldn’t use our brains to become more AI.”

He’s keen to point out that “any of these things can be used positively or negatively”. He recently had a conversation with American technologist Mary Lou Jepsen, who was concerned about the human rights implications of the whole brain-computer-interface idea and its capacity for being used as a form of torture. But nevertheless, Gabriel seems fascinated by the idea: he has a concept for something so vague, I don’t really understand it, called “the brain show”, that will “allow you to see how the brain affects us and how it might be manipulated” and which would feature some of the songs from o\i as part of its soundtrack. “It could be a virtual thing or a stage thing or both, but how it all works, and the story, I’ve got no idea,” he shrugs. “I’m at that stage where you can feel a sort of lump in the mist and you’re trying to imagine it becoming something, which I think is the way most people approach creativity.”

In the meantime, he has umpteen other ideas floating around. He’s intrigued by the concept of a virtual performance, somewhere between Abba Voyage and U2’s “wonderful and inspiring” shows at the Sphere in Las Vegas. There’s a plan to make a film based on The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, the 1974 concept album that preceded his exit from Genesis: you might have thought it was pretty much unfilmable, given that it features a scene in which the lead character has sex with three snake-like creatures, and another in which his recently amputated penis is snatched away by a passing raven, but Gabriel seems optimistic: he’s been working on the script with Argentinan writer Nicolás Giacobone of Digger fame.

And he wants to “dig into” another of Levin’s ideas, “that you might be able to communicate with cells and get them to behave in a certain way and sound might be a medium for it. I’m fascinated by explorations of consciousness,” he says, then goes on to tell me about experiments in the sentience of plants. “There was a cool guy at MIT who took a plant and put it in a sort of box with a computer on wheels, then moved the plant’s light source around the room and the plant was saying ‘OK’ and moving the box to follow the light around the room. I was wondering if you could do that with an oak tree. Like a sort of Jurassic Park, but with plants instead of dinosaurs. I mean, all these ideas are such great fun to explore.”

items.title: Framery's flexible pod subscription tackles office furniture waste issue
paragraphs: According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.
Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.
Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.
Framery aims to tackle this issue with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.
The Framery Subscribed subscription service allows organisations to scale up or down their pod quantities to suit changing needs.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”
“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.
With Framery Subscribed, an office’s subscription can be quickly modified or ended as an organisation evolves.
For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.
The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.
“Framery Subscribed reduces financial risk and allows us to react agilely to organisational changes,” said Serpola.
“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”
Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.
“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” said Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”
As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

According to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.
During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.
According to Framery, 97 per cent of pods have been returned under the scheme. Each Subscribed pod also comes with on-demand maintenance for the length of the subscription.
“A Subscribed pod only works if it is still worth subscribing to when the first customer gives it back,” says Antti Paavilainen, director of Subscribed at Framery.
“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”
Framery Subscribed is available in the UK, Denmark, Poland, Sweden, Germany, Austria, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands and Norway.

items.title: NextDC vows to keep future datacentres away from homes after community backlash in Melbourne
paragraphs: Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.

The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.
The share price has since recovered to over $9 a share, but not before rival Goodman Group bought a nearly 10% stake in the business.
Shareholders revolted against the company at the AGM, issuing a second strike against executive pay, but the resulting motion on whether to spill the board was resoundingly defeated on Friday.

The chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said it was his “hardest AGM” in 15 years, and that he ultimately took responsibility for “delivery, power, planning, approvals, construction and community support”.
“At M3, we needed to work more closely with our power and construction partners, and with the community,” he said. “We are now doing that.”
Scroggie said the community deserved to be heard earlier than they had been during the Jemena construction works, and it was NextDC’s job to do that.
“M3 has certainly changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours,” he said.

“For more than 15 years we’ve built datacentres right across the country, and what earned trust then is not enough now. Community expectations have moved in the age of artificial intelligence and we must move with them.”

In addition to a new community consultative committee, including a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders, NextDC has said it will have a dedicated project website and contact channels with defined response times for complaints and inquiries.
NextDC’s chair, Doug Flynn, also revealed that the company would change where it builds in future.
“Given community sensitivities, we do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties,” Flynn said.
“The pushback against datacentres is very different right now than it was … six or so years ago.”
Flynn said that the M3 site in inner Melbourne had been an industrial site for 100 years, and had petrochemical works on it before NextDC built the datacentre.
After the blowback to taller power poles led to a delayed expansion, Flynn said the Jemena employee overseeing community engagement left the business.
“They recognise that they were just charging ahead regardless of community,” he said. “And they got a bloody nose.
A spokesperson for Jemena declined to comment, but pointed to a September statement announcing its general manager for electricity networks had decided to step down.

items.title: GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2bn - industry estimate
paragraphs: Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.
Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.
Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.
The gaming studio has yet to announce when the game will release on PC and a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and do missions with others over the internet.
If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

items.title: Big tech is already building datacentres in Australia. Why is Labor so desperate to give them loopholes?
paragraphs: Right now, the prime minister faces a choice. Does he stand with Jimmy Barnes and the Working Class Man or does he stand with Big AI?

This week, some of the biggest names in Australian music, publishing, journalism and art have thrown down the gauntlet to the government. From Paul Kelly to Anna Funder and Peter Garrett, household names and Australian icons are all singing from the same song sheet.
Their message is simple: Australia, and our culture, is not AI’s to take.

Australia’s copyright protections must apply to everyone, even the world’s biggest tech companies. The stories, photographs and books that make Australia are not free building blocks for the world’s wealthiest corporations. Big AI wants access to the world’s vast creative library to train their models. They’re lobbying the Albanese Labor government for loopholes in copyright laws, so they can scrape and use other people’s hard work without having to pay or even ask for permission.
Big AI is dangling the promise of a seat at the table of the global AI boom, in exchange for unfettered access to our cultural treasures and a free pass to avoid the basic notion of property rights.

What this is really about is the need for Big AI to build datacentres in Australia. The enormous, power-hungry warehouses are packed with servers that power AI models like ChatGPT. These centres feed their machines vast amounts of data, including Australian music, books, journalism, culture and knowledge.

But here’s the thing: big tech is already building datacentres in Australia. They want our land, our water and our energy. The copyright debate only exists because Labor is desperate to offer yet another incentive to set up shop here.
Australian artists, creatives and journalists shouldn’t be the sacrificial lamb to big AI’s slaughter.
The price big AI wants us to pay is to undermine more than a century of copyright protections that give Australian artists control over their own work and the ability to earn a living.
Get this wrong, and it won’t just be our favourite musicians who pay the price.

Journalists risk having their reporting swallowed by AI models that reproduce their work and compete with their publications. Artists, authors, performers and screenwriters’ work could be used to churn out AI slop at the expense of their livelihoods.

First Nations artists are already having their work stolen and sold on platforms like Temu without permission or payment. It is outrageous that the world’s oldest continuing living culture should have to compete with computer servers.
Any Australian who has shared a photo, story or artwork online could have it scraped and fed into commercial AI systems without their knowledge or consent.

Make no mistake – for AI companies, this is a global play with big consequences. Any copyright loopholes Australia creates will undermine protections worldwide. Big AI will have a backdoor to scrape and steal cultural works everywhere, using Australian datacentres. Other countries have read the writing on the wall, strengthening copyright laws to protect their own culture and stop big AI exploiting their laws. Australia can’t afford to be the weak link in the chain.
We risk becoming the Cayman Islands of AI, a safe haven for big tech – a global pariah riddled with loopholes where AI can exploit culture and knowledge and dodge the laws that protect it.

The prime minister has promised to do the right thing by Australian creators. But words are cheap. The test is whether his laws guarantee consent, credit and compensation, rather than an opt-out system that forces artists, freelancers and small newsrooms to chase billion-dollar tech companies to protect their rights.

Australian music, films, and art are our memories, our connections to each other, our heartbreaks and our identity – the story of our nation. It’s not a bargaining chip for big AI and they are not AI’s to take.
Sarah Hanson-Young is a Greens Senator for South Australia

items.title: New Hunger Games cast say joining the franchise is 'nerve-racking'
paragraphs: Joseph Zada stars as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.
This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.
Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.
Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".
Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.
Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."
Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace play District 12 tributes Haymitch Abernathy and Maysilee Donner

Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.
Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.
It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.
Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.
Peak plays Lenore Dove, Haymitch's girlfriend.
Whitney Peak stars as Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove, who is left behind in District 12 while he fights in the games
Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.

Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".

He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".
Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".
This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.
"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.
"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.
Glenn Close plays an over-the-top government official from the Capitol in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

The film, which includes an ensemble cast of Ralph Fiennes, Maya Hawke, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning, is set during the 50th edition of The Hunger Games - with most elements of the brutal dystopian universe that fans have come to recognise from the previous films returning in this iteration.

Adapted from Collins' novels, the series is set in a post-apocalyptic North America, which is known as Panem, with the first trilogy focusing on a teenage Katniss Everdeen, who was played by Lawrence in the films.
Panem has 12 districts that participate in the yearly Hunger Games, produced and run by the governing area, the Capitol, as a punishment for rebellion.
Peak notes that being on set was an intense experience for the young cast and could "get overwhelming very quickly" on set, so they had to make sure to "keep it light between all the hard stuff".
"I don't think people realise how intensely bonding an experience like this is because we all spend days doing extremely physical and deeply emotional things," Grace says.
"It's like a little family on set; we've all been thankful to have each other," she added.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas now.

items.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
paragraphs: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

items.title: Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns
paragraphs: Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its £500m target.
In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures will be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.
The BBC welcomed the report and said it has "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".
The NAO's report also said the BBC's current measures are expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.
Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.
The NAO found the BBC's licence fee income fell by 26% in real terms over the last decade, due in part to the significant changes in audience habits.
The proportion of UK adults using BBC television, iPlayer, radio or online services on an average week also fell from 90% in 2021-22 to 81% in 2025-26, the NAO said.
The report noted the corporation's public service broadcasting operating defecit reached £209m in the last financial year.
The BBC has already announced plans to reduce spending by about 10%, including cuts to programming across its news, nations and content divisions.
Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank, Live At The Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and RuPaul's Drag Race UK are among the TV programmes to have been cut so far.
Radio programmes are also being dropped from the schedules, such as You and Yours and The World Tonight on BBC Radio 4.
The corporation has also announced plans to close the linear broadcast services of BBC Radio 4 Extra, BBC Three and BBC Scotland, with the latter two becoming online-only services.

The NAO said the BBC expects to face difficult choices about the scale and scope of its services as part of its latest savings programme, with further content reductions expected to have a greater impact on audiences.
It warned the corporation was likely to find it harder to identify further savings following its previous cost-cutting programmes.
The NAO also found the broadcaster had not properly monitored the cumulative impact of its previous savings on audiences, service quality and organisational capability.
It also raised concerns about the BBC's risk management and governance arrangements, and said stronger oversight would be needed to deliver the more demanding savings programme.

In response to the report, the BBC said it welcomed the findings, and added that it has had to "make tough decisions due to sustained financial pressures driven by declining licence fee income, changing audience behaviour, increased competition and rising costs".

Berangere Michel, the BBC's group chief financial officer, said: "We welcome this report and are pleased that the NAO has acknowledged the significant savings already delivered by the BBC, with the programme on track to meet its target one year ahead of schedule.

"The BBC must respond to significant cost pressures while reinventing for a changing world. This continues to require tough decisions, while ensuring that the impacts on audiences and colleagues are minimised.

"We accept the NAO's recommendations and have already begun implementing them to strengthen the delivery of our current savings programme, while recognising there are further opportunities to build on this progress.

She added: "We will continue to engage with government to secure a new Charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come."

items.title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
paragraphs: A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.
"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.
RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.
The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.
"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.
He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.
RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

items.title: Iraq Pushes to Reassert Control Over Jurf al-Sakhar, but Experts Question PM’s Ability to Confront Militias
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Iraq's government says it has reached a compromise with an Iran-backed militia that will government forces were to move into the group's stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.
Word of the government compromise with the Kataib Hezbollah militia comes from three senior security officials who spoke with Reuters news Agency.

The announcement came as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against ‌the group. However some observers question whether al-Zaidi has the political backing and security capabilities needed to challenge Iran-aligned armed groups.

Al-Zaidi assumed office in May through a political settlement among Shiite parties within the Coordination Framework rather than a direct electoral mandate. He faces resistance from Kataib Hezbollah, which has controlled the strategic area south of Baghdad for more than a decade.
On Thursday, Prime Minister al-Zaidi ordered the reopening of all closed roads in Jurf al-Sakhar, reaffirming that Iraqi security forces would assert state authority throughout the country.

The Iraqi government also established a joint command headquarters, scheduled to begin operations Friday, bringing together Iraqi army, federal police, Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and energy police units.
However up until now, Kataib Hezbollah has rejected demands to withdraw from the area or surrender its weapons.

Elizabeth Tsurkov, a researcher kidnapped by Kataib Hezbollah in March 2023, told VOA Prime Minister al-Zaidi and Iraq's chief justice, Faiq Zeydan, appear determined to confront the militias but face significant political obstacles.
"They have quite a narrow base of support inside the Coordination Framework," Tsurkov said.

She argued that most factions within the Shiite political alliance appear to favor a negotiated compromise that would allow both the government and Kataib Hezbollah to save face without fundamentally changing the balance of power.
Tsurkov also warned that militia penetration of Iraq's security institutions could undermine government operations.
She described the government's goal of bringing all weapons under state control by June 2027 as unrealistic without gradual reforms to reduce militia influence within security agencies.
Michael Pregent, a former U.S. military intelligence officer and analyst at the Hudson Institute, offered an even more skeptical assessment.

Pregent says that influential militia figures, including Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri and Kataib Hezbollah commander Abu Fadak, were involved in coordinating the operation, alongside Iranian Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani.
"This is not a real operation. It's cosmetic," Pregent told VOA. "It's a change of command. It's a rotation of forces. It is not a move by Iraq to reclaim its sovereignty from Iranian militias."
His account of the involvement of the militia leaders and Qaani have not been independently confirmed by the VOA.

In a November 17 statement to VOA, the U.S. State Department said, "The United States expects Prime Minister Al-Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable for engaging in violent and destabilizing activities throughout Iraq and the entire region."
The statement accused the militias of undermining Iraqi sovereignty, weakening the economy and stealing national resources through corruption to benefit themselves and Tehran.

Jurf al-Sakhar, approximately 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad, has remained under militia control since Iraqi forces and Iran-backed PMF fighters recaptured it from Islamic State militants in 2014.
An estimated 140,000 residents have been prevented from returning to their homes.
Tsurkov said the issue extends beyond allegations of oil smuggling to include enforced disappearances, secret prisons and suspected mass graves.
She called for investigations into alleged abuses and the return of displaced residents, whose numbers she estimated at between 120,000 and 180,000.

Meanwhile, Iraqi authorities are investigating allegations that millions of dollars' worth of crude oil has been stolen from pipelines crossing the restricted area since 2021. Kataib Hezbollah denies involvement.

Despite Baghdad's latest directives, the central question remains whether al-Zaidi can translate government orders into effective state control or whether the operation will ultimately amount to a negotiated reshuffling of forces without dismantling militia influence.

items.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
paragraphs: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

items.title: Afghan economy grows, but per capita income falls
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
Afghanistan’s economy is growing, but for the third straight year there is less to go around, according to the World Bank.

In a report released this week, the World Bank projected that Afghanistan’s economy would grow 3 percent in fiscal year 2026. But with the population growing by more than 6 percent, GDP per capita is expected to decline for the third consecutive year.
The World Bank attributed the economic growth largely to a strong harvest this year.
“Agriculture rebounded by about 8 percent after the 2025 drought and provided almost 90 percent of growth,” the report said.
The report said population growth of 6.6 percent would result in a 3.3 percent decline in GDP per capita.
“Population has grown by an estimated 24 percent since 2022, largely because more than 6 million Afghans have returned from Iran and Pakistan since 2024,” the report said.

In October, the UNHCR said that nearly 1.3 million Afghans had returned from Pakistan and Iran so far in 2026, including people who had been deported. The two countries have hosted most Afghan refugees.
The agency also reported that about 4.9 million Afghans returned to the country between 2023 and 2025.
The U.N. agency said the return of millions of Afghan refugees from Iran and Pakistan had put additional pressure on the Afghan economy.
The World Bank report projected that inflation would average 7 percent in 2026, almost double the 2025 rate.
It added that weaker labor demand and rising food prices were eroding household purchasing power, while private investment and exports had contracted.
According to the U.N., Afghanistan will remain one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises in 2026, with nearly 22 percent of the population in need of humanitarian assistance.

“Food insecurity and acute malnutrition continued to worsen in Afghanistan, with 15.9 million people facing crisis or worse levels of food insecurity (IPC Phase 3), including 3.4 million in Emergency (IPC Phase 4), while child wasting reached its highest recorded levels of the August-October period,” a UNICEF report said.

The World Bank projected that Afghanistan’s economy would grow by 3.3 percent in 2027 and 3.5 percent in 2028. However, output per person is expected to remain about 7 percent below its 2024 level in 2028.
The bank warned that a poor harvest, disruptions to trade routes, the return of more Afghan refugees from neighboring countries and further cuts in foreign aid could weaken economic growth.

The report said improving trade routes, creating more jobs in provinces receiving large numbers of refugees, and restoring access to education and employment for women and girls were key to improving living standards.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have barred girls from attending secondary schools and women from universities. Women are excluded from most government jobs and many private-sector jobs, including work for nongovernmental organizations. They are also prohibited from visiting public parks, gyms and public baths and are required to have a male relative, known as a mahram, accompany them on long-distance travel.

items.title: Bipartisan House probe targets Mercedes-Benz's Chinese business ties
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
A bipartisan House committee has launched an inquiry into Mercedes-Benz's Chinese shareholders, who together own about 20 percent of the company, and how much influence they have.

The investigation was announced in a letter dated November 16 and released Tuesday, by the House China Select Committee's chairman, Republican Representative John Moolenaar of Michigan, and its ranking Democrat, Representative Ro Khanna of California.

The letter asked Mercedes-Benz North America CEO Jason Hoff and the German automaker's chairman and CEO, Ola Källenius, to provide records and information about the company's relationships with Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC), Geely founder Li Shufu and other Chinese companies.

The lawmakers cited reports that BAIC and companies associated with Li together hold about 20 percent of Mercedes-Benz's shares, and that their voting power at shareholder meetings could be even greater, the lawmakers said.

"These records and responses will not only assist with the Select Committee’s oversight of national security and supply chain risks in the automotive sector but also inform Congress’s consideration of legislation to mitigate the profound threat presented by PRC cars in the U.S. market," the letter said.

The committee said it was concerned about the potential influence of these Chinese entities over Mercedes-Benz and their possible access to sensitive information. BAIC is a state-owned Chinese company, while Geely plays a leading role in Beijing's efforts to establish China as a dominant force in the global automotive industry, the lawmakers added.

The investigation will also examine Mercedes-Benz's expanding technology partnerships with Chinese companies, including lidar maker Hesai, technology giant Tencent and autonomous driving startup Momenta.

Among other issues, the committee wants to know how Beijing may influence Mercedes-Benz's strategic decisions, what technology the company shares with Chinese partners, and whether Chinese entities can access its proprietary research and development. It is also seeking information about Chinese-made components used in vehicles manufactured or sold in the United States and the company's contacts with Chinese government officials.
The committee has asked Mercedes-Benz to provide the requested records and information by December 1 and preserve all documents and electronic communications relevant to the inquiry.
The inquiry comes as Congress considers legislation to tighten restrictions on Chinese vehicles in the United States.

The Connected Vehicle Security Act, a bipartisan Senate bill, would ban the import, manufacture and sale of internet-connected vehicles and related software and hardware linked to China and other countries the U.S. considers foreign adversaries.
It would also bar automakers that are more than 15% owned by entities from those countries, a provision that could affect Mercedes-Benz.
The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in July but has since made little legislative progress. A similar bill has been introduced in the House.

In September, John Bozzella, the head of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, urged bipartisan congressional leaders to act before the end of the year and pass legislation, including the Connected Vehicle Security Act, to keep Chinese connected vehicles and related technology out of the U.S. market.

items.title: VOA interview leads to arrest of Iranian activists' family members
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Sepideh Gholian, a civil rights activist and former political prisoner, says security forces arrested and tortured three members of her family in a bid to force her to surrender, after she spoke to VOA’s Persian-language program “Omgh-e Meydan” (“Depth of Field”).

Authorities raided her family home in the southwestern city of Dezful on Nov. 16, arresting her father, Khodarahm, and her 17-year-old niece, Tahoura, according to rights groups. Her brother, Mehdi, was arrested when he went to ask about them.

Gholian said her father was severely beaten, and her niece was threatened with death and rape. Agents told the family that a suspended prison sentence against her had been activated because of her recent interviews and human rights work, rights groups reported.
Gholian’s brother, Mehdi Gholian, was also arrested when he went to ask about their father and niece and was transferred to Dezful Prison.
In her post, Gholian said agents told the family the three would not be released until she surrendered.

She said the Security Police, acting as the judicial officers in her case, told the family during the raid that a suspended five-year prison sentence from a previous case would be enforced because of her interview with VOA.
Gholian appeared on VOA’s “Omgh-e Meydan” on Sept. 12, 2026, where she spoke with Fahimeh Khezr-Heidari about the torture and mistreatment of political prisoners.

During the program, Gholian spoke at length about the torture inflicted on herself, other political prisoners, and protest detainees, including abuse during arrest, as well as inhumane prison conditions.

In January 2026, Gholian was arrested for attending the seventh-day memorial of Khosrow Alikordi in Mashhad and sentenced to five years of suspended imprisonment and six months of discretionary prison time on charges of "assembly and collusion against national security" and "propaganda against the system."

At the end of her post, Gholian wrote: "From right here, let me say to the prosecutor of Dezful or any unaccountable official who made this decision: we will not back down from our struggle. While my heart bleeds for my brother, my heart is warmed by your support, and I hope a good tomorrow awaits us."
Iranian authorities rarely comment on individual arrests and have not commented publicly on Gholian's post.

items.title: Protesters rally against Anthropic in New York and San Francisco after $2tn stock market debut
paragraphs: As the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic debuted on the US stock market at an eye-popping $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters from anti-AI groups rallied in front of the Nasdaq exchange at its New York City headquarters in Times Square and several were arrested. Similar demonstrations took place outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters.

“I think people are starting to get that there’s something wrong,” Jose Gonzalez, 46, one of roughly 30 protesters in New York City, said. Protesters carried flags reading “STOP TECH OLIGARCHS” and “FREEZE AI: END ICE, END WAR”.
Anthropic, founded in 2021, completed the largest initial public offering in history this week, raising about $81bn to continue developing its Claude family of generative AI models.

The Times Square rally featured a series of speeches from several community leaders, including Aber Kawas, a New York state senator, who said: “Investing in AI also comes at the direct cost of investing in people.”

Gonzalez took off work to rally in Times Square on Thursday morning. He works as a policy researcher for New York Communities for Change, a non-profit community organizing group that helped rally outside the Nasdaq building. He believes stricter regulations on AI progression nationwide are needed before people are more comfortable with AI research.
Environmental safety, national security, Flock cameras and AI’s connection to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and law enforcement were among the largest concerns for protesters.

“It’s all connected,” Jes Vesconte, 30, said after wrapping up the New York rally. “The same capitalist imperialism is causing the affordability crisis and the climate emergency and atrocities that ICE is doing.”
Vesconte works for a local worker agency in New York. He said he’s encouraging his peers not participate in the stock trading for Anthropic.
“If we did not have the profit motive, we wouldn’t be having these issues,” he said. “This is the epitome of that with the largest IPO ever.”

Outside Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco, about three dozen protesters from two different groups gathered before 11am. One activist held a fake stock certificate for a single share of “Misanthropic”.

Sydney Von Arx with the group Ban RSI said she was there to draw attention to the dangers she sees with “recursive self-improvement”, a technical process in which AI trains itself to become more advanced. Von Arx thinks Anthropic’s IPO is “a time to reflect on how these AI companies that started as small startups with lofty goals have turned into giant corporations that have put profit before safety and security”.

She wants a global ban on recursive self-improvement. “We should not have AI building AIs,” she said. “It’s going to go too fast at a pace that no humans can keep up with.” Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, previously warned that recursive self-improvement could outrun human’s ability to control the systems.

Adam Kaufman, who works at an AI safety non-profit, held a sign saying: “The only winning move is not to RACE,” with the “A” rendered to mimic the Anthropic logo. Kaufman said the sign was a reference to the movie WarGames, in which a nuclear strategy computer, after simulating numerous nuclear wars, concludes the only winning move is not to play.

items.title: Rob Brydon says he invented his own fake agent to negotiate fees
paragraphs: Rob Brydon has revealed he pretended to be his own agent at the start of his career when he was working as a TV and radio presenter in Wales.

The actor, best known for playing Stacey's Uncle Bryn in the hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, told BBC One's Graham Norton Show, external he used to step into the role of his fake agent to arrange bookings for events.
"I would get asked to go and do things, and I didn't really have an agent at that time so I invented a guy called Richard Knight," Brydon told the show.
The fictional agent would phone organisers and negotiate a fee for Brydon's appearance, he said.
The actor, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, shared an anecdote about being invited to a fundraiser and managing to get a fee for it.
"I'm terribly embarrassed," he told the show's host and fellow guests Cynthia Erivo, David Tennant and Laura Linney.
"They were all there for the good of their hearts," he said.

Brydon, known for his ability to mimic a range of celebrities, went on to impersonate the fictional Richard Knight asking for money in return for an appearance, with the agent describing Brydon as "an angel".
"I would go to these events and they would say 'oh I spoke to Mr Knight, he's quite a character', and I would say 'more than you realise'," Brydon told the show.
Dylan Brady, Ada Player, Harry Baxendale and Yasmin Al-Khudhairi join the cast as Bill's student lodgers Christian, Hettie, James and Zahra.
Brydon praised the young actors, saying he "loved being around them, partly because of their energy".
He said he also enjoyed hearing their perspective on the industry.
"They knew who was being cast in what, who was directing which projects and it reminded me of how I used to be," he said.
The actor also remarked on the "odd" feeling of being told by some of the actors that they grew up watching him on television.
He said: "I remember that at the end of filming, one of them said to me, 'Thanks for being nice and for spending time with us between set-ups'.
"My reaction was, 'Well, of course I did. We're all actors on this show.'"
Bill's Included will be available on BBC iPlayer and BBC One from 20 November.

items.title: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface
paragraphs: Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.
According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”
“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”
“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”
Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.
The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.
“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.
“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”
“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.
Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.
It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.
The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.
The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.
It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.
To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.
GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.

The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.
Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.

The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.

Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled ‌on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.
The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”

Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”
The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.
Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.
