The Medici family history itself is more labyrinthine than can be captured in a single exhibition, even for diehard historians (or, I dare say, bingers of the 2016 Italian-British TV series), and the Wallace eschews dense background reading here. It has a dual obligation to impart the artwork’s historical significance in relation to its existence in the Wallace Collection, which is perhaps why it omits significant details regarding Cosimo’s role in founding the Uffizi Gallery and expanding the Pitti Palace in Florence. We get the key grounding, however, in that in 1537, the 17-year-old Cosimo was elected as the new duke of Florence. This followed swiftly after the assassination of the last male heir of the senior branch of the Medici family, Alessandro, leaving a power vacuum at threat from republicanism.

And, crucially, it demonstrates that it is not necessarily the most “beautiful” works that are the most compelling. It’s always secretly thrilling to encounter a fresco that’s been hacked off the wall (removal videos are nail-biting stuff), and a 1464 fresco of the young Cicero reading taken from a Milanese branch of the Medici bank even has chunks at its base missing, the snap-lines used to mark out its design in wet plaster clearly visible up close in raking light, and somewhat hilariously mounted in an incongruous wooden frame. Among its usual Wallace location the clunky fresco medium would usually pale next to its fine art neighbours – now it shines in the spotlight.

We are told how the statesman Cicero was a model of civic virtue and morality and hence adopted as a symbol of the Florentine republic. He is envisaged here (in a commission by Cosimo the Elder, not Cosimo I as is the case for every other piece – pay attention at the back!) as a studious young figure with a sense of industry and success, implying similar connotations for the benefacting Medici family.

The varying amount of iconographic content – ie, the visual symbolism deliberately used by Cosimo I for dynastic purposes – does highlight the limitations of working within Wallace’s collection. Certainly, a parade helmet (c1550) and sword (1546-69) bear a plethora of imagery and were inventoried in the Medici armouries as alluding to Hercules, who was commonly said (by Florentines) to have founded Florence. Cosimo’s heraldry sits next to an Order of the Golden Fleece, of which Cosimo was a member, and topped by a ducal crown, despite his only becoming grand duke in 1569. In short, the iconographic picture and dynastic assertion is bright and clear.

Yet the show’s (literal) centrepiece, a 1574 earthenware wine cooler, bears only Cosimo’s personal emblem, a turtle with a sail, alluding to the motto festina lente (make haste slowly), which was itself pinched from Roman emperor Augustus. The rest of the glazed iconography is a combination of fanciful mythological whimsy, satyrs and monstrous figures. It bears a naval battle which it is noted can only with certainty be linked to its purpose for holding liquid. Unlike the armour for which its display purpose – and audience – was obvious, we can only speculate on the audience for such an object other than banqueting and revelry. Perhaps we can – only half-jokingly – look to the glaringly formidable testes of the carved monsters supporting the bowl for further declaration of dynastic strength and rigour.

Such a sparse but precise display is welcome as a contrast with the Wallace’s visual overwhelm, using close and precise old-school art historical analysis to draw out one strand of its many contained histories. Even the choice of terracotta wall colour instantly imparts a Florentine flavour – a smart touch. Its limitations remind us that the collection is based on personal, not curatorial choice, : we don’t even have a portrait of Cosimo himself in the collection, despite Bronzino having churned out dozens of them. Yet hopefully there will be more studies like this to enjoy.

items.title: Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.
Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

“How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”
“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”
With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.
She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.
“I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”
In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.
Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.
“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.
Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).
These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.
“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”
“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”
“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.
In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.
She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

“I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me.”
“I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”
It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.
Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.
“That has been super important for me,” she said. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.
“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she said, before pausing.
“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”
Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”
Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.
“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.
“So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”
Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.
A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.
This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.
It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.
Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.
“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.
“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”
Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.
And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.
In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.
She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.
For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.
“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she said.
“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI protagonists, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, against the backdrop of the Miami-inspired Vice City. Rockstar Games hide caption

I want to tell you about the time I saw Bigfoot. I want to tell you about sitting in the rain on a city street in a muscle car and prepping to rob a bank while lightning split the sky between high-rise condo towers in the distance and the drum fill from In The Air Tonight played on the radio. I want to tell you about gunfights and fistfights, the perfect satire of radio commercials and how the sunrise looks over Ocean Beach. But more than any of that, I want to tell you about the time an alligator bit my mom.

It happened in the backyard of an abandoned house with a rotting inground pool. My mom, Mia Caminos (mother of Lucia Caminos, one of the two leads in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI, probably the most highly anticipated video game sequel of all time), was thrilled by the pool. Standing there, amid the artfully rendered weeds and trash, she spread her arms and told me to use my imagination, to see her vision for this ruin of a house with its upmarket water feature, in a scabby neighborhood on the outskirts of Vice City. She speaks in tones of increasingly frantic desperation because she has already put money down on this house, sight unseen. All of her money, actually, in hopes of flipping it and selling it fast to keep her startup real estate business afloat.
Lucia begins her epic as a petty criminal. Rockstar Games hide caption
The pool is still half full of water. There's a dirty, sodden mattress floating in it. And as if this is the main thing standing between her and success, Mia is fixated on getting it out of the pool.

And, dutifully, I do. Playing as Lucia, I grab hold, mash buttons, help my mom drag away the wet, heavy, stinking mattress. And just as we get it up and over the lip of the pool that's going to be the thing that makes this wreck of a house suddenly desirable – that's when the alligator lunges out of the murky water, grabs my mom by the arm and tries to drag her back in.

This is a story about folly, fixation, unrealistic expectations of success at the ass-end of late capitalism, and the vicious, whip-crack cruelty of predators who lie in wait for anyone trying to improve a terrible situation.

But then I shoot the alligator in the head before it can eat my mom. Because this is also a story about violence, and how sometimes (maybe all the times), the loud, cathartic rip of gunfire is the only solution left for people who have already lost so much and can't bear to see one more thing taken from them.
It's a story about my mom and an alligator, sure.
Grand Theft Auto VI returns to Vice City and its Florida-inspired environs. Rockstar Games hide caption

But let's back up a little. For anyone who has somehow missed the shrieking, neon-and-swamp-water marketing onslaught over the past several days, weeks, months and years, Grand Theft Auto VI is the newest release from Rockstar Games. It is a Bonnie and Clyde love story, a knife-edged satire of modern American culture and politics, an unapologetic murder simulator, a love letter to 50 years of crime movies, and a thoughtful, emotional meditation on the sacrifices, small and large, that we make for family. A massive open world game set in the fictional state of Leonida (based on the very real state of Florida), it represents a return to a location that Rockstar hasn't visited in-depth since its 2002 release of GTA: Vice City, and is the first new game in the franchise since GTA5 launched in 2013. According to estimates, it already earned over $1.5 billion in pre-sales and will likely make a total of $3 to $5 billion in its first week, which could make it the largest single entertainment product launch ever.

Fans have been waiting years for it. They have created libraries worth of lore and theories and dissected trailers frame-by-frame. To discount the overheated environment into which this singular work of art is being released would be doing a disservice both to it and the legions of salivating prognosticators who have made guessing the number of bird species included in-game, or speculating on the square mileage of its map, their entire personalities.
While Vice City remains the game's hub, most of its map is actually rural or wild. Rockstar Games hide caption

Now, though, they know it all. We all do. We know that GTA6 is expansive, covering everything from the Keys (where the game starts) to the hilly, forested north, with Vice City in all its grimy, pastel-colored splendor at the beating heart of it. It is a playground, equal parts gorgeous and maniacal, and in all that space the developers have given us a thousand different things to do. You can rob a bank or take a bike ride, go fishing, hunt trophy animals, visit strip clubs, rob random civilians, street race, fly drones, eat a sandwich, work out, manage your family savings account, jump a sports car off the top of a building, steal a plane, punch out a convenience store clerk, fight a bear or, yes, just wander out toward the horizon and study the birds. And while some of that is fun and all of it is diverting (at least for a little while), none of it is the ostensible point. The game-y part of the game — the hundred extras and time-wasters that players have come to expect from open-world projects in general, and GTA specifically — is not what makes it matter.

What matters is Mia and the alligator, Lucia and the gun. It's the multi-pronged, exquisitely balanced narrative about poverty and rigged systems that makes it hard to turn away from GTA while you're playing and impossible not to think about when you're away.
Jason and his pal, Cal, shoot pool. Rockstar Games hide caption

Lucia is an ex-con, a car thief and a small-time criminal who got caught trying to rob a payday loan joint and starts the game in jail. Her partner, Jason Duval, is a veteran, dishonorably discharged, now making a living flying loads for a local coke dealer down in the Keys and living rent-free in one of his properties. Jason skims a little on the coke deals, wears flip-flops and drinks beer in the sun, and goes fishing with his best friend Cal (played with genius-level goofy, drunken paranoia and dopey bravado by Bobby Moynihan). Jason and Lucia have a kid, Tomás, who is currently living with Lucia's family, and every plan they have is about getting right by the law, making a few bucks and grabbing a chance at finally being a family.

Only there are complications — surprisingly banal ones at first (like not being able to open a checking account because of their bad credit) — that slowly ramp up into huge ones across 60-odd hours of main story gameplay that see Jason and Lucia (both of whom are playable characters) graduate from knocking over liquor stores in a beat-up El Camino, to pulling off elaborate heists in the middle of Vice City which will have you dangling from a net suspended from a cargo helicopter hauling 200 tons of cocaine. It goes from Badlands to Die Hard with the speed of a muscle car, all bright chrome and barking straight pipes. From True Romance to Heat like that's just the natural arc of any American love story.

And what's remarkable about the whole bloody delight is that it remains, until its final operatic moments, so surprisingly grounded. This is a somewhat more mature GTA than its predecessors, trading aliens, cannibal cultists and whacked-out drug trips for wellness influencers, local politics and the music industry. Jason and Lucia's relationship is the superstructure around which the entire narrative is built, and it's a dynamic thing that must be maintained in a dozen little ways — making coffee in the morning, opening doors for each other, date nights (even if that means robbing a jewelry store together), or holding hands as you walk toward yet another betrayal by someone you thought you could trust. You can switch freely between them, or just call the other one to come drive the getaway car. Let their relationship dwindle and the narrative shifts, flattens. But when they're together, the two of them talk and talk: In bed, in the car, by the pool. They reveal pieces of themselves in quiet moments, joke, tease, flirt, make plans for a future that always seems right around the next corner. And you love them for it. You can't help but love them for it, and root for them, and want good things for them, because they're just two hard-luck kids trying to do right in a world where "right" sometimes means petting a dog or helping a farmer spray manure all over his boss's house, and sometimes means stealing $10 million from South American drug lords.
The couple that robs together, stays together. That's the hope, anyway. Rockstar Games hide caption

In so many ways GTA6 is an example of inspired synthesis. Rockstar made a killing with the sunlit beauty and craziness of GTA5 more than a decade ago, a game built on deconstructing Hollywood myths and male friendships. Then it made art with a slow-burn meditation on loyalty, death and obsolescence in Red Dead Redemption 2. And this? It is the middle path charted between those two bright stars. It has seriousness and weight and something to say. And also, you accidentally end up starring in a porno movie. Through mechanical tweaks and narrative railroading, the game trades abject chaos for consequences that force you to actually live in its world rather than just murder your way through it, but then makes the dullest, most quotidian chores (like going grocery shopping or answering your mom's texts) feel like a long, slow breath taken between gasping moments of panic.

Yes, you have to sleep. Yes, you have to eat. Yes, you have to work out and put gas in the (stolen) car. But after a while, I found myself actually wanting to do those things because doing them felt like roleplaying; like added opportunities to fully exist within the fiction of Jason or Lucia's world. And in what will no doubt enrage a million over-testosteroned 15-year-olds who want nothing more out of GTA6 than a shinier, brighter, higher-resolution playground in which to jack a Lambo and mow down pedestrians, certain mechanical adjustments in the game (like cars that exist without the tools immediately available to steal them, or how you no longer carry every gun you've ever touched, but store them in the trunk of your ride) have made it harder to jump right in and create mayhem from hour one.

Plus, the police response has been overhauled. Commit brazen crimes and cameras will capture your appearance. Witnesses will describe your clothes or getaway car. Wanted levels now measure not just the size of the armed response, but its sophistication, so speed and stealth become vital. Do a job cleanly, destroy the evidence, get out fast without tripping alarms or blowing stuff up and you're golden. Go loud and cops will search whole regions for you, using helicopters and canine units. They'll hunt you until you change your appearance, swap cars, or simply flee.
Do your best to evade or overcome the police in GTA6. Rockstar Games hide caption

To call the game a masterpiece seems like a cheap, throwaway declaration because after years of development and hundreds of millions of dollars spent, a masterpiece feels… expected, right? Like if it wasn't a masterpiece, that would feel somehow personally insulting. Like they just didn't try hard enough. But the truth is, these things can go wrong so easily. They are enormous, unwieldy, lumbering projects that can fall apart for any number of reasons — and do all the time.

But this one didn't. There is a gloss on it that feels like love. A polish so fine that if you're not looking for it, you might not even notice the way the palm fronds move in the wind when there's weather coming in, or the light on the edge of a storm; how Lucia hangs her head out of a convertible when Jason is driving, or the way the sound of your tires changes depending on whether you're cruising on macadam or blacktop. Does it drag a little in the third act? Sure. Are there NPC glitches, targeting hang-ups and moments where you have to stop to puzzle out exactly who is betraying whom and how they're all connected? Absolutely. But at almost any point, you can walk away from the narrative for a while, call your better half, hop in your car and just drive. Everywhere you go, Leonida is alive around you in a way that no game has ever been before. There are a million stories here just waiting to be discovered or created. Pick one. See where it leads you.

But remember Mia and the alligator. Because at its core, GTA6 will always be a story about predators and prey. And no matter where you go or how powerful you think you are, you can never, ever be sure which one you are.

Jason Sheehan knows stuff about food, video games, books and Star Blazers. He's the restaurant critic at Philadelphia magazine, but when no one is looking, he spends his time writing books about giant robots and ray guns. Children of the Flying City is his latest book.

items.title: I want to know if toxic lagoon fire caused my husband's rare deadly cancer
paragraphs: The council said it took "its responsibilities for protecting public health and the environment extremely seriously" and had carried out "extensive investigations over many years" into the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Wrexham council added that concerns about the health of firefighters who attended the fire were raised with their contaminated land officer twice.
The first was in February 2004 by the fire officer in charge at Wrexham fire station and on another occasion by a fire officer, who was told to speak to the health authority.

On the risk of another fire on the site, Wrexham council said that in 2006 advice was sought from the fire service about this, but they were told a number of "specific circumstances" would need to occur for this to happen.
An emergency response plan has been drawn up, and it was revisited in 2017.
North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it was not in a position to comment on the fire in 1980.

It added: "We recognise the importance of understanding the potential long-term health impacts associated with firefighting. Approaches to occupational health, wellbeing and health monitoring continue to be developed nationally as evidence, research and understanding across the sector evolve."
The Welsh government announced in its draft budget on Tuesday that it would commit £2m to "kick-start a new approach to managing contaminated land".
"We are developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land," the government said in a statement.
"We also continue to press the UK government for funding to address the legacy of Wales's industrial past, including the remediation of contaminated land."

items.title: Harvard GSD students propose alternatives to Trump's arch
paragraphs: Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

The students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, worked with Washington DC non profit organisation The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) on the designs. The aim was to engage the public in the design process, as the team views the government did not properly open the arch up for review.

“By recognising Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” said Dvorak and Geitner.
The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum.
“As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum’s course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation,” they said.
“The current administration’s assertion of authority over national memory presented an opportunity to put these convictions into practice.”

The first proposal treats Memorial Circle as “a void along the historic axis between Washington and Arlington”. The designers chose to fill the central roundabout circle, currently covered by grass, with a low-lying pool of water.
A natural stone perimeter surrounds the pool and is inscribed with words of “belonging and unity”.
It’s design is “restrained” according to the team, and primarily meant to be viewed from a vehicle while passing through the traffic circle.
The second proposal does away with the traffic circle entirely and instead inserts a straight thoroughfare to Arlington Memorial Bridge.

Two circular fountains would be located on either side of the road. Additionally, a large pool of water, mirroring the perimeter of the former traffic circle, would fill up the site during commemorative events when the bridge is closed.
It draws upon previous historical proposals for Memorial Circle and seeks to pay homage to the precedent of the site.

“[The fountain] geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity,” said the designers.
“In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”

Trump’s proposed arch was announced late last year with renderings by US studio Harrison Design. It features gilded statues and a neoclassical design and has been dubbed the “Arc de Trump” – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Construction on the arch was set to begin in September with the government barreling ahead, but it was halted in early November by Judge Tanya S Chutkan.
Trump has claimed the arch will serve as a “military complex” with snipers in an attempt to use national security as a pretext for construction.

Many take issue with the arch blocking views to adjacent Arlington Cemetery, including members of the Kennedy family, who filed a lawsuit to block construction, claiming that the arch would cast shadows over the grave of president John F Kennedy.
The US Commission of Fine Arts (CFA), which reviews projects in the capital city, approved the project in May.

The proposals also follow recent efforts by the legislature to change Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of proposed projects on historic properties.

Earlier in November, protesters gathered in Washington DC in opposition of the administration’s proposed rewrite of these protections. They are couched within the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill recently introduced to Congress.
Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation

items.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
paragraphs: The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck.

The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber.

This artist who worked in Flanders at the end of the middle ages paints like an alien who has hidden his flying saucer in a barn outside Bruges and gone into town to observe the humans. Every detail of earthly life seems new to him. A woman with a big, blunt face looks at us from under the gold-ribboned horns of her fashionable hennin headdress. Van Eyck records the shine, moisture and green-greyness of her eyes but she remains a mystery to him. She is his wife.

If it seems fanciful to see Van Eyck as an alien, stories about him in the Renaissance were nearly as extreme. Vasari believed he was some kind of alchemist who chanced not on gold but the new medium of oil painting. It’s a powerful fable for there is something occult about a painter who can create gold by a trick of the brush. In Van Eyck’s portrait of Jan de Leeuw, a Bruges goldsmith, your eyes are hypnotised by his tiny ring like a real nugget of gold magically inserted into the illusory space of the painting.

The modern artist Willem de Kooning said oil painting was invented to depict human flesh – he was probably thinking of Titian’s lush nudes. Van Eyck reveals the mystery of flesh just by painting a face. No one before looked at the world the way he does. He didn’t invent oil painting but he was the first fully to exploit its multiplicity of slowly built-up layers to create a mirror-like image of reality. Van Eyck is surely looking at himself in a mirror, gazing with piercing, even merciless eyes in his portrait of a man with his head wrapped in crimson cloth. We see the laughter lines in his gold-tinted skin, the pink flush in his cheeks, the beginnings of age or ill health, for Van Eyck would die at around 50. I think it’s timid not to call it a self-portrait.

He depicts smooth youth too, in his portrait of a young man glowing in a brilliant twilight, perfect for ever, behind a parapet with the inscription “Léal Souvenir”, which means something like “loyal remembrance”. This portrait is surely an aid to mourning, a souvenir of loss.

That’s fundamental to what Van Eyck does. His portraits are phenomenal acts of preservation. Behind the clinical exactness of each wrinkle, each chin hair, is a desperate attempt to freeze time, defeat death, make loyal memories of people who will soon be gone, even if they are monstrous.

The Burgundian courtier Baudoin de Lannoy looks a total bastard. He gazes to the side sulkily under his huge, felt-rimmed hat. His eyes are hooded orbs, his long face pummelled by jousts and battles. Yet he is preserved for ever, the shape of his ear meticulously recorded as if in a criminal profile. Uglier still is the Italian merchant in the Arnolfini Portrait, his thin, pasty face half in shadow. The shady side of his face has a droopy, rheumy eye. Has he got a palsy? His sickly face couldn’t contrast more with the pearly beauty of his wife. They seem an ill-matched couple: Death and the Maiden.

Yet a portrait of the same man alone, done around two years later, shows him with bright eyes. Is he being flattered here or insulted in the Arnolfini Portrait? Van Eyck is not a camera, passively recording his world. His paintings are full of imagination, even whimsy. His only surviving drawing, which is in this show, is a study of the stubbly old man. Comparing the drawing with the painting, you see that the sketch is more respectful: in the finished painting he elaborates wildly on swags of skin, the vortex of the ear.

The weird geology of ears, chins and wrinkles anticipates the impulsiveness and chaos of Hieronymus Bosch. Van Eyck’s portraits are brooding creations of north European melancholy. Entering his world is perfect as winter deepens.
Van Eyck: The Portraits is at the National Gallery, London, 21 November to 11 April

items.title: OpenAI announces new AI safety program; researchers worry it won't be enough
paragraphs: The OpenAI logo is displayed on a smartphone screen placed on a reflective surface onto which the company's logo is projected in Creteil, France, on Nov. 6, 2026. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images hide caption
AI safety researchers say OpenAI's new third party evaluator program falls far short of what the company promised, raising concerns about its effectiveness.

The company announced Monday that staff from four AI safety and research organizations will become "embedded assessors" to "give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing [potential] risks."

"Getting an outside opinion on the safety work and the robustness of these systems is going to be increasingly important and valuable," CEO Sam Altman said at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.
However, many AI safety researchers say the new program is a far cry from Altman's vow in September that independent evaluators would have "employee-like access" to internal company systems.

Altman's promise came after details of the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI's autonomous systems shook the AI field. Worries of the technology's catastrophic risk captured public attention, and rival Anthropic said it would set up such a program.

"We are giving deep access to some of the most sensitive tools and models our researchers use...that are the most important for assessing key, relevant and timely safety claims," said Lama Ahmad, OpenAI's frontier assurances lead, on X.
Prior to these new embedded evaluation programs, AI companies have brought in outside researchers to assess the capabilities of AI models and identify safety loopholes the companies have missed.

The work of outside evaluators have already helped shed light on the companies' work, and have raised public awareness of safety risks that the technology poses. One recent report about Anthropic using AI to significantly speed up model development has prompted concerns in the field about how close the top companies are to using AI to autonomously build even more powerful models, a stage known as recursive self-improvement. Some in the field worry that if this happens, the velocity of development could lead to catastrophic consequences for humanity and are calling for new regulation against the practice.
Researchers say the actual announcements of how these programs will work suggests something more limited than what Altman promised.
"The assessors have very narrow scopes to their access, and only two of them seem to really be allowed to talk to employees," said Sydney Von Arx, founder of AI safety research group Nightingale.

One of the announced assessors, Apollo Research, outlined its limited access to OpenAI employees. If employees that haven't been whitelisted, or pre-approved, reach out to the embedded assessors, then the assessors will have to loop OpenAI in before having substantive conversations with the employees.
It's important for outside researchers to be able to interview employees, Von Arx said. "They help you find your blind spots. They tell you what you're missing."

Another glaring omission: "Nobody has access to internal Slack," Von Arx said, referring to the corporate messaging tool, which would allow assessors to see what employees are talking about with one another. "Imagine being an 'employee' and only being allowed to talk about company information with whitelisted coworkers and having no Slack."

In a statement to NPR, OpenAI said there's currently no standards for embedded evaluations. "We expect to deepen these relationships over time and share what we learn to help establish best practices for effective embedded assessments across the industry," OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila said. The company also said assessors can ask to talk to employees that haven't already been whitelisted, and that there is a process in place to get statements from OpenAI about things they've learned informally.

The third-party organizations will focus on various aspects of AI safety, according to OpenAI. Some of the work is related to preventing models from trying to engage in undesirable behavior, and other parts are related to catching bad behavior when it happens. The assessors will have access to some internal models, training processes and some OpenAI employees. The assessors will be able to publish their findings after OpenAI redacts confidential information, the company said.

OpenAI's commitment to embedded evaluations was questioned when three employees who worked on safety were fired. They subsequently said they were worried OpenAI is walking back from its promise of having embedded evaluators.
One of the fired employees, Tomek Korbak, was OpenAI's technical point of contact for two outside evaluators that investigated the Hugging Face attack.

"Embedded auditing will only fulfill its aims if the auditors really get employee-level access as opposed to being hired to do a specific job," he posted on X in response to OpenAI's announcement. "Sadly, OpenAI makes it clear now that [Sam Altman's] September tweet about 'employee-like access' was just an awkward overpromise that the company wants to quietly walk back."

items.title: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
paragraphs: Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

items.title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
paragraphs: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.
What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.
It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.
"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.
"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common, external, particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.
We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.
The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."
As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.
In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.
So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?
"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.
"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

items.title: 'Real life' family ghost story inspires 'nightmarish' new TV drama
paragraphs: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".
"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.

In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.
They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.
Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm.
"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.
After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.
Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.
"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."
He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.
Robins also hopes to raise the question - "do ghosts exist?", sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.
"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.

The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy, who recently starred in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.
She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."
Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."
Robins said The Witch Farm was "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.
He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in its creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."
The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from 22 November

items.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
paragraphs: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
paragraphs: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

items.title: US moves to restrict China's remote access to advanced SI chips
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. Commerce Department announced new restrictions Monday on remote access to advanced super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence), chips and servers, technology. The new restrictions are meant mainly to stop Chinese companies that are getting around U.S. limits on chip sales by using or renting computer time in other countries.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule developed at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.

Under the new rule, U.S. chip suppliers will need government permission before selling advanced chips to data centers that let Chinese companies rent or use large amounts of that computing power. The limit is roughly equal to the power of about 330 of Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
It also requires licenses for chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, which Commerce says pose a higher risk that chips will be diverted.

The rule requires data centers, overseas chip manufacturers and chip exporters to conduct enhanced due diligence on customers, including determining whether they are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by Chinese state-owned enterprises or entities in Macau.
In addition to China, the restrictions cover Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The Commerce Department said the rule is intended to bring safeguards governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities into closer alignment with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.

The department said the United States remains the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the legitimate commercial use of American technology worldwide. But it warned that rapid advances in cloud computing and super intelligence infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.

China's Foreign Ministry criticized the new restrictions, accusing Washington of interfering in China's trade and technology cooperation with other countries. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Tuesday that the United States was "overstretching the concept of national security."
He added that the measures violated understandings reached between the two countries, warning that "China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests."
Chairman of the House Select Committee on China and Republican Representative John Moolenaar of Michigan, welcomed the announcement of restrictive measures by the U.S. government.
In a statement Monday, Moolenaar said the rule “sends a message to the CCP that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years.”

Moolenaar called the measure an important step toward preventing sensitive chips from falling into the wrong hands, strengthening U.S. national security laws and protecting America's leadership in the race for super intelligence.

In January, the House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which seeks to restrict foreign adversaries, including the Chinese Communist Party, from obtaining access to U.S. technology through cloud computing services.

Rush Doshi, who served as director for China affairs on the National Security Council during the Biden administration, said in a post on X that the Trump administration's new remote-access rule was driven by the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who U.S. authorities believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to The New York Times. China rejects the report.
The announcement also comes amid differences within the Trump administration over how to approach Megaspeed.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that the Treasury, State and War departments, along with the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, had favored placing Singapore-based Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List for months.

The list identifies foreign individuals and entities considered to pose risks to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests. U.S. companies generally need a license to export certain items to listed entities, with the licensing policy varying by entity and product.
Bessent said the Commerce Department controlled the decision, adding that it was up to the department to explain its internal process.

President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that there were "two different views" on how to approach the issue. He described one as favoring a friendlier approach and the other as being willing to risk a confrontation. Trump said both positions were acceptable and that he understood both sides.

Trump departed Monday for the Philippines to attend a special U.S.-ASEAN summit in Manila. He is also scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' informal meeting and hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

items.title: US Congressman-elect Dan Koh has a message for North Korea
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.
President Donald Trump will be in China this week for an Asia-Pacific summit, and he has floated possibility of meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
An incoming Korean American congressman says he is open to engaging adversaries, if it serves the interests of the United States and South Korea.
In an interview with VOA, newly elected Democratic Representative Dan Koh had his own message for the people of North Korea.
“I am thinking of you, and I hope that one day we will be able to work side by side," he said.
Koh, who won Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in the November 3 midterm elections, spoke with VOA on November 12.

On the possibility of resuming U.S.-North Korea summit talks, Koh said he does not “oppose meeting with adversaries or those with whom the United States disagrees." However, he stressed that any such engagement should serve the national interests of both the United States and South Korea.

"This is something I will hold very close to my heart and prioritize during my time in Congress," he told VOA. "I will work to ensure that the relationship between South Korea and the United States remains very strong.”

While outlining plans to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Trump said he might also meet North Korean leader Kim, adding that such a meeting would be welcome.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told VOA during an October 31 press briefing in Atltanta that he believes Trump would be willing to engage in talks again “if there’s something productive that can come out of it.””
Rubio also discussed North Korea during a question-and-answer session with reporters on November 13 at the Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention in Washington.

While stressing that he was not defending atrocities committed in North Korea, Rubio said Kim Jong Un, unlike Iran’s leadership, seeks regime survival rather than expansion and is not seeking to invade Japan or China.
Incoming Democratic Representative Koh also underscored South Korea’s importance as a U.S. ally and expressed opposition to tariffs on South Korean products.

“Of course, I think there are certain critical technology sectors where tariffs may be appropriate to protect the United States,” Koh told VOA. “But South Korea is not our enemy, and what we’re doing right now is destabilizing all of our allies around the world.”

In an April executive order on tariffs, President Donald Trump "declared that foreign trade and economic practices have created a national emergency" and the "order imposes responsive tariffs to strengthen the international economic position of the United States and protect American workers."

Koh also addressed report of discrimination against U.S. companies operating in South Korea, including against Coupang, South Korea’s biggest online retailer, often called “the Amazon of South Korea."
The information comes from a July report by the House Judiciary Committee. Koh said it was important to ensure that American companies are treated fairly in South Korea.

The report, titled “Closed for Competition: South Korea’s Discriminatory Attacks on American-owned Businesses,” says that the Korea Fair Trade Commission aggressively targeted U.S.-owned companies through early-morning raids and threats of criminal charges.
It also says that South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission discriminated against Coupang by imposing a fine of more than $410 million, in June over a personal data breach.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry rejected the report, saying it reflected only Coupang’s arguments.
About his Korean heritage, the fresh congressman expressed deep pride in his family heritage and Korean American identity.

“It is a tremendous honor to be able to give a little bit of pride back to the hometown and family of my grandfather, who came to America against all odds,” Koh said.“I think this is such an exciting time for Korean American culture, and I am incredibly proud to be a part of it."

items.title: Taliban ban cricket broadcasts in Afghanistan's Kandahar province
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The Taliban have ordered local radio stations in the southern Afghan province of Kandahar to stop airing news and information about cricket, the country’s most popular sport.
The Taliban’s provincial Department of Information and Culture issued the order on Saturday.
“Both commentary and news coverage, or even reporting about their winning results, is also banned,” the source in the department told AFP, requesting anonymity for security purposes.

Three chief editors and managers of private radio stations in Kandahar told Radio Azadi on Monday that they have received verbal instructions from the Taliban’s provincial authorities prohibiting all cricket-related broadcasts.

An official in Afghanistan’s Cricket Board, who requested anonymity as he was not authorized to speak to the media, told VOA that the board was aware of the development but said the “restrictions are limited to the Kandahar province,” and that the board is currently in discussion with the provincial authorities.
Cricket is the most popular sport in Afghanistan, particularly among younger people.
Afghans, who had been living in refugee camps in Pakistan, are credited with bringing the game to their impoverished South Asian nation.

Cricket flourished in Afghanistan after the U.S.-led coalition toppled the Taliban in 2001, when the country became an associate member of the International Cricket Council, the world’s cricketing body.
Afghanistan became a full member of the ICC’s elite club of 12 countries in 2017, and it enjoys the status of a test-playing nation.
Since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the national team has mostly trained and played outside the country.
The Afghan team won widespread admiration during the 2023 Cricket World Cup, defeating three former champions: Pakistan, England and Sri Lanka.

The international community has not formally recognized the Taliban government mainly for restricting Afghan women’s access to education, employment, sports, and public life at large. The curbs have prompted some countries to boycott bilateral cricket competitions with Afghanistan.
The Afghan men's team, however, has become increasingly competitive internationally, reaching the semifinals of the 2024 Men's T20 World Cup for the first time.
Afghan players have also become prominent figures on international cricket teams.

items.title: Iran continues crackdown on women: teacher’s retrial denied, Baha’i citizen sentenced
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iran has rejected a request for a retrial by Kokab Bodaghi Pegah, a teacher's union advocate living in Izeh, for a second time, and referred her case for enforcement of her one-year prison sentence, the Coordinating Council of Iranian Teachers’ Trade Associations reported Sunday.
Bodaghi Pegah was convicted of “propaganda against the regime” over her union activism.

According to the council, the Supreme Court upheld the teacher’s one-year prison sentence after the Khuzestan Province Court of Appeals fully affirmed the initial one-year sentence issued by Branch 101 of the Ahvaz Criminal Court in late July of this year.
In September 2025, Bodaghi Pegah was also sentenced to a three-month suspension from service by the Administrative Violations Appeals Board of the Khuzestan Province Department of Education.

Also on Sunday, the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Nazanin Abedini Kafshgari, a Baha’i resident of Qaem Shahr, was sentenced by the Sari Revolutionary Court to three years in prison and an eight-year ban on social rights, such as holding public sector jobs.

According to HRANA, the sentences were issued on November 9 by Branch 1 of the Sari Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Ammar Ramezani. The court charged the Baha’i citizen with "propaganda against the Islamic Republic system" and "propaganda in favor of groups or organizations opposed to the Islamic Republic system."
HRANA stated that the court cited her educational and religious activities—including teaching Baha’i beliefs to children and her social media activity—as the basis for her conviction.
