HRANA further reported that Fariba Asadi, a social activist detained in connection with the 2025–2026 protests, has been sentenced to six years in prison along with supplementary punishments.

According to HRANA, the Islamic Republic charged the female protester with "assembly and collusion, acting against national security, and participating in protests." In addition to the prison term, she was sentenced to a two-year travel ban, a two-year ban on membership in social groups and organizations, and dismissal from government and public service jobs.

Her verdict was issued by Branch 2 of the Karaj Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Sabzevari. Asadi, a resident of Karaj, was arrested by Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence agents on January 26, 2026.

Separately, the Hengaw Organization for Human Rights announced that Golaleh (Nazanin) Elyasi, a resident of Mahabad, was arrested on Saturday, November 14, after being summoned to the city’s Sentence Execution Unit, and was transferred to the women's ward of Urmia Central Prison to begin serving her two-year sentence.

According to Hengaw, Elyasi was sentenced to two years of imprisonment in August 2026 by Branch 1 of the Mahabad Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Ahad Siami, on the alleged charge of "assembly and collusion to commit crimes against national security."

In its reports on religious freedom in Iran, the U.S. Department of State has specifically documented the persecution of Baha’is, Iran's largest non-Muslim religious minority. According to the State Department, they face arrest, imprisonment, and social restrictions for peaceful religious activities, including teaching their beliefs.

The State Department has repeatedly designated Iran as a "Country of Particular Concern" for "particularly severe violations of religious freedom," emphasizing that Baha’is in Iran face systematic discrimination in areas including education and employment. The United States has consistently called for the release of prisoners of conscience and the dropping of charges that violate the universal right to freedom of religion or belief.

items.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
paragraphs: The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

items.title: US Army seeks faster access to emerging defense technology
paragraphs: At the annual Association of the United States Army (AUSA) exposition in Washington on October 12 - 14, 2026, Army leaders called for faster access to new technologies as defense companies showcased systems designed for the modern battlefield. VOA's Julie Taboh reports.

paragraphs: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK.
Find out how to listen to other BBC stations
The latest two minute news summary from BBC World Service.
Video gaming is huge - it's more lucrative than the movies and music combined.

Tuvalu looks like paradise – a cluster of islands, with white sandy beaches lined with palm trees, surrounded by the deep blue of the Pacific Ocean. But the tiny nation, which is roughly midway between Australia and Hawaii, is facing the existential threat of rising sea levels, caused by climate change. The 11,000 or so inhabitants are reckoning with a future where their country may no longer be habitable. With world leaders meeting at the UN COP31 climate talks, we bring together three young women to share their experiences of life in Tuvalu. “I want my children to understand [Tuvaluan] values, to know the language,” Moeli tells us. “To know more about Tuvalu, you have to sit down, respect the elders, no talking when elders are talking, everything like that.” (Photo: Moeli and Kalita, sisters from Tuvalu. They are both wearing a bright blue cotton top, with white floral design and a crown of flowers. leaves and reeds. items.title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
paragraphs: Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16

Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."
Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter, external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."
And Time Out's four-star review, external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

items.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
paragraphs: He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?
Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.
The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.
"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.
Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."
Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".
Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external.
"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external.
"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."
Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."
Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."
So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?
Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)
Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.
"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.
"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.
"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external.
"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".
Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.
"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.
However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.
Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.
"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.
"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."
Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.
"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.
"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.
"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.
"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."
Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.
It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero.
"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."
Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.
The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced.
"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."
Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

items.title: Giant lunar sculpture has visitors over the moon
paragraphs: The Moon sculpture is hanging at the St Helier Methodist Centre
People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.

Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir.
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.

"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."
Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to channel.islands@bbc.co.uk, external.

items.title: Freshers' flu left me deaf in both ears - I'm now helping people like me drive
paragraphs: Darcie, from Dronfield in Derbyshire, said she went to university a year early, at the age of 17, and became deaf in the first few weeks.
"I just had freshers' flu, and it deteriorated my inner ear on both sides," she said.

Darcie added: "I assumed that me not being able to hear was just part of the illness and I didn't know it was a medical emergency, so I didn't get it checked until a week later and I still couldn't hear.
"And that's when they told me, because it's been so long, we can't get it back."
She said the condition was called sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL).
Darcie said it was not easy doing a music degree but she had to "find ways around things".
"So it didn't ruin in my life, it just changed how I had to do things," she added.
However, Darcie said it was challenging finding someone who felt comfortable teaching her.
She said: "I reached out to God knows how many driving instructors, and they all said the same thing of 'I'm not confident I can accommodate that'.
"So when I contacted Dave, I didn't say anything and he was like, 'yeah, no worries. I can fit you in this day'.
"And then at the end I put, 'oh yeah, by the way, I'm deaf', and that was it - we had to work together because he'd never worked with a deaf person before."
She said they soon found ways of working around her hearing loss.
These included for the emergency stop when the instructor usually shouts "stop", he instead puts his hand out in front of him really quickly.
Darcie said during the lessons, they realised they could help share this knowledge.
She said: "If I'm having this problem, I know that there's gonna be other people that are gonna need instructors that are deaf aware, can maybe sign a little bit.
"Me and Dave just looked at each other one day, and were like, 'we should make a course', and he goes, 'yeah, we should'.
"I created the course myself and I sent it to Dave, and he loved it."
Dave Leverton, from Handley Driving School, said he made adaptations for Darcie's lessons, including adding an extra mirror in a position where she could see him.
"[This] meant that we could use some verbal communication," she said.
"Then Darcie taught me things... simple sign language that we could manage on the move so that she knew where she was going and what she was going to do.
"It was a constant process of her teaching me so that I could teach her."

Franki Oliver, audiology manager at the Royal National Institute for Deaf People, said: "If you suddenly lose your hearing - either in one or both of your ears - getting treatment quickly is key. A sudden change in hearing is not always serious, but it could be a medical emergency.
"Sudden hearing loss can affect one or both ears, can happen instantly or over the course of a few weeks, and you might also have tinnitus or balance problems.
"Causes vary, and can include ear wax build-up, infection or physical injury. Recovery depends on the cause and how badly you're affected.
"Getting urgent treatment for sudden hearing loss increases your chance of recovering your hearing."

items.title: Iranian Kurdish opposition groups reject amnesty-for-surrender deal
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Iranian Kurdish opposition leaders based in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region have ruled out turning themselves in to Tehran as part of potential amnesty deal, citing lack of trust in Iran to guarantee their safety.

Their comments come after Iraqi officials reported progress in negotiations involving Baghdad, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and Iran over the future of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have a maintained presence in northern Iraq for decades.

Iraq's Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein confirmed last week that one of the options discussed during the trilateral talks included potential amnesty for the Iranian Kurdish armed group members who wished to return, if they felt safe.

Amanj Zibaee, a member of the central committee of the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), an armed opposition group seeking greater autonomy for Kurds in Iran, and the party’s representative in Erbil, told VOA that his group categorically rejects the prospect of surrendering to Iranian authorities.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran makes many promises but offers nothing in practice. Surrendering to it is something we completely reject, and it is not even an option we have discussed,” he said.
Zibaee said his party would wait for an official announcement over the proposal discussed between Baghdad, Tehran and Erbil before determining its response.
“Once the Iraqi government and the Kurdistan Regional Government officially announce their positions, the KDPI leader will make an appropriate decision,” he said.
He said his organization has acted responsibly and has not used Iraqi territory to attack Iran, a key demand by Baghdad.
“We have never used the Kurdistan Region of Iraq as a base to launch attacks against a neighboring country. We have acted responsibly, and we will continue to do so,” Zibaee said.
Khalil Nadri, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Freedom Party, also dismissed the possibility of accepting an Iranian amnesty.

“We have an agreement with the Kurdistan Region that we will not conduct military operations against Iran from its territory. Our struggle against Iran takes place inside Iran, in Eastern Kurdistan,” Nadri told VOA, referring to predominantly Kurdish areas of western Iran.
He said his party had respected Iraqi sovereignty and helped defend the region against the Islamic State and Iran-backed armed groups, including the Popular Mobilization Forces.
“Iran is not in a position to grant us amnesty,” Nadri said. “Our homeland has been occupied. We will return when our homeland is liberated and the enemy has withdrawn.”

Iran has repeatedly over many years launched missile, and drone strikes targeting Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq that have been fighting for Kurdish regional autonomy or independence in Iran. The attacks surged following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East as Iran launched retaliatory attacks against neighboring countries.
The Iranian Kurdish armed opposition Komala party said Monday that two missiles struck the entrance to one of its bases in the Balisan Valley in Iraq's Kurdistan Region.
Idris Kolahdozi, a member of the party's Central Committee and its head of relations in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA that the attack caused no casualties or property damage.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of who carried out the attack.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Hussein said the latest round of negotiations between Iraq, Iran and the Kurdistan Regional Government that started in October in Baghdad are continuing and that several options were under consideration.
In an interview with France 24, Hussein said the parties had reached a degree of understanding about how to address the opposition groups’ presence in Iraq.
He raised a possible amnesty deal that could allow Iranian Kurdish opposition members to return to Iran, provided they received credible guarantees for their personal safety.

Earlier this month, Iraqi government spokesperson Haider Aboudi told VOA that discussions had reached an “advanced stage” and that Baghdad hoped to resolve the issue soon, though no final deal has been publicly disclosed.
Aboudi emphasized that Iraq was determined to prevent its territory from being used to attack neighboring countries.
KRG spokesperson Peshawa Hawramani similarly told VOA that the regional government would not allow its territory to be used to harm neighboring states.

The negotiations come amid continued Iranian pressure on Baghdad and Erbil to remove Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from Iraqi territory. Tehran has repeatedly accused the groups of threatening its security, allegations the opposition parties deny.
Last month, KDPI spokesperson Khalid Azizi told VOA that his party had largely complied with Iraqi requests to withdraw from areas near the Iranian border.
He said the party had engaged in discussions with Iraqi and Kurdish authorities, with United Nations involvement, over the region's security for several years.

items.title: US, nine partners sign SI supply chain accord ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The United States and nine partner countries have signed a declaration to protect super intelligence, commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI, supply chains, the State Department announced Sunday.
News of the signing comes days before President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to discuss SI at a summit in Shenzhen.
The San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity establishes a shared security framework for supply chains supporting AI.

Joining the United States are the U.K., Japan, South Korea, Australia, India, Singapore, Israel, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. All participate in Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative to strengthen technology supply chains.
The declaration underscores Washington’s efforts to secure SI supply chains with partners while pursuing discussions with Beijing on managing the risks from increasingly powerful systems.

The State Department released the wording of the declaration that calls for coordinated action against "economic coercion, supply chain disruptions, and non-market policies and practices and their market-distorting effects..."
The declaration also seeks to protect "private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth..."
Its framework focuses on two areas: sensitive technology and critical infrastructure.

Sensitive technology includes the "goods, software, materials, knowledge, components, and inputs used to produce them." The signatories say they will work together to stop the theft, or smuggling of AI technologies that could pose significant national security risks.
Critical infrastructure includes ports, transportation, communications, energy and computer networks that SI supply chains rely on. Attacks on these systems or data leaks could cause serious harm.

Pax Silica was formally launched last December, when Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg and representatives from Japan, Australia, Singapore, South Korea and Israel signed its founding declaration in December 2025.

At the time, the State Department said the initiative aimed to reduce “coercive dependencies,” meaning reliance on suppliers that could use that leverage to pressure other countries, and that it wasn't meant to isolate any one country.

Asked Monday whether the agreement could affect the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said SI should benefit all humanity. She said China opposed dividing countries along ideological lines or forming closed, exclusive groupings in the sector.
Mao said Beijing and Washington remained in communication about the leaders’ meeting.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, their third meeting this year.
Trump said last week that he would not raise the alleged spy allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, although he expected Xi to bring up the matter.
Despite their technological rivalry, Washington and Beijing have been exploring cooperation on AI safety.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that the two sides would use the APEC talks to work out ways to warn each other about SI safety problems and to share ways of testing advanced AI systems, according to Reuters.
Three people briefed on preparations told Reuters that other planned talks would focus on ways to manage potential misuse of the technology.

The news outlet reported that Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed an emergency mechanism for notifying each other of serious AI incidents in September, but that has yet to become operational.

The mechanism is intended to prevent SI incidents or misunderstandings from escalating into national security crises. Communications so far have relied largely on direct contact between senior officials, the sources told Reuters.

items.title: OIC voices support for Afghan women amid doubts over change in Taliban’s policies
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

In his recent address to the international conference on women empowerment, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian, Cultural and Social Affairs Tarig Ali Bakheet restated the organization’s “solidarity with ... women in Afghanistan in their pursuit of their right to education and employment.”
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have imposed strict restrictions on women in Afghanistan, where they are barred from education beyond primary school, employment and public spaces
The United Nations reported that the group has issued more than 100 decrees and edicts curbing women’s basic rights in the country.

Despite pressures from the international community, including OIC and Muslim-majority countries, on the Taliban to change their policies toward women in Afghanistan, the group has not reversed any of its restrictions.
Afghan political expert, Obaidullah Burhani told VOA that OIC’s stance is ‘commendable,” however, it lacks concrete measures and action.
“Their efforts are limited to issuing declarations, and I see no prospect for change,” Burhani said, adding that OIC’s leverage is limited “because the organization lacks executive authority.”
He said that OIC member countries lack shared will.

“There are political and security-related calculations and disagreements [among member states]. However, regardless of what they may be, I do not believe they will have any significant impact on the situation [of women’s rights] in Afghanistan, which has remained unchanged thus far.”

In July, the OIC ministerial conference in Islamabad, Pakistan, issued a declaration expressing disappointment and regret at the Taliban’s restrictions on women, calling it inconsistent with Islamic values.

The Taliban’s ban on women’s education and employment “tarnishes the essence and image of Islam and stresses the importance of commitment to guaranteeing equal participation of all women and girls, without distinction, in public life within the Afghan society as per Islamic values and principles,” said the OIC declaration.
The Taliban’s spokesperson Zabiullah Mujahid told TOLOnews in July that women’s rights in Afghanistan are “ensured all the rights” of women “required under Sharia [Law].”

Fazl Hadi Wazin, an Islamic scholar and president of Movement for Understanding and Reform of Afghanistan, however, told VOA that the Taliban’s leadership position that girls should not pursue education beyond sixth grade “contradicts Islamic teaching.”

“Unfortunately, some members of the Taliban’s leadership, based on their flawed interpretation [of Islam], argue that girls should not continue their education beyond the sixth grade. This position is not consistent with Islamic teaching,” he said.
Wazin said that he sees little hope for the reopening of girls’ schools as long as Taliban leaders who oppose girls’ education continue to hold power within the group.
“I don’t believe they will allow girls to attend schools or universities,” he said.

items.title: From Batman to Bond - how Robert Pattinson landed the role of 007
paragraphs: Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman

Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.
He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.
His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.
Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.
Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noir
Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.
His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.
"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.
"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.
"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."
He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.
Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.
Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.
He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.
"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.
"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."
Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'
"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."
The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.
By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external.
"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.
Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.
Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.
Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018
With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.
But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.
Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external.
"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.
"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."
Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
paragraphs: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.
This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

items.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
paragraphs: With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”
“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

items.title: Donating kidney to daughter a 'no-brainer', says dad
paragraphs: Walker said Noa-Rae was a healthy child until he noticed her face becoming swollen at the age of two.
"It all started when she was quite young," he said.
"She would wake up with a swollen face that would last for hours.
"We took her to the doctors and they originally thought she had a skin or eye problem, but we did a blood test and the results came back saying she had nephrotic syndrome."
NHS England says nephrotic syndrome causes the kidneys to leak large amounts of protein into the urine, which reduces the amount of protein in your blood.
The condition can lead to the "swelling of body tissues, a greater chance of catching infections and blood clots", the NHS said.
It can be detected through a urine or blood test.
"At the time, me and my wife had no idea what nephrotic syndrome was because it's such a rare condition," said Walker.
"It's quite hard because you go from living a normal life to having multiple days and weeks in and around hospital."
Walker said his daughter's kidneys were removed when she was three due to the severity of the condition.
Noa-Rae then began dialysis, causing her to miss school and other day-to-day activities as she spent much of her time in hospital.
"She's been an absolute trooper, all she really knows is hospital appointments," said Walker.
After having her kidneys removed, Walker said the next step "was always going to be a transplant".
"Doctors mentioned that the parents would have quite a high chance of being a match," he said.
"I think any parent in their right mind would think straight forward to helping out their kids.
"To sacrifice one part of yourself to better your own kid's life should be a no-brainer really."
NHS Blood and Transplant says kidneys may be rejected by the body when its immune system recognises the kidney has come from a different person and thinks it is not supposed to be there.
But, doctors said they hoped Walker's kidney would keep working until Noa-Rae is "at least the age of 16".
He said organ transplant and donation was "super important" and was urging other people to consider being a donor.
"It'll make a massive difference to whoever it needs to go to," said Walker.
"It could last one day, it could last years, but as long as she keeps getting them, she could live as much of a normal life as possible."
NHS Blood and Transplant said 539 people in the East Midlands were on the kidney transplant waiting list at the end of October.
Between April 2025 and March 2026, 196 kidney transplants were carried out in the region, including 141 from deceased donors and 55 from living donors.
A total of 158 people donated a kidney in the past year with 108 deceased donors and 50 living donors.
Walker said his family were now looking forward to life beyond hospital appointments and treatment.
"There should hopefully be a bit less hospital time," he said.
"She will still have check-ups once a week, which will slow down to once a month and progressively even less.
"She'll be at school full-time, which she really enjoys, so that'll be a good thing."

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
paragraphs: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council
